en: Śrī Śuka said:
Having performed the slaughter of the Daityas, Kṛṣṇa, accompanied by Balarāma and surrounded by the Yadus,
brought down the burden of the earth while bringing forth the Kali age with its swiftest onset.
Having made those sons of Pāṇḍu— who had been greatly provoked by their rivals through foul gambling,
insults, the seizing of their hair, and other such acts—
the pretext for bringing them together with one another, [the Lord acted].
Having slain the kings and removed the burden of the earth,
the Lord, the immeasurable one, reflected while the armies of those kings who were the earth’s burden were being driven away by the Yadus, who were protected by His own arms.
I consider that even though the burden has been removed from the earth, it has indeed not departed;
for alas, the Yādava clan remains unbearable.
No other source could possibly cause its humiliation in any way.
Having eternally brought about internal strife within the Yadu clan— which has always relied upon me and been swollen with prosperity— I shall enter my own abode, like fire entering a bamboo thicket.
O King, having thus resolved, the omnipresent Lord, whose will is truth,
withdrew His own lineage under the pretext of the brahmins' curse; He who,
by His own form— the source from which all worldly beauty emanates— was the delight of the eyes of men.
"By means of these songs, may they steal away the hearts of those who remember me; by my footprints, may they seize the activities of those who behold them.
Having spread abroad my glorious fame, I shall easily cross over the darkness of this world. Thinking thus, the Lord returned to his own abode.
The King said: How did the curse of the brāhmaṇas come to pass upon the Vṛṣṇis— who were devoted to the brāhmaṇas, charitable, ever-servant to their elders, and whose minds were fixed on Kṛṣṇa?
O best of the twice-born, tell me everything regarding that curse— what its cause was and what its nature was— and how there can be division among those who are of one essence. Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Bearing a form of perfectly beautiful proportions, performing auspicious deeds upon the earth with all desires fulfilled,
and delighting in his own abode, he of noble fame—
Having performed his remaining duties—
deeds that were a mass of merit, most auspicious, and which,
when sung, remove the impurities of the Kali age from the world— he desired to withdraw the universe.
While He, whose nature is Time, was dwelling in the house of the Yadu deity,
the sages Viśvāmitra, Asita, and Kaṇva were sent forth and arrived at Piṇḍāraka.
Durvāsas, Bhṛgu, Aṅgiras, Kaśyapa, Vāmadeva, Atri,
Vasiṣṭha, Nārada, and others.
While playing, the princes, the delights of the Yadu clan, approached them;
having greeted them, though they were undisciplined, they questioned them as if they were well-disciplined.
They then dressed Sāmba, the son of Jāmbavatī, in female attire.

"O brāhmaṇas, this dark-eyed woman, who is pregnant, asks you; yet, being bashful to ask in person, she asks through me. O you of unfailing vision, please tell her directly: what will she, desiring a son and about to give birth, actually bring forth?"
O King, thus mocked, the sages became enraged and said to them:
"O fools, he shall produce for you a pestle that will destroy your lineage.
Hearing this, they were utterly terrified and suddenly released their brother from their bellies.
They saw a pestle made of iron belonging to Sāmba there.
Thinking, "What have we, of such meager fortune, done? What will people say of us?
they became distraught and went home, taking the pestle with them.
Having brought that [club] into the assembly, they reported it to the King, whose facial luster had faded, in the presence of all the Yādavas. O King,
having heard the infallible curse of the brāhmaṇa and having seen the club, [the King was struck with fear].
The inhabitants of Dvārakā were struck with wonder and seized by fear.
Having pulverized that club, King Āhuka, the lord of the Yadus,
cast it into the waters of the ocean, along with whatever iron remained of it.
A certain fish swallowed the iron filings that had been carried by the waves; these, it is said, became eraka-grass when they were washed up and stuck on the shore.
That fish was then caught in the ocean by fishermen along with other fish using a net.
The hunter placed the iron arrowhead into its belly;
though the Blessed Lord is the Sovereign who knows all things and could have made it otherwise, He did not wish to do so, but as the embodiment of Time, He acquiesced to the brahmin’s curse.
Śrī Śuka said:
O best of the Kurus, in Dvārakā, which was protected by the arms of Govinda,
Nārada dwelt constantly, longing for the worship of Kṛṣṇa.

O King, who indeed that possesses sense-control would not worship the lotus feet of Mukunda, which are the refuge for those subject to death from all sides and are worshipped by the best of the immortals?
On one occasion, Vasudeva [honored] that celestial sage who had come to his home.
Having offered worship to him as he sat comfortably, and having greeted him, he spoke thus.
Śrī Vasudeva said:
"O Blessed One, your journey is for the well-being of all embodied beings."
Just as the conduct of parents is for the sake of their wretched children,
and the behavior of gods toward living beings results in both suffering and happiness,
so too the conduct of the virtuous— such as yourself, whose soul is fixed on Acyuta— is for the sake of happiness alone.

As the gods reciprocate with those who worship them in that very same way, so too do the saintly ones— who are compassionate toward the distressed— act as companions in the performance of one's duties like a shadow;
nevertheless, O Brahmin, we inquire from you about the bhāgavata-dharmas.
Having heard these with faith, a mortal is liberated from all fear. Indeed,
in the past, for the sake of progeny, I worshipped the Infinite One on earth— who bestows liberation— yet I did not worship Him for the sake of liberation, being deluded by the divine illusion.
"O observer of noble vows, please instruct us so that we may truly and directly be liberated from these various calamities and from fear on all sides.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having been thus questioned by the wise Vasudeva,
the celestial sage, delighted and reminded of the qualities of Hari, spoke to him. Śrī Nārada said:
O bull among the Sātvatas, you have rightly resolved this matter,
in that you inquire about the bhāgavata-dharmas which bring welfare to the entire universe; for these,
when heard, recited, meditated upon, honored, or approved, [yield great fruit].

Indeed, the true dharma instantly purifies even those who are enemies of the gods and the universe; for today, O most auspicious one, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa— the hearing and chanting of whose names is meritorious— has been brought to my mind by you.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history:
the conversation between the sons of Ṛṣabha and the high-souled King of Videha.
There was a son of Svāyambhuva Manu named Priyavrata.
From him [Kṛṣṇa] was born Agnīdhra, from whom Nābhi was born; Ṛṣabha is remembered as his son.
They say that he [Ṛṣabha] was an expansion of Vāsudeva who descended with the desire to proclaim the dharma of liberation.
He had one hundred sons who had mastered the Vedas.
Among them, Bharata was the eldest and was solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa;
it is after his name that this wonderful land became renowned as Bhārata-varṣa.
Having renounced this world once he had enjoyed its pleasures, he departed to seek Hari through austerity.

By worshipping him, he indeed attained his state through three human births. Of them, there were eighty-one twice-born ones who were the lords of the nine islands on all sides and the originators of the systems of ritual action (*karma-tantra*).
There were nine highly fortunate sages who expounded the true meaning:
Śramaṇa, Vātarasana, and those proficient in the science of the Self;
as well as Kavi, Havis, Antarīkṣa, Prabuddha, and Pippalāyana.
Then Āvirhotra, Drumila, Camasa, and Karabhājana—
these, perceiving the universe, which consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest, as the form of the Blessed Lord and non-different from their own selves, wandered the earth.
Those liberated ones, whose desired movements are unimpeded, wander through the worlds of the gods, Siddhas, Sādhyas,
Gandharvas, Yakṣas, humans, Kinnaras, and Nāgas, as well as those of the sages, Cāraṇas, and lords of the spirits.
At one time, those [demigods] who preside over the worlds of the Vidyādharas, the twice-born, and the cows, arrived by chance at the sacrifice of the high-souled Nimi,
which was being performed by sages on the island of Ajanābha.

O King, seeing those great devotees who resembled the sun, the sacrificer, the sacrificial fires, and all the brahmins stood before them. Videha, perceiving that they were solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa, [honored them].
Delighted, the king honored those nine, who were seated upon their thrones according to their rank,
who were radiant with their own luster, and who resembled the sons of Brahmā;
being supremely pleased, he bowed down with humility and questioned them, O King.
Śrī Videha said:
I consider you to be the direct associates of the Lord, the enemy of Madhu;
for as manifestations of Viṣṇu, you move about for the purification of the worlds.
The human body, which is subject to momentary destruction, is difficult for embodied beings to obtain;
even so, I consider the sight of the beloved of Vaikuṇṭha to be rare among them.
Therefore, O sinless ones, we ask you about that ultimate security.
In this cycle of worldly existence, even half a moment of association with the virtuous is a treasure for men.
If it is possible for us to hear them, please speak of those *bhāgavata* duties by which the Unborn Lord,
being pleased, will grant even His own self to one who has surrendered.
Śrī Nārada said:
O Vasudeva, having been thus questioned by Nimi, those most exalted ones,
after honoring the king along with his assembly and officiating priests, spoke with affection.
The venerable poet said:

I consider that for one whose mind is agitated by the sense of a non-real self, constant service to the lotus feet of Acyuta here provides freedom from fear from all quarters; for it is there that fear ceases through the Universal Self.
Know those means for the attainment of the Self which were indeed proclaimed by the Blessed Lord to be the direct path for men who lack knowledge; for they are the *bhāgavata* methods,
O King, by resorting to which a person shall never fall into negligence.
Whether running with eyes closed, one should not stumble or fall here;
whatever one does with body, speech, mind, senses, intellect, or soul, following one's own nature,
one should offer all that to the Supreme Nārāyaṇa.
Fear arises from attachment to a second [entity]; for one who has strayed from the Lord, there occurs the opposite state, which is forgetfulness.

Therefore, the wise man, regarding his guru as God and himself as the Self, should take refuge in that One Lord with exclusive devotion, for even though duality does not exist, it appears to the meditator through the power of His *māyā*, just like dreams and mental fantasies.

The wise man should restrain that mind which conceives of and discriminates between actions; from that, fearlessness shall arise. Listening to the auspicious accounts of the births and deeds of the Discus-wielder as they exist in the world, and singing the names that signify those deeds, he should wander about free from shame and unattached.
One who maintains such a vow, having developed intense attachment through the chanting of the Lord’s beloved names, becomes one whose heart is swiftly moved;
he laughs loudly, weeps, cries out, sings, and dances like a madman, indifferent to worldly conventions.
He regards the ether, air, fire, water, earth, the luminaries, living beings, the directions, trees, and so forth [as equal].
One should bow down with undivided devotion to the rivers and oceans, to the body of Hari, and to whatever being exists.
Devotion to the Supreme Lord, the experience of Him, and detachment from everything else— this triad occurs simultaneously,
just as for one who is eating, there arise satisfaction, nourishment, and the cessation of hunger at every morsel.

"O King, for one who worships the feet of Acyuta with such constant devotion, there arise devotion, detachment, and realization of the Lord; from that, he directly attains supreme peace. Śrī Rājā said:

"Now, tell me of the devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata): what is his duty, what is his nature among men, how he conducts himself, what he speaks, and by what characteristics he is dear to the Blessed One.
Śrī Havir said:

He who perceives the nature of the Blessed Lord within all beings, and perceives all beings within the Blessed Lord as his own self— he is the most excellent devotee. [This applies] toward the Lord, those dependent on Him, the ignorant, and even His enemies.
He who practices love, friendship, compassion, and equanimity is a middling devotee.
He who strives with faith to worship Hari only through the ritual image,
but not toward His other devotees, is considered a materialistic devotee.
He who, even while perceiving objects through the senses, neither feels aversion nor rejoices,
but views this world as the *māyā* of Viṣṇu— he indeed is the best of devotees (*bhāgavata*).
He who [remains unaffected] by the birth, dissolution, hunger, fear, thirst, and sufferings of the body, senses, vital breath, mind, and intellect...
One who is not deluded by the attributes of worldly existence, who is preeminent among the devotees of Hari through constant mindfulness,
and in whose mind the seeds of desire and action no longer take root— he who has Vāsudeva as his sole abode is indeed the best of the bhāgavatas.
He for whom the sense of "I" does not cling to this body because of its birth or actions, nor because of caste, stage of life, or species— he is indeed dear to Hari.
He for whom there is no distinction between "self" and "other," nor between possessions or the self itself— [he is dear to Hari].

He who is equal toward all beings and tranquil is indeed the best of devotees (bhāgavatottama). Even for the sake of the prosperity of the three worlds, his mindfulness remains unimpaired; he is sought after by the gods and others who have not yet conquered their own selves.

He who does not waver from the lotus feet of the Blessed One even for half a moment or a mere flicker of an eye is indeed the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas; he whose heat of suffering has been dispelled by the moonlight of the jewel-like nails on the toes of the Blessed One’s feet of great prowess.
How can that Lord again prevail over those who have taken refuge in His heart, just as the heat of the sun cannot prevail when the moon has risen?
He from whose heart Hari— the destroyer of the multitude of sins— does not depart even when addressed involuntarily,
and who holds the lotus feet [of the Lord] with the cord of devotion, is declared to be the foremost among the devotees (bhāgavatas).
The King said:
"O venerable ones, we wish to understand the illusory power (māyā) of Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, which deludes even the masters of illusion; please speak to us."
"I am not satiated while enjoying your words, which are the nectar of Hari’s stories—
the medicine for the fever of worldly existence for a mortal scorched by that very suffering.
Śrī Antarīkṣa said:

O mighty-armed one, by means of these great elements, the primordial Self of all beings created various high and low creatures for the sake of establishing their own nature through their respective essences. Thus, having created the beings, He entered them with His five constituent elements.
Dividing himself into one or ten forms, he enjoys the modes of nature; that Lord, experiencing the modes through the modes manifested by his own self,
considers himself the creator of this world and thus becomes attached to it.
Performing actions with their motives through further actions, the embodied soul,
receiving the various fruits of those deeds, wanders here in this world from happiness to its opposite.
Thus, as a person follows the paths of karma, which carry many misfortunes, he continues on.

Until the dissolution of all beings, he experiences creation and destruction helplessly; when the dissolution of the elements is imminent, Time— without beginning or end— draws away the manifest world, which consists of substances and qualities, back into the unmanifest.
Indeed, a terrible drought lasting for a hundred years will occur upon the earth;
then, the sun, heated by the accumulated heat of that time, will scorch the three worlds,
starting from the depths of the netherworld (pātāla) with the fire from the mouth of Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Burning with upward-pointing flames and fanned by the wind from all sides, it increases;
for a hundred years, the Saṃvartaka cloud-mass poured down rain,
and the Virāṭ dissolved into the water in streams as thick as an elephant's trunk.
Then, O King, having abandoned Virāj,
the Person born of Virāj (Vairāja) enters the subtle Unmanifest, like a fire without fuel.
The earth, its fragrance carried away by the wind, becomes fit for the state of water.
Water, having its essence withdrawn, is prepared for the state of light;
but light, its form withdrawn by darkness, dissolves into the wind. The wind, its touch withdrawn by space, dissolves into the ether.

O King, by the nature of time, the ether, its qualities having been withdrawn, merges into the self; likewise, the senses, the mind, and the intellect, along with the products of the *sāttvika* mode (*vaikārika*),
enter into the ego, which, together with its own qualities, merges into the *ahaṃkāra*.
This illusory energy (māyā) of the Blessed One, which effects creation, maintenance, and dissolution, has been described by us as having three modes (tri-varṇā). What more do you wish to hear?
Śrī-rāja said:
"O great sage, please tell this: how may those of dull intellect easily cross over this divine illusion (māyā), which is so difficult for those of unrefined self to surmount?
Śrī Prabuddha said:
One should observe the reversal of results for men who, moving in pairs, undertake actions for the sake of happiness and the destruction of suffering;
for with wealth that is constantly distressing and as fleeting as one's own death, it is difficult to find true fulfillment.
What joy is there in a home, children, relatives, and cattle— things acquired through effort yet ever-fickle?
Thus one should know this world to be perishable, constructed by karma,
subject to equality, superiority, and destruction, just like the realms of those who rule over mandalas.

Therefore, one who desires the highest good should take refuge in a guru who is thoroughly proficient in the Vedic scriptures and in the Supreme Brahman, and who is the very embodiment of tranquility. There, regarding the guru as both oneself and the deity, one should learn the duties of a devotee of the Lord (bhāgavata-dharma).
Hari, the Self who bestows the self, is pleased by those who follow Him with sincerity; first, by non-attachment to everything else and attachment to the virtuous,
and truly, as is appropriate, by compassion, friendliness, and humility toward all living beings.
Purity, austerity, forbearance, silence, self-study, straightforwardness,
celibacy, non-violence, equanimity toward the pairs of opposites,
constant contemplation of the Self as the Lord in all things, solitude, and homelessness.

Wearing secluded garments of bark, contentment with whatever may come, faith in the scripture concerning the Lord, and likewise freedom from censure toward others; as well as the restraints of mind, speech, and action, truthfulness, and both internal and external tranquility.

Hearing and chanting about Hari, whose deeds are wonderful, as well as reflecting upon His births, activities, and qualities, and performing every action for His sake— whatever sacrifice one has made, whatever gift given, austerity performed, mantra chanted, or whatever virtuous deed one has done that is dear to oneself— [all this is offered unto Him].
The offering of one’s wife, children, home, and even life to the Supreme;
likewise, friendship toward those men who have Kṛṣṇa as their soul and Lord;
and service rendered to both—the great and the saintly among men.
The mutual narration of the purifying glory of the Lord brings about mutual delight,
mutual satisfaction, and mutual cessation from worldly activity for the self; thus,
by remembering and causing one another to remember Hari, who removes the multitude of sins, they attain liberation.
With devotion born of devotion, they bear their bodies with hair standing on end;
at times they weep from thinking of Acyuta, and at times they laugh, rejoice, and speak like those beyond the mundane world.
They dance, sing, and practice [meditation] upon the Unborn;
having attained the Supreme, they become silent and perfectly tranquil.
Thus, one should learn the duties of the devotees of the Lord with devotion arising from that [realization].
"One who is devoted to Nārāyaṇa easily crosses over the insurmountable *māyā*.
Śrī Rājā said:
"Of the Supreme Self, the Brahman designated as Nārāyaṇa..."
"You ought to tell us the ultimate conclusion, for you are the best among those who know Brahman.
Śrī Pippalāyana said:
"He is the cause of the maintenance, origin, and dissolution of this world, yet he is himself without cause."
O King, know that to be the Supreme, by which the body, senses, life-force, and heart are enlivened and by which they move within and without during dreaming, waking, and deep sleep.
Neither the mind, nor speech, nor the eye, nor the self, nor the vital breaths and senses can enter into this [Supreme], just as flames cannot enter their own source, fire;
even sound, by its very nature of negating that which perceives it, has the Self as its ultimate root.
He states what was implied by the word "artha": that without which the establishment of prohibitions is not possible.
In the beginning, the one [Brahman] became threefold as goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas);
they call this the thread (sūtra), the Great One (mahat), the ego (ahaṃkāra), and the individual soul (jīva).
By virtue of its two great powers in the form of knowledge, action, their objects, and their fruits,
Brahman alone shines forth as both the existent and the non-existent, that which is beyond them both.
This Self was never born, shall not die, and does not increase.
For one who knows the ritual of extraction, [the merit] is never exhausted, even for those who deviate; indeed, it is everywhere, eternal, and unfailing— a mere perception,
just as the vital breath (prāṇa) is differentiated by the power of the senses.

In eggs, in embryos, and in trees where [the self] is not yet determined, the vital breath indeed pursues the individual soul (jīva) here and there; when the aggregate of the senses has subsided and the ego is dormant, the Knower of the Field (kūṭastha) remains apart from the latent impressions—may we have remembrance of That.
When, through intense devotion to the lotus-footed Lord, one yearns for His feet...
One should cleanse the impurities of the mind born of the modes and their activities; when that mind is purified, the reality of the Self is perceived directly,
just as the light of the sun is seen by those with clear vision.
The King said: Please describe to us the yoga of action (karma-yoga), by which a person,
being purified, quickly shakes off all actions here and attains the supreme state of freedom from action (naiṣkarmya).
"Previously, I asked this same question to the sages in the presence of my father;
the sons of Brahmā did not answer. Let the reason for that be told.
Śrī Āvirhotra said:
"Action, inaction, and misaction"—this is the Vedic teaching, not a worldly one;
for the Veda has the Lord as its soul, and even the wise are bewildered therein.
This Veda speaks in indirect language; it is an instruction for the immature.
For the sake of liberation from karma, the Lord indeed ordains ritual actions, just as one prescribes medicine for healing.
But he who, being ignorant and having his senses unsubdued, does not personally perform what is declared in the Vedas,
falls from death to death through such improper action and unrighteousness.

One who performs only that which is enjoined by the Vedas, free from attachment and offering it to the Lord, attains the perfection of actionlessness (*naiṣkarmya-siddhi*); the scriptural mention of rewards is for the purpose of inspiring interest. This applies to one who desires to quickly sever the knot of the heart regarding the Supreme Self.
One should worship Lord Keśava according to the injunctions prescribed in the Tantras. Having received grace from the teacher and having been shown the traditional scripture by him,
one should worship the Great Person (Mahāpuruṣa) through whichever form is most dear to oneself.

Pure, seated facing the deity, and having purified the *piṇḍa* through breath-control (*prāṇāyāma*) and other means, one who has performed the ritual protection (*sannyāsa*) should worship Hari with whatever offerings are available, both in the image and within the heart.
Having prepared the ritual materials, the ground, and his own body as the lingas, and having sprinkled the seat with water,
he should then arrange the water for the feet and other offerings; then, being composed,
having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the heart and other limbs with the *hṛdaya* and other mantras, he should worship with the root mantra.
One should worship each respective form, along with its limbs, sub-limbs, and attendants, using its own specific mantra,

offering water for the feet (*pādya*), respectful oblation (*arghya*), water for sipping (*ācamanīya*), and so forth, as well as bathing materials, garments, ornaments, perfumes, garlands, unbroken grains (*akṣata*), flower wreaths, incense, lamps, and food offerings.
Having worshipped the Lord along with His attendants according to the rules and having praised Him with hymns,

one should bow down to Hari while meditating on oneself as being composed of Him; then, having placed the remnants upon one's head and having respectfully bid farewell to the image of Hari, one should dissolve it into one's own abode.
Thus, he who worships the Lord— the Self— in fire, the sun, water, and so forth, as well as in the guest and in his own heart, is indeed quickly liberated. Śrī Rājā said:
"Whatever deeds Hari performed, performs, or will perform here through his various voluntary incarnations— let those be told to us.
Śrī Drumila said:
Or rather, one who would attempt to enumerate the infinite qualities of the Infinite One is of childish intellect;
he might somehow count the particles of dust of the earth over time, but never those of the Abode of all powers.
When [the Lord], having created the five elements from Himself...
Having fashioned the Virāj city,
the primordial deity Nārāyaṇa entered it by means of a portion of himself and assumed the designation "Puruṣa."
That whose body is this arrangement of the three worlds; by whose senses the two types of senses of embodied beings [exist];
whose knowledge is self-born, from whose breath comes strength, vigor, and effort.
In the beginning, through the mode of goodness (sattva), he was the creator of maintenance, dissolution, and creation; through passion (rajas), he became Śata-dhṛti for its creation;
and as Viṣṇu, he became the Lord of Sacrifice and the bridge of dharma for the twice-born during its maintenance.
"Rudra also, that primordial Person, [goes] to dissolution through darkness"— thus do creation, maintenance, and dissolution perpetually occur among living beings.
Then, through his form, he was born from Mūrti, the daughter of Dakṣa, for the sake of Dharma.
Nārāyaṇa, the most excellent of sages, the tranquil Nara,
spoke of and practiced the path characterized by actionlessness (naiṣkarmya),
he whose feet even today are served by the best of sages.
Indra, suspecting that [Nara and Nārāyaṇa] desired to seize his own abode,
dispatched Kāma along with his attendants to the place known as Badarī,
accompanied by hosts of apsarases, the spring season, and gentle breezes.
The primordial deity, who knows the greatness of his own power, pierced them with arrows in the form of glances at the women; having recognized the transgression committed by Śakra,
he laughed and spoke to those trembling ones, his own astonishment having vanished.
"Do not fear, O Lord! O Madana, Māruta, and you divine consorts,
accept our offering and ensure that this place is never empty!"—
thus spoke the gods to the God who grants fearlessness, O King.
With their heads bowed in shame, they spoke to him with compassion:
"O All-pervading Lord, this is not surprising in You, the Supreme and Unchanging,
whose lotus feet are bowed to by multitudes of wise sages who find delight in their own selves."
For those who serve you, many obstacles created by the gods arise as they cross beyond their own abodes to reach your supreme station—
not so for others who offer their own portions as oblations upon the sacrificial grass.
If You, our protector, place Your foot upon the head of obstacles,
then some of us shall cross over the shoreless ocean of hunger, thirst, the three times, the qualities of nature, wind, the tongue, and the genitals.
"They fall under the sway of fruitless anger; they sink into the mire of the cow's hoofprint and waste their efforts by performing difficult austerities in vain"—
as they were thus speaking, women of most wonderful appearance appeared before them.
The omnipresent Lord revealed Himself to those women who were performing service and honoring Him with their own worship.
Seeing those women— who were like the goddess Śrī incarnate— the followers of the gods were enchanted by their fragrance, their own splendor eclipsed by the nobility of her beauty.
The Lord of the gods of gods, as if smiling, said to those who were prostrate before him:
"Choose one of these women, who are of your own caste and the ornaments of heaven. Having received his command with the word "Om," those praised by the gods bowed down to him.
Placing Urvaśī, the foremost of the Apsarases, at their head, they went to heaven.
Having bowed before Indra in the assembly while the inhabitants of the triple heavens listened, they described the power of Nārāyaṇa; Śakra was struck with wonder and became afraid.
The Lord Acyuta, in the form of a swan, spoke of self-yoga; the blessed Kumāra, our father Ṛṣabha, was given [this teaching];
and Viṣṇu has descended with a portion of Himself for the welfare of the worlds.
By Him, the slayer of Madhu, the Vedas were recovered from the mouth of Hayagrīva;
at the end of the age, Manu and the medicinal herbs were protected by Him in the form of a Fish;
and as a Boar, lifting the earth from the waters, He slew the son of Diti.
In the *Kūrma* incarnation, he bore the mountain upon his own back during the churning for the nectar;
in the *Varāha* incarnation, he released the distressed king of elephants who had sought refuge from the crocodile;
and in the *Nṛsiṃha* incarnation, he protected the *śramaṇas* and sages who were praising him as they fell before him.
And Śakra, having slain Vṛtra, had entered into darkness;
the celestial women, helpless, were confined in the house of the asuras;
therefore, in the form of the Man-Lion, he slew the lord of the asuras for the sake of the fearlessness of the virtuous.
In the war between the gods and the asuras, having slain the lords of the Daityas for the sake of the gods, He established the worlds with His portions during the intervening periods;
then, having become Vāmana, He took away this earth from Bali.
Under the pretext of begging, he gave [the earth] to the sons of Aditi;
and Rāma,
who was like the fire of Bhṛgu’s lineage that consumed the Haihaya clan, cleared the earth of kṣatriyas twenty-one times.
He bound the ocean, slew the ten-faced Rāvaṇa along with Laṅkā;
victorious is the Lord of Sītā, whose fame destroys the impurities of the world.
To relieve the burden of the earth, the Unborn One was born among the Yadus.
Once born, he will perform deeds difficult even for the gods;
through his arguments, he will delude those who perform sacrifices yet are unworthy of them,
and at the end of the Kali age, he will destroy the Śūdra kings who rule the earth.
"O mighty-armed one, such births and deeds of the Lord of the universe, whose fame is vast, have been described in great number. Śrī Rājā said:
"Those who consider themselves the best knowers of the self generally do not worship the Blessed Lord Hari.
What is the ultimate goal for those whose desires are unappeased and who have not conquered their own minds?
Śrī Camasa said:
From the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet of the Supreme Person, along with the stages of life (āśramas),
the four social orders (varṇas)— the Brahmins and the others— were separately born according to their respective qualities.
Among these, he who [knows] the Lord as the manifest Person, the source of his own self...
Falling from their station, they do not worship [the Lord] but despise Him, and thus they fall downward.
Some keep the stories of Hari far away, and others keep the chanting of Acyuta’s names far away;
such as women, Śūdras, and the like, are indeed objects of compassion for those like you.
Even a brāhmaṇa, a kṣatriya, or a vaiśya who has reached the presence of Hari,
as well as those who recite the Vedas, may still be bewildered by their Vedic birth;
they are unskilled in action, stubborn, foolish, yet imagining themselves to be learned scholars.

Deluded by passion, making terrible resolves, lustful, and as venomous as snakes, these hypocritical, arrogant, and sinful men utter flattering words with honeyed speech, eager for their own ends, and they mock the beloved devotees of Acyuta.
In their homes, where they are devoted to sexual union with women they have served, they speak to one another of their worldly desires;
ignorant of the Truth, they sacrifice animals for their livelihood, offering no prepared food, no ritual arrangements, and no sacrificial fees.
[They boast] of their fortune, power, noble lineage, learning, renunciation, beauty, strength, and ritual acts.
Filled with pride, the wicked, their intellects blinded, disregard the virtuous who are dear to Hari, even though those virtuous ones are accompanied by the Lord himself;
for they fail to recognize the Self, the beloved Lord, who eternally dwells within all embodied beings just as space pervades all.

The ignorant do not hear that which is sung in the Vedas; they speak only of the news of their own mental desires. In this world, the pursuit of sexual intercourse, meat, and liquor is constant for living beings; indeed, there is no scriptural injunction regarding them.
Among them, marriage, sacrifice, and the drinking of wine are prescribed as established practices; however, among these [latter groups], cessation from such acts is desired.
For wealth indeed has dharma as its sole fruit, which leads to knowledge, realized wisdom, and ultimate peace.

In their homes, people are occupied with the body and do not perceive death, whose power is inexhaustible. That which is ordained as the smelling of wine and the immolation of an animal is not, in truth, violence.
Thus, sexual union for the sake of progeny and not for pleasure is their pure self-duty; yet they do not know this.
But those who do not know this, being wicked, stubborn, and falsely conceited, they confidently harm animals and, after death, they are eaten by them.
Hating the Lord Hari, who is their own self, within the bodies of others,
and being bound by affection for this corpse along with its attachments, they fall downward— those who have not attained liberation and those who have passed beyond the state of delusion.
For those who pursue the three goals of worldly life (trivarga) are impatient; they destroy themselves.
These self-killers, lacking peace and falsely imagining they possess knowledge when they are ignorant, sink down, their purposes unfulfilled, as their desires are destroyed by time.
Having abandoned their homes, children, friends, and wives— which were created by the illusory energy (māyā) of the Self—
those who have turned their backs on Vāsudeva enter into darkness against their own will.
Śrī Rājā said:
"At what time is that Blessed One worshipped by men; what is his color and what is he like? By what name or by what ritual is he adored? Let this be told here.
Śrī Karabhājana said:

In these ages— the Kṛta, Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali— Keśava is worshipped according to various rituals, with diverse colors, names, and forms. In the Kṛta age, he is white, four-armed, with matted hair, and clothed in bark garments.
Wearing a black antelope skin, a sacred thread, and a rosary, and carrying a staff and a water-pot,
human beings at that time— peaceful, free from enmity, friendly, and impartial—
worship the Divine through austerity, tranquility, and self-restraint.
He is celebrated as Haṃsa, Suparṇa, Vaikuṇṭha, Dharma, Yogeśvara, Amala,
Īśvara, Puruṣa, Avyakta, and Paramātman.
In the Tretā age, he is red in color, four-armed, and wears three girdles.

Then those most righteous men, exponents of the Veda, worshiped that Lord Hari— who consists of all the gods, possesses golden hair, and is characterized by the sacrificial ladle (*sruk*), the dipping-spoon (*sruva*), and other implements— by means of the threefold Vedic knowledge (*trayi-vidyā*).
Viṣṇu, Yajña, Pṛśnigarbha, Sarvadeva, Urukrama,
Vṛṣākapi, Jayanta, and Urugāya— thus he is glorified.
In the Dvāpara age, the Blessed Lord is dark-complexioned, clad in yellow garments, and bearing his own weapons.

O King, mortals who desire to know the Supreme then worship that Person— who is characterized by the Śrīvatsa and other marks and signs— as the emblem of the Great King, according to both the Vedas and the Tantras.
Salutations to You, Vāsudeva; salutations to Saṅkarṣaṇa; salutations to You, the Blessed One, Pradyumna and Aniruddha. Salutations to Nārāyaṇa, the Sage, the Supreme Person, the Great Soul.
"Obeisances to the Lord of the Universe, the Universal One, the Self of all beings"—
thus, O Lord of the Earth, they praise the Lord of the World in the Dvāpara age;
hear now how it is likewise done in the Kali age through various ritual systems.

The wise indeed worship Him who is dark-complexioned, yet not black in luster, together with His limbs, secondary limbs, weapons, and attendants, primarily through sacrifices consisting of congregational chanting (*saṅkīrtana*). He is always to be meditated upon as the destroyer of humiliation and the fulfiller of all desires.

O Great Person, I worship Your lotus feet— the abode of all holy places, praised by Śiva and Viriñca, the refuge, the destroyer of the suffering of Your servants, the protector of those who bow to You, and the boat for crossing the ocean of worldly existence.
Having renounced the royal fortune so difficult to abandon and so desired by the gods, he, being most righteous, went to the forest at the word of his elder brother;
yet he pursued the illusory deer desired by his beloved.

"I bow to Your lotus feet, O Great Person. Thus, O King, Lord Hari, the sovereign of all auspiciousness, is worshiped by the men living in each age according to the requirements of that particular yuga.
The noble ones, who recognize virtue and partake of its essence, honor the Kali age,
for in it all one's goals are attained through mere chanting alone;
indeed, there is no greater gain for embodied beings wandering here than this.

From him one may obtain supreme peace, and the cycle of worldly existence is destroyed. O King, in the Kṛta and other ages, people desire birth; however, in the Kali age, they shall indeed become devoted solely to Nārāyaṇa.
In various places, O Great King, and especially in abundance among the Draviḍas,
there are the river Tāmraparṇī, the Kṛtamālā, the Payasvinī,
the highly meritorious Kāverī, and the great western river, the Pratīcī.
O lord of men, those humans who drink their water are generally devotees of the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, possessing pure hearts.
O King, such a person is neither a servant nor a debtor to the gods, sages, spirits, kinsmen, humans, or ancestors.

For one who has gone for refuge with his whole being to Mukunda, the worthy protector— having abandoned all other duties and devoted himself solely to the root of Hari’s own feet— the Supreme Lord Hari,
dwelling within the heart, shakes off every ill deed that may have arisen by any chance.
Śrī Nārada said:
Having thus heard the Bhāgavata duties, the Lord of Mithilā,
together with his preceptor, joyfully honored the sages, the descendants of Jayanta.
Then, while all the world looked on, the perfected ones (siddhas) vanished;
the king, having followed these duties, attained the supreme goal.
You too, O highly fortunate one, [should follow] these Bhāgavata duties which you have heard.
Established in this with faith and free from attachment, you shall go to the Supreme.
Indeed, by the glory of you two, husband and wife, the entire world has been filled;
for the Blessed Lord Hari, the Sovereign, has become your son.

O Kṛṣṇa, by seeing, embracing, and conversing with you, and by sharing your bed, seat, and meals, our very selves have been purified as you both exercise parental affection toward your son. Even those kings— Śiśupāla, Pauṇḍraka, and others— who [opposed you] out of enmity...
Śālva and others, whose minds were captivated by His gait, graceful movements, glances, and so forth, meditated upon Him while lying down, sitting, or in other postures;
they attained identity with Him— how much more so, then, for those whose hearts are devoted?

Do not entertain the notion that Kṛṣṇa is merely your offspring; he is the Supreme Lord, the Soul of all, the ultimate immutable reality whose divine sovereignty is concealed by his illusory human form.
He has appeared for the destruction of the demon kings who are a burden to the earth, and for the protection of the virtuous.
"The glory of Him who has descended is spread throughout the world for the sake of liberation.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having heard this, the highly fortunate Vasudeva was greatly amazed.
And the highly fortunate Devakī abandoned her delusion regarding herself. Whoever, with a concentrated mind, retains this meritorious history,
having shaken off all impurity in this world, becomes fit for union with Brahman.
Śrī Śuka said:
Then Brahmā, surrounded by the gods born of his own self and the lords of progeny, arrived;
and Bhava, the lord of the past and the future, went forth surrounded by hosts of spirits.
Indra with the Maruts, the Lord [Brahmā], the Ādityas, the Vasus, the two Aśvins,
the Ṛbhus, the Aṅgirases, the Rudras, the Viśvedevas, and the Sādhyas— these are the deities;
as well as the Gandharvas, Apsarases, Nāgas, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, and Guhyakas.
The sages, the ancestors, along with the Vidyādharas and Kinnaras,
all approached Dvārakā, desiring to behold Kṛṣṇa,
by whose form the Blessed One enchants the world of men.

While that city was shining brilliantly, enriched with great opulences, he spread his fame throughout the worlds— which removes the impurities of all people— and they gazed upon Kṛṣṇa, whose appearance was wonderful, their eyes never sated.
Covering the best of warriors with garlands brought from the celestial gardens,
they praised the Lord of the Universe with hymns of wonderful words and meanings.
The glorious gods said:
O Lord, we bow down with our intellect, senses, vital breaths, mind, and speech to Your lotus feet,
which are meditated upon within the heart by those seeking liberation who are endowed with devotion, as the means to release from the bond of the body born of karma.
You, who are difficult to conceive within the self due to Your own illusory energy consisting of the three modes...

O Unconquered One, You manifest, maintain, and dissolve the manifest universe while abiding within its modes; yet You are not tainted by these actions, for You, being faultless, delight in Your own unimpeded bliss.

O Bull among men, for those whose souls are established in goodness, purification does not come through learning, sacred tradition, study, charity, austerity, or ritual acts as it does for those of evil intent who worship you,
O Lord of expanded glory.
May Your lotus feet— the comet that destroys inauspicious intentions— be ours, through hearing performed with true faith,
just as they are carried by sages whose hearts are moist with love for the sake of ultimate security.

He who is worshipped at each sacrifice in the ritual array by self-realized Sātvatas of equal spiritual power for the sake of transcending the celestial realms— he who is meditated upon with palms joined in reverence before the sacrificial fire.

O Lord, having accepted the oblation according to the rules prescribed by the three Vedas, You are worshipped through the yoga of the supreme self by the yogis who desire to know Your own illusory power (ātma-māyā), those most exalted devotees of the Supreme Lord.

O All-pervading Lord, this forest garland of Yours, though worn for a night, is like the goddess Śrī herself; it vies with her as a rival wife. We have not offered You a well-prepared worship worthy of such a guest.
May Your foot always be the comet that destroys those of evil intent— Your foot which, joined with the three strides and bearing three descending banners,
brings fear to the armies of the asuras and fearlessness to the gods.
O Infinite One, may the lotus feet of the Blessed One— which lead the virtuous to heaven and others to the opposite state— purify the sins of us who worship You,
under whose control all beings exist like oxen bound by a nose-rope.
May the feet of the Supreme Person, who is the ultimate beyond both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, grant us peace— He by whom Brahmā and the other embodied beings are being tormented by Your Time (*kāla*).

You are the cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of this world, as well as of the unmanifest, the individual soul, and the mahat-tattva; they call You Time. This very Time, possessing three naves, is engaged in the destruction of everything.
Time, with its profound current, is You, the Supreme Person;
from You, O one of unfailing potency, the male [the individual soul] receives that by which he conceives a great embryo within himself.
Accompanied by her, he emitted from himself the golden egg-shell, endowed with external coverings;
you are the sovereign lord of both that which is stationary and that which moves.
O Lord of the Senses, although You enjoy the objects brought forth by the transformations of the qualities arising from Your own māyā, You remain unstained;
whereas others, though they have renounced them of their own accord, are still afraid of them.

But his sixteen thousand wives were struck by the arrows of the bodiless god (Kāma), who was skilled in the secret mantras of amorous play conveyed by the movements of his eyebrows— movements that captivated the heart with even a fleeting glance accompanied by a smile.

The rivers flowing from the three worlds, which carry the waters of Your nectar-like stories, are not capable of washing away the impurities of those whose senses cannot be subdued by their own instruments; yet these rivers of water from Your feet are able to destroy all such stains.
Those who sit in purity partake of the two holy waters: the revealed scripture born from his feet through their ears, and the water from his limbs through physical contact.
Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said:
Having thus praised Hari along with Īśa, the hundred-fold sustainer (Brahmā), together with the gods,
bowed down to Govinda and, taking his place in the sky, addressed him.
Śrī Brahmā said:
O Lord, O Soul of all, long ago we requested you to remove the burden of the earth; that has been accomplished exactly as requested by you.
Furthermore, true dharma has been established among the virtuous who are faithful to their promises through your grace.
And your fame, which removes the impurities of all the worlds, has been spread in every direction;
having descended into the lineage of Yadu and assuming a supreme form,
you have performed deeds of unrestrained vigor for the benefit of the universe.
O Lord, O Supreme Person, those virtuous men who in the Kali age hear and chant Your deeds as You have descended into the Yadu dynasty will easily cross over the darkness of ignorance.
O Lord, more than one hundred and twenty-five autumns have passed;
O Support of All, there is now no longer any remainder of the work for the gods to be done by You.
Furthermore, this lineage has become almost entirely ruined by the curse of the brahmins.
"Therefore, enter your own supreme abode if you so desire;
protect us, the world-guardians of your realm, who are the servants of Vaikuṇṭha.
The Blessed Lord said:
O Lord of the gods, that which you have spoken has been understood by me:
"Your entire task has been accomplished; the burden of the earth has been removed.
Yet this Yādava clan remains arrogant with its prowess, heroism, and splendor.
This world, which I desired to uphold, has been obstructed by them like the great ocean by its shore.
If I depart without destroying this vast clan of the arrogant Yadus, this world will perish due to their overflowing tide.
"Now the destruction of the lineage, born from the curse of the twice-born, has begun.
O sinless Brahmin, at the conclusion of this, I shall go to my own abode.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus addressed by the Lord of the World, the self-born god Brahmā, having prostrated before him along with the hosts of deities, returned to his own abode. Then,
great portents arose in Dvāravatī.
Beholding the assembled elders of the Yadu clan, the Blessed Lord spoke;
the Śrī-Bhagavān said:
"Indeed, these very great portents are arising here on all sides."
And a curse upon our lineage from the Brāhmaṇas has become insurmountable;
O noble ones, we who wish to live must no longer dwell here.
We shall go this very day to Prabhāsa, which is exceedingly meritorious; do not delay.
Having bathed there, the wicked King Ugrasena, who had been seized by consumption due to Dakṣa’s curse,
was immediately freed from his sin and regained his former prosperity. And we, having immersed ourselves therein and offered libations to the ancestors and the gods, [attained our desires].
Having fed the Ṛṣis and brāhmaṇas with food possessing various excellent qualities,
and having indeed sown great gifts with faith into those worthy recipients, we shall cross over our sins by means of these gifts, as one crosses the ocean by means of boats.
Śrī Śuka said:
O descendant of Kuru, having been thus instructed by the Blessed One, the Yādavas resolved to depart for the sacred ford and harnessed their chariots.
O King, having observed that [vision], having heard what was spoken by the Blessed One, and having seen the terrible omens, Uddhava— who was constantly devoted to Kṛṣṇa—
approached the Lord of the lords of the worlds in a secluded place.
Bowing his head with devotion at His feet and joining his palms in reverence, he addressed Him.
Śrī Uddhava said:
"O Lord of the gods of gods, O Master of yoga, whose hearing and chanting are meritorious!"
Having surely withdrawn this family, you will surely abandon the world;
for although you were capable of it, O Lord, you did not counteract the curse of the brahmins.
O Keśava, I shall not leave your lotus feet even for half a moment.
O Lord, I am unable to abandon [this world]; lead me, too, to Your own abode.
O Kṛṣṇa, Your divine pastimes are the supreme auspiciousness for men;
having obtained them as nectar for the ears, people renounce all other desires.
In sleeping, sitting, walking, standing, bathing, playing, eating, and so forth—
how indeed could we, your devotees, ever abandon You, our beloved Self?
For we are adorned with the garlands, perfumes, garments, ornaments, and unguents that have been enjoyed by You.
"O Lord, we are Your servants who eat the remnants of Your food; may we indeed conquer Your illusory power (māyā).
Those sages who are clothed by the wind, the ascetics who churn the upward-flowing breath—peaceful, stainless, and having renounced all attachments—they attain Your abode known as Brahman."
But we here, O Great Yogin, wandering upon the paths of karma,
shall cross over the darkness difficult to traverse by means of Your news,
while remembering and chanting Your deeds and Your words.
His walking, smiling, glancing, and playful movements were imitations of the ways of the human world.
Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having been thus petitioned, the Blessed Lord, the son of Devakī, [responded].
The Blessed Lord spoke to His beloved devotee Uddhava, who was solely devoted to Him.
The Blessed Lord said:
"O most fortunate one, that which you have told me is indeed what I desire to do."
Brahmā, Śiva, and the guardians of the worlds desire residence in heaven for themselves;
indeed, the work of the gods has been completed by me here in its entirety. For this purpose I descended with a portion of Myself, having been entreated by Brahmā.
The lineage, consumed by mutual strife and cursed, shall perish;
for on the seventh day, the ocean will indeed submerge this city. Indeed, when I have abandoned this world, its auspiciousness destroyed.
O virtuous one, before long Kali will cast you out;
when I have abandoned this earth, you shall no longer dwell here. O gentle one, in the Kali age, people will take pleasure in what is inauspicious.
But you, having completely renounced all affection for your own kinsmen and relatives,
and having properly fixed your mind on Me, wander the earth with an even vision.
Whatever is done by means of the mind, speech, eyes, ears, and other senses—
Know that which is perceived as perishable to be composed of the mind through *māyā*.
For a person who is not disciplined, the delusion of manifold objects brings about both virtues and defects.
The distinctions between "action," "inaction," and "misdeed" arise from the perception of virtue and defect.
Therefore, with the senses restrained and the mind composed, behold this world as pervaded by the Self, and behold the Self within Me, the Supreme Lord—
endowed with both theoretical knowledge and realized wisdom, having become the very Self of all embodied beings.
With your soul satisfied by the experience of the Self, you are not hindered by obstacles;
having transcended both [good and evil], you do not desist from what is prohibited because of the perception of fault,
nor do you perform what is enjoined because of the perception of merit, just like a child.

Being a friend to all beings, peaceful, and firm in the certainty of theoretical and realized knowledge, one who perceives the entire universe as having Me as its essence shall indeed never again fall into calamity. Śrī Śuka said:
O King, having been thus instructed by the Blessed One, the great devotee Uddhava, desiring to know the ultimate truth, prostrated himself before Acyuta and spoke. Śrī Uddhava said:
O Lord of Yoga, O You who apply yoga, O Soul of Yoga, O Source of Yoga!
For my ultimate liberation, You have explained renunciation characterized by the state of a renunciant (saṃnyāsa).
O Infinite One, this renunciation of desires is difficult to perform for those whose minds are absorbed in sense objects.
It is my conviction, O Soul of All, that this is especially true for those who lack devotion toward You.
Thus, with a deluded mind steeped in the notions of "I" and "mine," I am immersed in this self along with its attachments, which has been fashioned by Your illusory power (māyā).
That has been explained by you directly;
O Blessed One, instruct your servant as to how I may accomplish it.
For You, who are Truth, self-perceiving, and the Self, there is nothing other than Yourself.
O Lord, even among the gods, I do not see anyone who can describe You;
for all these embodied beings, beginning with Brahmā, have their intellects deluded by Your māyā and perceive only external objects as real.

Therefore, O Lord, I— my mind despondent and tormented by misfortune— approach You, who are faultless, infinite and boundless, omniscient, the Sovereign, whose abode is the unimpeded and transcendent Vaikuṇṭha.
"I take refuge in Nārāyaṇa, the friend of Nara.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Generally, men in this world are experts in discerning the true nature of the world."
For one uplifts oneself from an inauspicious disposition by means of oneself alone;
for a person, especially, the self is one's own teacher,
since it is through direct perception and inference that one finds what is beneficial.
And when I am in the form of a person, the wise, who are proficient in Sāṅkhya and Yoga,
perceive me most clearly as augmented by all my potencies—
whether as having one, two, three, four, or many feet, or even as footless.
Many cities have been created by Me; among them, the city of Puruṣa is My favorite.
Here they truly seek Me, the Lord, through disciplined reasoning and by means of the qualities perceived as signs, though I am ungraspable through inference.
In this regard, they cite this ancient history:
the conversation between Avadhūta and Yadu of immeasurable splendor.
[They tell of] a certain Avadhūta wandering about, free from the two-fold bonds and fearless of anything.
Beholding the youthful sage, Yadu, who was conversant with dharma, questioned him.
Śrī Yadu said:
"O brāhmaṇa, from where has this highly proficient intelligence come to you, who are a non-doer?"

Having attained which, you, though wise, move through the world like a child; for generally, men strive by means of specific motives for virtue, wealth, pleasure, the desire for knowledge, and for longevity, fame, and prosperity.
You, however, are wise, skillful, capable, fortunate, and one whose speech is immortal;
yet you do nothing and desire nothing, like one who is dull-witted, insane, or a ghost,
while people are being consumed by the forest fire of lust and greed.
Released from the fire, you do not suffer, like an elephant standing in the waters of the Gaṅgā.
O Brahmin, please tell us who ask you the cause of your bliss within yourself— how is it for you, who are devoid of touch and are the absolute Self?
The Blessed Lord said:

O twice-born one, having been thus questioned and honored by the highly fortunate Yadu, who was devoted to Brahman and possessed of great intelligence, He spoke to him as he stood bowed with humility.
The venerable brāhmaṇa said:
O King, I have many gurus who have taken refuge in wisdom; having acquired wisdom from them, I wander here as one liberated. Hear about them.
Earth, wind, ether, water, fire, the moon, and the sun;
the dove, the python, the ocean, the moth, the honeybee, and the elephant;
the honey-thief, the deer, the fish, Piṅgalā, the osprey, and the child.
The girl, the arrow-maker, the snake, and the spider-weaver—
these twenty-four were my teachers, O King; having approached them,
I learned from them here how to train myself through their various disciplines and modes of livelihood.

O son of Nahuṣa, O tiger among men, listen as I tell you exactly what I have learned and how I have practiced it; understand it thus. Even when assailed by beings who follow the power of destiny, a wise man remains steadfast.
Knowing this, one should not deviate from the path; one should learn the vow of the Earth.

A saint whose every effort is eternally for the sake of others, and whose sole existence is for the benefit of others, should learn from the Mountain—the disciple of the Earth—how to realize the identity with the Supreme Self.
A sage should be satisfied with the mere maintenance of life alone, and not with the objects dear to the senses,
so that his knowledge may not perish nor his speech and mind become scattered.
When entering among various objects and diverse duties from all sides, the yogi [should remain thus].
One whose self is free from the qualities and defects of nature should not become attached, like the wind;
though entered here into earthly bodies and taking refuge in their qualities,
the yogi who perceives the Self is not joined by those qualities, just as the wind is not joined by odors.

And having become invisible among moving and stationary beings through the realization of the self as Brahman and through pervasive union, the sage should contemplate the sky-like nature of the all-pervading Self— uninterrupted and unattached—
as being obscured by entities composed of fire, water, and earth, such as clouds and the like, driven by the wind.
Just as the sky is not touched by the qualities created by time, so the person (puruṣa) is not touched by them. Pure by nature, affectionate, sweet, and a source of sanctity for men,
the sage— a friend to the waters— purifies others through his sight, touch, and praise.

Radiant with splendor, blazing with austerity, and possessing an insurmountable stomach, he consumes all things; yet, though he eats everything, his disciplined mind does not take on impurity, just like fire.
Sometimes hidden and sometimes manifest, he is to be worshipped by those who desire the highest good.
The omnipresent Lord, consuming the prior and subsequent inauspiciousness of all donors everywhere,
has entered this world— which He created by His own *māyā* and which is characterized as both real and unreal— and moves about assuming various forms, like fire within fuel.
The states of the body, beginning with birth and ending with the cremation ground, do not belong to the self,
just as the phases of the moon occur through time by its unmanifest path;
for by the force of the current of time, there is the arising and passing away of all beings.

Although they are eternal, they are not perceived, just as the flames of a fire are not distinct from the fire itself. By means of the *guṇas*, the yogin assumes the *guṇas* according to the time, yet he does not become attached to them, just as a cowherd is not joined with his own cattle.

Just as one situated in a physical form perceives it through its manifestations, so too the Self, though residing within, is not perceived as distinct by those of dull intellect; yet it is observed to be present like the sun.
One should not cultivate excessive affection for, nor attachment to, anything whatsoever, nor toward anyone.
One who acts [otherwise] will experience distress, like the pigeon of feeble intellect.
A certain pigeon, having built a nest in a tree in the forest,
lived there for several years together with his wife, the female pigeon.
The two pigeons, their hearts overflowing with affection as householders,
bound themselves to one another— eye to eye, limb to limb, and mind to mind—
whether in lying down, sitting, walking, standing, conversing, playing, or eating.
Having united as a couple, they wandered with confidence through the forest groves. O King, whatever she desired, that compassionate woman would satisfy her;
yet he, whose senses were unsubdued, failed to fulfill even those desires despite his great effort.
A female dove, having first conceived a fetus, when the time arrived,
laid her eggs in her nest while remaining in the presence of her husband. In due course, from those eggs were born the limbs of Hari, perfectly formed.

With their delicate limbs and body hairs invigorated by powers that are difficult to conceive, the couple, affectionate toward their children, nurtured their offspring with joy; they were filled with bliss as they listened to the warbling of those children and their sweet, melodious speech.
With their soft-touching wings, their charming warbling, and their innocent movements,
as they came forward to meet them, the two parents—
whose hearts were bound by affection for one another through the illusory power of Viṣṇu— attained great joy.
Deluded and dejected in mind, they reared their children and progeny.
Once, those two householders went out for the sake of food for them; seeking it, they wandered for a long time throughout that forest.
A certain hunter wandering in the forest by chance saw them;
having spread out his net, he caught the pair as they were moving near their own dwelling.
Both the male and female pigeon were constantly intent on nourishing their offspring.
Having taken food for their journey, the two returned to their own nest. Seeing her young offspring ensnared in the net, the female dove,
crying out in intense distress, ran toward them as they cried out.
Repeatedly moistened with affection by her own delusion born of a distressed mind,
she herself became bound by the snare, losing her memory even as she watched her bound children—
pigeons dearer to her than herself.
Distraught and deeply afflicted by grief, he lamented for his wife, who was equal to himself:
"Alas! Behold my ruin, I of meager merit and wicked mind; while still unsatiated and with my purpose unfulfilled, the home that provided the three goals of life has been destroyed."
My wife, who was devoted to her husband as a deity and perfectly suited to me,
has abandoned me in this empty house and gone to heaven with her virtuous sons;
thus, I am wretched in this empty home, with my wife dead and my children gone.
Or for what purpose does one who is destitute and lives in misery wish to live? Seeing those very people— enveloped by their own actions, seized by death, and struggling—
and though himself pitiable, seeking instruction, and even seeing them, the ignorant man fell [into delusion].
Having obtained that domestic pigeon, the cruel hunter,
his purpose fulfilled, departed for home with the female pigeon and their offspring.
Thus, like the bird, the householder whose mind is unpeaceful delights in the pairs of opposites.
A wretched man who, along with his family, sinks under the weight of maintaining a household—
having attained this human world which is an open door to liberation— is known as one who has fallen from his high station after having ascended it, like a bird clinging to its nest.
The venerable brāhmaṇa said:
O King, the pleasure derived from the senses—whether in heaven or even in hell—is for embodied beings nothing but suffering; therefore, a wise person should not desire it.

Whether the morsel be well-prepared or tasteless, large or even small, one should swallow it as it happens to come by chance, remaining inactive like a python. One should lie down for many days without food, making no effort to procure it.
If he does not take food, like a great serpent subsisting on its destined portion, then—
even though possessing senses— he would not desire anything while lying down, his body devoid of activity yet endowed with vigor, stamina, and strength, and free from sleep.
The sage is serene and profound, difficult to fathom and difficult to transcend;
indeed, he is infinite in extent and unshakeable, like an ocean with still waters.
Whether his desires are fulfilled or he is destitute, the sage is solely devoted to Nārāyaṇa.
He would neither overflow nor dry up, like the ocean with its rivers; yet,
seeing a woman— the illusion of the gods— and being enticed by her charms, he whose senses are unsubdued falls into blinding darkness like a moth into a flame.
The fool, his mind deluded by illusion, is enticed by objects such as women, gold, ornaments, and garments created by Māyā;
with his vision destroyed, he perishes like a moth through the desire for enjoyment. One should swallow food little by little, only so much as is required for the body to subsist.
A sage, not causing harm to householders, should adopt the "bee-like" mode of livelihood (*mādhukarī-vṛtti*).
A skillful man should extract the essence from all scriptures— both small and great—
just as a bee gathers nectar from flowers.
A mendicant should not store up what was begged for the evening or for the morrow;
with his hand as his bowl and his stomach as his vessel, he should not be a hoarder like a fly.
A mendicant should not store up what was begged for the evening or for the morrow.
Like flies gathering around filth, he who clings to her perishes along with her.

A mendicant should not touch a young woman even with his foot, nor even one made of wood; by touching her, he would be bound like an elephant that has come into physical contact with a female elephant.
A wise man should never approach a woman, for he may meet his own death;

he might be slain by those superior in strength, just as one elephant is slain by other elephants. Furthermore, that which has been accumulated with great suffering by the greedy should neither be given away nor enjoyed.
Even that [which he eats] is consumed by another who knows the meaning of the *madhu-hēva* hymn;

for the ascetic (*yati*) indeed eats before the *madhu-hēva* [sacrifice], while those householders (*gṛhamedhin*) eat with wealth acquired through great hardship, hoping for blessings from their homes.

A renunciant wandering in the forest should never listen to vulgar songs; he should learn from the deer how to remain unattached even when they are captivated by the songs of the hunter. One who indulges in the dancing, instrumental music, and vulgar songs of women [is lost].

Their plaything and submissive servant was Ṛṣyaśṛṅga, the son of a deer. A person whose intellect is unwholesome, being utterly deluded by the taste of objects through the excessively agitating tongue, meets with death, just as a fish is caught by hooks.
Wise men who abstain from food quickly conquer the senses;
however, with the exception of the tongue, those [other senses] continue to grow for one who is without food.
A man may have conquered his other senses, yet he cannot be considered one who has mastered his senses as long as the tongue remains unsubdued.
One cannot conquer everything until the tongue is conquered; when the sense of taste is conquered, all is conquered.
O son of a king, listen to something I learned from a prostitute named Piṅgalā in the city of Videha in ancient times.
Once that unchaste woman, intending to bring her lover to the rendezvous,
was standing at the outer gate at the appointed time, assuming an exquisite form;
O bull among men, she saw men approaching on the road.
Desirous of wealth, she considered those wealthy suitors who had paid the bride-price as her lovers; yet, when they had arrived and departed, that woman who lived by secret appointments thought:
"Perhaps some other wealthy man, a liberal giver, will come to me."
Thus, with her hopes frustrated, she whose sleep was destroyed stood leaning against the door;
as she went out and came back in, the night arrived. Her mouth was parched by her craving for wealth, and her mind was dejected.
Supreme detachment arose within her, which is the cause of contemplation and brings happiness. Listen to the song of me, whose mind was thus detached:
"For a person, detachment is indeed like a sword for cutting the bonds of worldly hope."

O King, one who has not developed detachment toward the limbs of the body does not desire to abandon the bondage of the physical form, just as a man devoid of true knowledge cannot relinquish his sense of "mineness.
Piṅgalā said:
Alas! Behold the vast expanse of my delusion, I who have failed to conquer myself;
for like a fool, I desire lustful passion from an unreal woman, while neglecting this eternal lover who is ever-present, who bestows delight and grants all wealth.
"I am ignorant; I worship that which grants no desires and bestows only suffering, fear, mental anguish, delusion, and vanity.
"Alas! I have needlessly tormented myself with a life of hypocritical conduct and highly censurable pursuits.
"From men who are slaves to women and thirst for wealth—objects of pity—I desired pleasure for myself by means of what was purchased with my riches."
This body is a leaking house with nine doors, constructed with the ribs as its rafters and beams, the spine as its pillars, and bound together by the skin, hair, and nails.
What else can I resort to when I am filled with feces and urine?
For in this city of the Videhas, I alone possess a deluded intellect,
since they desire from Acyuta— who gives his very self— merely a worldly object that is unreal.
He is the friend, the dearest one, the protector, and the very Self of all embodied beings.
Having sold Him with my own self, I take delight in Him just as Lakṣmī does.
How much more dear must He be to you than those men who grant desires, who distribute only so much pleasure?
The gods, along with their wives, are subject to beginning and end, driven away by Time;
surely the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu has been pleased with me through some past action, since this disillusionment from my wicked desires has arisen within me, bringing such happiness.
"Let not such misfortunes, which cause despondency, befall me, an unfortunate woman; for by means of them a person casts off worldly attachment and attains peace.
Therefore, accepting this favor upon my head, I shall associate with those who dwell in the village."
Having abandoned evil desires, I take refuge in that Supreme Lord;
being contented and full of faith, I live upon whatever comes by chance, and I sport with Him alone as my own soul and my delight.

Who else is the sovereign lord capable of protecting one who has fallen into the well of saṃsāra, whose vision is stolen by sense objects, and who is seized by the serpent of Time—were it not for oneself?
For the self alone is the protector of the self; this is so when one becomes weary of everything.
Being vigilant, one should behold this world devoured by the serpent of Time.
The illustrious brāhmaṇa said:
Thus resolved in mind, [he abandoned] that wicked hope born of thirst for his beloved.
Having cut [off her desires] and established herself in tranquility, she sat down upon her bed.
For hope is the supreme suffering, and freedom from hope is the supreme happiness; just as Piṅgalā slept happily after completely severing her hope for her lover.
The venerable brāhmaṇa said:
Indeed, whatever is most dear to men leads to suffering through its possession;
however, the wise man who possesses nothing attains infinite happiness.
Other powerful birds, being without meat, killed the osprey who possessed meat;
by renouncing that meat, he attained happiness.
For me, there is neither honor nor dishonor, nor anxiety regarding home or children.
I wander here like a child, sporting with the Self and finding delight in the Self;
we two alone are liberated from anxiety, immersed in supreme bliss—
he who is deluded, inert, and childish, and he who has gone beyond the modes of nature.
In one place, O King, a young maiden, having invited them to her home, personally honored those who had come as suitors while her kinsmen were away; in another,
she prepared fine rice in secret for their meal.
As she was pounding [the grain], the conch shells resting upon her forearms produced a great sound.
Thinking that this was loathsome, the noble lady then became deeply ashamed;
she broke the conch shells one by one, leaving only two in each hand.
The sound of both her own conch shells arose as she struck them;
yet, while one produced a resonant note, no sound issued from the other.
O subduer of enemies, I learned this lesson from her instruction.
Wandering through these worlds with the desire to understand the true nature of the universe, he reflected:
"Conflict arises among many living together, and even between two there is talk;
therefore, one should dwell alone, like a bangle on a maiden's wrist."
One who has conquered his breath and mastered his posture should fix the mind on a single point,
remaining vigilant through the yoga of dispassion and practice, while holding it steady. That state upon which the mind, having found its footing, gradually sheds the dust of karma— this is the goal.
When goodness has increased, having shaken off passion and ignorance, one attains the fuel-less extinction (*nirvāṇa*).
At that time, with the mind thus withdrawn into the self, one knows nothing either external or internal;
just as the arrow-maker, his soul absorbed in the arrow, did not see the king passing by his side.
Wandering alone, without a fixed abode, vigilant, dwelling in the cave of the heart,

the sage should remain unobserved in his conduct, solitary, and sparing in speech. Indeed, the undertaking of a household leads only to suffering for one whose self is impermanent and whose efforts are fruitless.
A snake enters a dwelling made by another and prospers in comfort; so too,
at the end of the kalpa, the Lord Nārāyaṇa alone, by his own māyā and through the movement of time, withdraws this universe that was previously created.
He alone was without a second, self-supported, and the refuge of all;
when his powers— sattva and the others— had been brought to equilibrium by time through the power of his own nature,
he remained as the Original Person, the Lord of Pradhāna and Puruṣa.
He dwells as the supreme among the high and the low, known as Kaivalya; He is the mass of bliss consisting of absolute experience, free from all limiting adjuncts.
By the power of His own self-experience, He [perceives] His own Māyā, which consists of the three guṇas.
O subduer of enemies, at the beginning, agitating that [nature], He creates the *sūtra* (the thread) by means of it;
they call that the manifestation of the three qualities (*tri-guṇa-vyakti*), which emanates in all directions,
and in which this entire universe is woven and by which the person (*puruṣa*) transmigrates.
Just as a spider, having extended a thread from its heart and from its mouth,
plays with it and then swallows it again, so does the Great Lord.
Wherever an embodied being holds the mind with the intellect upon the All-pervading, [there he remains].
Out of affection, hatred, or even fear, one attains the very nature of that object; O King, just as a worm, while meditating on a silkworm, enters a wall made by it and,
without abandoning its former form, attains the state of being identical with it.
Thus has this understanding been taught to me by these gurus;
now, O Lord, hear from me as I speak the wisdom I have learned from my own self.
My body is my guru, for it is the cause of detachment and discrimination.
Bearing this body, which is the abode of the material mode of goodness (*sattva*) and which results in constant suffering,
I reflect upon the principles of reality; nevertheless, having concluded that it belongs to another, I wander about free from attachment.

That body, which— having its wealth restricted— is exhausted within the mind as it expands its efforts to provide for and do what is pleasing to the group consisting of wife, children, wealth, cattle, servants, home, and kinsmen, is truly a source of misery.
Having produced its seed, the tree withers according to its nature;
on one side the tongue drags it away with thirst,
on another the genitals, on another the skin and belly, and from somewhere else the ears.
The sense of smell is drawn elsewhere, the restless eye wanders, and where is the power of action?
Like many co-wives, they tear at the master of the house.
Having created various worlds by His own power, the Unconquered One [remains].
Displeased with trees, reptiles, beasts, birds, and venomous serpents,
the Lord, having fashioned a Puruṣa whose intellect was fixed on the vision of Brahman, attained joy.
