Having obtained this human birth— which is extremely difficult to attain at the end of many existences, which grants all goals, and though transient in this world— the wise man should strive quickly, lest he fall again into death after death.
Indeed, for the sake of the supreme good, one should withdraw from all sense objects.
Thus, having developed detachment and possessing the light of realized knowledge within myself,
I wander this earth free from attachment and devoid of egoism.
Indeed, knowledge from a single guru would not be very firm nor very complete;
for this Brahman is sung as non-dual by many seers.
The Blessed Lord said:
Having spoken thus to Yadu, that brahmin of profound intellect took his leave;
honored and well-worshiped by the king, he departed contentedly as he had come.
Having heard the words of the Avadhūta, our ancestor, the elder brother of our forefathers...
Completely liberated from all attachments, he indeed became even-minded. The Blessed Lord said: "With me as your refuge, remain attentive to your own duties as declared by Me."
One whose mind is free from desire should practice the conduct appropriate to one's social class (varṇa), stage of life (āśrama), and family;
being pure in soul, one should observe through meditation on reality the failure of all undertakings among embodied beings who are attached to sense objects.
Just as the perception of objects by one who is asleep, or the mental construction of one who is meditating,
is fruitless because it lacks a real self-nature, so too is the cognition of a separate self produced by the modes of nature.
One who is devoted to Me should cultivate renounced action (*nivṛtta-karma*) and abandon active worldly duty (*pravṛtta-karma*).
One who has set out in the inquiry [into the Self] should not heed the injunctions for ritual action;
rather, being devoted to Me, one should constantly practice the restraints (yamas) and occasionally the observances (niyamas).
One should serve a peaceful teacher who knows Me and whose very self is Me.

One who is free from pride, devoid of envy, skillful, without the sense of "mine," firm in friendship, not impetuous, desirous of knowing the ultimate truth, free from malice, and whose speech is never in vain; [who is thus detached] from wife, children, home, fields, kinsmen, wealth, and the like—
Remaining indifferent, seeing the same self-interest in all beings,
the Self is distinct from the gross and subtle bodies; it is the witness of the self, self-luminous,
just as fire is the burner and illuminator, distinct from the wood that is burned.
The Supreme Being, having entered within, assumes the qualities produced by those [modes]— namely, cessation, origination, atomicity, and magnitude— as well as the various qualities of the body;
for this body is indeed composed of the modes for the sake of the Person (puruṣa).
This cycle of worldly existence and its cause belong to the person; knowledge is the cutter of the self's bonds.
Therefore, by means of inquiry, one should unite with the Self—the solitary Supreme residing within the self—and gradually eliminate the perception of this [world] as a substantial reality.
The teacher is the lower fire-drill (araṇi), and the student is the upper fire-drill;
their union is the instruction, which is the junction of knowledge that brings happiness.
That intellect, which is self-confident and exceedingly pure, shakes off the illusion born of the material modes.
When one has burned away these qualities and this self, it becomes extinguished by itself, like a fire without fuel. Furthermore,

there is a diversity among these agents of action, performers of deeds, and enjoyers of pleasure and pain, as well as among the worlds, time, the scriptures, and the self, due to their eternal nature.
You consider that the structural arrangement of all entities is indeed innate;
thus, according to the distinctions of their respective forms, the intellect is born and differentiated.
Even so, my dear one, for all embodied beings, this occurs through their connection with a body.
Through the divisions of time, states such as birth and so forth occur repeatedly;
even therein, the lack of independence of the agent of actions is observed.
What purpose, indeed, could there be for the enjoyer who must experience pleasure and pain while being powerless?
Not even for the wise does any happiness exist for embodied beings, nor does suffering exist for the deluded; rather, their egoism is merely in vain—
provided they understand the attainment and destruction of pleasure and pain.
Even they do not truly know the yoga by which death might not prevail.
What object of sense gratification, or even desire, can bring him happiness when death is so near?
It yields no satisfaction, like that of a victim being led to the place of execution.
And that which is heard [through scripture] is as flawed as that which is seen, due to rivalry, envy, transgression, and loss;
furthermore, because of the many obstacles inherent in desire, it is as fruitless as agriculture.
If dharma is performed according to one's own capacity, provided it is not obstructed by impediments, [it is fruitful].
Listen now to how one who has conquered even that place departs:
by performing sacrifices here to the deities, the sacrificer goes to the heavenly world (*svarloka*) and enjoys there,
like a god, the divine pleasures he has earned for himself.
In a bright celestial chariot acquired through his own merit,

he sports in the midst of goddesses, wearing attire that captivates their hearts, while being sung of by Gandharvas; he travels by a vehicle that moves at will, adorned with a network of tinkling bells, accompanied by women.
Playing and finding delight in the pleasure gardens of the gods, he does not perceive his own downfall;
he rejoices in heaven for as long as his merit lasts. Once his merit is exhausted, driven by time, he falls back down against his will.
If, through association with the wicked, one becomes devoted to unrighteousness, has his senses unsubdued,
is lustful, wretched, greedy, henpecked, and a violator of living beings;
and if he sacrifices animals contrary to the prescribed rules, worshipping hosts of spirits and ghosts— *Bhagavata Purana 11.10.27–28*
Having gone helplessly to the hells, a living being goes to intense darkness;
performing actions that result in suffering with a body, he again assumes a body through those very actions. In that state, what happiness can there be for one subject to the nature of a mortal?
Even for the worlds and their guardians who live for an entire kalpa, there is fear of me;
even for Brahmā, whose lifespan lasts two parārdhas, there is fear of me.
The modes of nature produce actions, and the mode produces further modes.

But the individual soul (jīva), conjoined with the modes of nature, experiences the fruits of its actions; as long as there is an inequality of the modes, so long does the multiplicity of the self persist.
Indeed, as long as there is this multiplicity of the self, so long does its state of dependence remain.
"As long as there is a lack of independence for this [individual soul], so long will there be fear of the Lord.
Those who worship this [limited self] become deluded and are overwhelmed by grief.
Time, the Self, destiny, the world, inherent nature, and even religious duty—"
"Thus they describe me in many ways when there is the intermingling of the *guṇas*.
Śrī Uddhava said:
"Even while abiding within the *guṇas* born of the body, one remains unenveloped [by them]."
O All-pervading Lord, how is it that the embodied soul is not bound by the *guṇas*, or how indeed is he bound?
How should he conduct himself, how should he sport, and by what characteristics is he to be known?
What should he eat, or what should he excrete; should he lie down, sit, or move about?
"O Acyuta, O best among those who know how to answer questions, please explain this to me:
my confusion is whether the eternally bound and the eternally liberated are truly one and the same.
The Blessed Lord said:
The designations "bound" and "liberated" are explained by Me as being due to the modes of nature, not in reality;
since the mode is rooted in *māyā*, for Me there is neither liberation nor bondage.
Sorrow, delusion, pleasure, pain, and the assumption of a body are all through *māyā*.

Just as a dream is a manifestation of the self and not real, so too is this cycle of worldly existence (saṃsṛti). O Uddhava, know that knowledge (vidyā) and ignorance (avidyā) are my two bodies for embodied beings;
these two, which cause liberation and bondage respectively, are fashioned by my illusory power (māyā).

O great-minded one, for the individual soul (jīva), who is indeed a single portion of Me, bondage is beginningless through ignorance (avidyā), and likewise, its opposite [liberation] occurs through knowledge (vidyā). Now, I shall describe to you the distinction between the bound and the liberated.
O dear one, these two birds, though possessing contradictory natures, abide upon a single tree; they are similar to one another and are friends, having by chance built their nests in that tree.
One of them eats the fruit of the *pippala* tree, while the other does not eat at all, yet he is superior in strength.
The learned Apippalāda knows both himself and the other, but Pippalāda does not.

He who is joined with ignorance is eternally bound; he who consists of knowledge is eternally liberated. Although situated in the body, the wise man is not situated in the body, just like one who has awakened from a dream.
Though not situated in a body, the one of dull intellect appears to be situated in a body, like one seeing a dream;
whereas the wise man, being immutable, does not form the notion of "I" when the senses are engaged with sense-objects or when the qualities are perceived within the modes of nature.
In this body, which is subject to destiny, the ignorant person, acting through karma that is itself produced by the modes of nature, becomes bound by the thought, "I am the doer.
Thus detached from lying down, sitting, walking, and bathing, [he remains free].
In seeing, touching, smelling, eating, hearing, and so forth,
the wise man is not bound in that way as he encounters the qualities (guṇas) here and there; though situated in material nature (prakṛti), he remains unattached, like space, the sun, and the wind.
With doubts severed by the sharp sword of fearlessness, freedom from attachment,
and discernment, he turns away from the perception of multiplicity, just as one awakened from a dream.
This occurs when the volitional constructions of the vital breaths, senses, body, and intellect have vanished for him.

He who is liberated from the functions [of the senses] is indeed free from the qualities of the body even while remaining in it. For the wise man is not perturbed whether his self is harmed by violent beings or honored by someone somewhere, or whatever occurs to him by chance.
A sage who perceives with equanimity should neither praise nor blame those performing good or evil deeds; being free from attachment to virtues and faults,
he should not do anything, speak anything, or meditate upon what is good or evil.
Delighting in the Self, the sage should wander about with this mode of life like one who is dull-witted;
if he is proficient in the Word-Brahman but does not become proficient in the Supreme,
his labor is as fruitless as that of one who tends a cow that yields no milk.

O dear one, he who protects a cow that yields no milk, an unfaithful wife, a body dependent on others, and worthless offspring; and wealth that has not been offered to worthy recipients, and speech devoid of Me—he suffers misery upon misery.
O dear one, for such a person, there is no purifying action of Mine regarding this world’s maintenance, creation, or dissolution.
A wise person would not uphold that barren speech which claims a desire for birth in a divine pastime (līlāvatāra).
Thus, having dispelled the delusion of multiplicity within the Self through inquiry,
one should rest with a stainless mind, offering it to Me, who am all-pervading.
If you are unable to hold the mind steady upon Brahman,
perform all actions for Me without expectation,
while listening with faith to My auspicious stories that purify the world.
O Uddhava, by singing, constantly remembering, repeatedly enacting my deeds and births,
performing acts of virtue, desire, and wealth for my sake, and taking refuge in me,
one attains unwavering devotion to me, the eternal.
"By means of devotion obtained through the association of the saintly, he shall worship Me in Me;
indeed, he who is shown the path by the virtuous attains My state directly.
Śrī Uddhava said:
O Lord of Excellent Renown, what kind of person is considered by You to be a saint, O Master?
What kind of devotion toward You is practiced and esteemed by the virtuous?
This, O Overseer of Men, Overseer of the World, Lord of the Universe, [I ask] of You.
"Tell it to one who is bowed down, devoted, and has sought refuge.
You are the Supreme Brahman, the ether, the Puruṣa beyond primordial nature;
O Blessed One, you have descended here, having assumed a distinct form by your own will."
The Blessed Lord said:
Compassionate, free from malice toward any embodied being, patient,
whose essence is truth, whose nature is irreproachable, impartial, and a benefactor to all.

One whose intellect is unassailed by desires, self-controlled, gentle, pure, and possessing nothing; free from worldly striving, moderate in eating, peaceful, steadfast, a sage who has taken refuge in Me;
vigilant, profound in soul, resolute, and having conquered the six internal enemies—[such a person attains Me].
Free from pride, bestowing honor upon others, composed, friendly, compassionate, and wise— he who, having understood these qualities and defects taught by me even though they be his own,
abandons all such duties and worships Me alone, he indeed is the most excellent of beings.

Whether they know Me or do not know Me, those who worship Me with undivided devotion— whatever My extent may be, and who I am, and of what nature— they are considered by Me to be the most perfect devotees.
[This includes] the sight, touch, and worship of My emblems and My devotees.
Service, praise, and the chanting of the qualities and deeds of the one who is bowed down;
O Uddhava, faith in hearing My stories, meditation upon Me,
the offering of all gains, and the surrender of oneself through the spirit of servitude.
The narration of my births and deeds, the celebration of my festivals,
and the festivities in my temple with songs, dances, instrumental music, and assemblies;
as well as processions and the offering of oblations on all annual festival days.
Vedic and Tantric initiation, the observance of my vows,
faith in the installation of my image,
and the spontaneous effort of working together in the construction of gardens, groves, pleasure parks, cities, and temples;

Serving my household with sincerity, like a servant— by sweeping, smearing, sprinkling water, and drawing decorative circles— and by being free from pride, devoid of hypocrisy, and not boasting of what has been done for me.
One should not even use the light of a lamp offered to Me;
whatever is most desired in the world and whatever is exceedingly dear to oneself— that one should offer to Me, for that conduces to infinity.

O auspicious one, the sun, fire, brāhmaṇas, cows, the devotees of Viṣṇu, the ether, the wind, water, the earth, the self, and all living beings are My objects of worship. One should worship Me in the sun with the threefold Vedic knowledge and in the fire with oblations.

O dear one, by means of hospitality toward the foremost of brāhmaṇas; by providing grass and fodder for the cows; by honoring kinsmen who are devotees of Viṣṇu; by steadfast meditation on the Lord within the heart;
by regarding the wind as the primary element; and by offering water preceded by other ritual substances into the water.

On the sacrificial ground, with mantras and heart-essences, one should worship Me— the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)— within oneself by means of offerings, and within all beings through equanimity; likewise, one should worship My form upon these altars, characterized by the conch, discus, mace, and lotus.
With a concentrated mind, one should worship Me while meditating upon Me as endowed with four arms, peaceful,
and composed. He who, being thus composed, worships Me alone through his sacrifices and meritorious works,
attains true devotion to Me and the constant remembrance of Me by serving the saintly.

O Uddhava, generally there is no means other than the yoga of devotion and the company of the virtuous; for I am indeed the ultimate goal of the saintly. Now, O delighter of the Yadus, listen to this supreme secret as you hear it.
"Though it is very secret, I shall speak it to you, for you are my servant, my well-wisher, and my friend.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Neither yoga, nor Sāṅkhya, nor even religious duty (dharma) restrains Me."
Neither Vedic study, austerity, renunciation, nor sacrifices and charitable works, nor sacrificial fees; neither vows, rituals, Vedic meters, sacred fords, nor observances and restraints—
association with the virtuous alone secures Me, for it removes attachment to everything else.
Indeed, by association with the virtuous, the Daityas, Yātudhānas, beasts, birds,
Gandharvas, Apsarases, Nāgas, Siddhas, Cāraṇas, Guhyakas,
Vidyādharas, humans, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, women, and those of the lowest castes [are all purified].
In each successive age, many of *rajasic* and *tamasic* nature have attained My state, such as the son of Tvaṣṭṛ, Kāyādhava, and others;
Vṛṣaparvan, Bali, Bāṇa, Maya, and Vibhīṣaṇa.
Sugrīva, Hanumān, the bear, Gaja, the vulture, Vaṇikpatha, the hunter, Kubjā, the cowherd women in Vraja, the wives of the sacrificers, and others—
none of them had studied the collection of the Vedas, nor had they served the most exalted sages.
Those who have not performed austerities through vows have reached me simply by association with me. Indeed, by pure devotion alone, the cowherd women, the cows, the trees, the deer,
and others— beings of deluded intellect as well as the serpents and the perfected ones— have easily attained me.
Even one who strives through yoga, Sāṅkhya, charity, vows, austerity, sacrifice, exposition, Vedic study, and renunciation might not attain Him;
yet those whose hearts were devoted to Me when I was led to Mathurā along with Rāma by the son of Śvaphalka [attained Him].

Due to their deep-seated love, they perceived no other remedy for the intense anguish of separation from Me; those various nights were spent by them as if they were half a moment when they were with Me, their dearest one, in the realm of Vṛndāvana, yet when deprived of Me, O dear friend, those same nights became equal to a kalpa.

With their minds bound by attachment to Me, they did not perceive themselves, nor Me, nor this world; just as sages in deep meditation do not perceive name and form when they have entered the waters of the ocean.
Those women, desiring Me, regarded Me as a lover, for they did not know My true nature.
By hundreds of thousands, they have attained Me, the Supreme Brahman, through [the cessation of] attachment.
Therefore, O Uddhava, casting aside both injunction and counter-injunction,
as well as engagement and withdrawal, and even what is yet to be heard and what has already been heard.
"Come to Me alone as your sole refuge, the Self of all embodied beings, with the realization that I am the Self of all; thus you shall be free from fear from every quarter.
Śrī Uddhava said:
O Lord of the lords of yoga, this doubt that has arisen within me as I listen to Your words does not subside, even though it resides in my own self; by this, my mind is bewildered.
The Blessed Lord said:

This very *jīva*, born from the cavity [of the heart], has entered the cave [of the heart] with the resonance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*); having assumed a subtle form consisting of mind, it becomes gross through its measures (*mātrā*), accents (*svara*), and phonemes (*varṇa*). Just as fire, the companion of the wind in the sky, when wood is vigorously churned, becomes heat.
"The minute atom grows by means of the oblation; even so, this manifestation of mine is speech.
Thus [arise] speech, action, movement, excretion, smell, taste, sight, touch, and hearing;
as well as volition, discernment, and egoism—the thread [of the subtle body], which is a transformation of the qualities of passion, goodness, and darkness.

For this individual soul (jīva), threefold, born from the lotus-womb, unmanifest, and one, is primordial by age; though its powers are distinct, it appears as if manifold, just as seeds do when they reach the womb [of the soil]. In Him this entire universe is woven like warp and woof, just as a cloth rests upon the expansion of its threads.

This ancient tree of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), whose nature is action (*karman*), produces two kinds of flowers and fruits. It has two seeds, a hundred roots, three stalks, five trunks, and yields five kinds of sap.
It has eleven branches, two nests for birds, three layers of bark, and two fruits; it is pervaded by the sun.
Vultures and village-dwellers eat one fruit of this tree, while forest-dwellers eat another;
the swans [eat yet another]. He who knows that which is one yet manifold, consisting of illusion (*māyā*) and worshipped through rituals—he truly knows the Veda.
Thus, by means of service to the guru and singular devotion, the wise man, with the sharpened axe of knowledge, [cuts down the tree of worldly existence].
Having carefully severed the seat of the individual soul and having thus unified yourself with the Self, then cast aside your weapon.
The Blessed Lord said:
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities of the intellect (buddhi), and not of the Self (ātman).
One should destroy the other two [modes] by means of goodness (*sattva*), and indeed, one should destroy goodness itself by means of goodness.
From increased goodness, there arises in a person dharma characterized by devotion to Me; through the practice of goodness, goodness increases, and from that, dharma proceeds.
Dharma, which increases the quality of goodness (sattva), destroys passion (rajas) and ignorance (tamas);
when these two are destroyed, unrighteousness (adharma), which is rooted in them, quickly perishes.
[The factors determining the nature of action are: scripture, water, progeny, place, time, and birth.
Meditation, mantra, and ritual purification—these ten are the causes of the modes of nature.
Among these, whatever the elders proclaim as being characterized by goodness (sāttvika), that is indeed so;
whatever they censure as characterized by darkness (tāmasa), that is so; and whatever they disregard as characterized by passion (rājasa), that is so.
A person should cultivate only those things that are characterized by goodness (*sāttvika*) for the sake of increasing their own goodness.
From that arises righteousness, from that knowledge, until there is the removal of all forgetfulness.
Just as fire produced by the friction of bamboo stalks is extinguished after burning up that forest, so too does the fire of ignorance subside.
Thus, the body born of the transformation of the *guṇas*, along with its activities, comes to rest.
Śrī Uddhava said:
Mortals generally perceive sense objects as the very seat of calamities.
"Nevertheless, O Kṛṣṇa, they still eat; how is that possible, like dogs, donkeys, and pigs?
The Blessed Lord said:
"The notion 'I am [the body]' is a perverted cognition in the heart of one who is heedless."
From that, the terrible *rajas* rises up, and from it arises the *vaikārika* mind.
For the mind joined with *rajas*, there is conceptualization accompanied by mental constructs (*savikalpaka-saṅkalpa*).
Then, from meditation upon the qualities (*guṇa-dhyāna*), desire becomes unbearable for the one of wicked intellect.

One who has not conquered his senses and is under the sway of desire performs actions that result in suffering, being utterly deluded by the force of passion (*rajas*). Even a learned man, when his intellect is distracted by *rajas* and *tamas*, [acts in this way] once again.
Undertaking yoga with an unwearied mind, perceiving faults [in worldly objects], one does not become attached; remaining vigilant, one should practice while gradually fixing the mind upon Me,
without despondency, at the proper times, having mastered the breath and the posture.
"This much alone has been taught as yoga by my disciples, Sanaka and the others:
how the mind, withdrawn from all directions, is to be directly absorbed in Me.
Śrī Uddhava said:
"O Keśava, I desire to know that form in which you instructed Sanaka and the others in yoga. The Blessed Lord said:
The sons of Hiraṇyagarbha, Sanaka and the others, who were born of his mind,
questioned their father regarding the subtle and exclusive path of yoga.
Sanaka and the others said:
"O Lord, the mind enters into the modes of nature, and the modes enter into the mind.
How can there be a mutual relinquishing of these two for one who desires liberation and wishes to cross beyond them?
The Blessed Lord said:
Thus questioned, the Great God, the Self-born, the Creator of beings,
though reflecting upon the seed of the question, could not grasp it, for his intellect was fixed on ritual action.
That Lord then thought of me, desiring to cross over to the further shore of the inquiry.
At that time, I went into his presence in the form of a swan.
Seeing me, they approached, offered obeisances at my feet, and placing Brahmā at their head, asked: "Who are you?"
O Uddhava, listen to me as I relate what I said at that time when I was questioned by those sages who were desirous of knowing the truth.
Since the reality of the Self is non-dual, such a question as this [is appropriate].
O brāhmaṇas, how could such a thing be possible for you, or what basis could there be for my speaking?
Since the five elements are identical in their essential nature, your question "Who are you? is merely a verbal fabrication and is indeed meaningless.

"Understand clearly: 'I alone am that which is grasped by the mind, speech, sight, and the other senses; there is nothing other than Me. The mind enters into the modes of nature (guṇas), and living beings enter into the mind."

For the individual soul whose self is Me, both the body and the mind are composed of the modes of nature. By constantly serving the modes, the mind enters into them; yet the modes themselves arise from the mind. One should therefore abandon both, for they are My forms.
Waking, dreaming, and deep sleep are the functions of the intellect according to the modes of nature; the living entity is determined to be distinct from them by virtue of being their witness.
When this bondage of worldly existence—which bestows the functions of the modes upon the self—[is overcome...]

Established in the Fourth State (turya) within Me, one should abandon that renunciation which pertains to the mind of the modes of nature; having become dispassionate through knowledge, one established in the Fourth State should cast off the bondage created by egoism, which is the subversion of the self's true purpose, as well as all anxiety regarding worldly existence.
As long as a person’s perception of manifold objects does not cease through reasoned arguments,
the ignorant one remains as if dreaming even while awake, just like one who dreams while in a state of waking.
Because other entities besides the Self are non-existent, the distinctions created by them [are likewise unreal].

The destinies and causes of this [individual soul] are as false as the visions of one who dreams; for while awake, he experiences objects that change moment by moment through all his senses, yet perceives within his heart things corresponding to those very same objects.
In the dream state and in deep sleep, that one Lord withdraws [the senses];
through the continuity of memory, He is the witness of the functions of the three qualities and the master of the senses.
Having thus reflected upon the three states of the mind according to the qualities (guṇas), [one realizes the Self].

Having reached the certain conclusion that "these have been fashioned by my illusory power within me," sever the mental affliction of all doubt and worship Me with the sharp sword of knowledge— sharpened by inference and authoritative scripture— which cuts through the heart's core.
One should perceive this world as a delusion, a play of the mind, seen and then vanished, as fleeting as a whirling firebrand;
it is the single consciousness that appears manifold through illusion.
Dreaming is a mental construction produced by the emission of the three *guṇas*.
Therefore, withdrawing one's vision from that, with craving ceased,
one should remain silent, experiencing one’s own innate bliss, free from worldly effort.
If this [body] is perceived as a non-entity and abandoned with such an understanding,
it will not lead to further delusion until death;
for whether the perishable body is currently standing or has already fallen, it remains transient.
The perfected one does not perceive that from which he attained his true nature—
whether it has departed due to destiny or returned by the power of destiny—
just as one blinded by the intoxication of wine does not notice a garment that has been put on.

Even the body, subject to destiny, remains under the influence of its own originating karma until the end; however, one who has ascended to the yoga of samādhi perceives that very body along with its phenomenal expansion as being accompanied by the vital breath.
One who has awakened to reality no longer clings to the dream state.
O brahmins, I have thus declared to you this secret of Sāṅkhya and Yoga;
know that I have come as a sacrifice, with the desire to proclaim your dharma.
O best of the twice-born, I am the ultimate refuge of yoga, of Sāṅkhya, of truth, of righteousness, and of splendor; I am the goal of prosperity, fame, and self-restraint.
All these qualities resort to me, who am devoid of material attributes and free from all expectations.

"He is my friend, dear to me, and my very self; equanimity, non-attachment, and other such qualities are His"—thus their doubts were severed by Me. Then the sages, Sanaka and the others, having honored Me with supreme devotion, praised Me with hymns of praise.
Having been properly worshiped and praised by those supreme sages, I returned to my own abode while the Supreme Lord Brahmā looked on. Śrī Uddhava said:
O Kṛṣṇa, those who discourse on Brahman speak of many paths to the highest good;
among these, is there a predominance of optionality, or is there one primary goal?
O Lord, You have described the yoga of devotion as independent of all else.
"By casting off all attachment, by what means may the mind enter into You? The Blessed Lord said: "This speech known as the Veda was lost over time during the dissolution."
In the beginning, I proclaimed this dharma, whose essence is myself, to Brahmā;
he, in turn, proclaimed it to his first-born son, Manu.
From him, the seven great sages, headed by Bhṛgu, received it.
From those Pitṛs were born their sons: the Devas, Dānavas, Guhyakas, humans, Siddhas, Gandharvas, along with Vidyādharas and Cāraṇas;
as well as Kindevas, Kinnaras, Nāgas, Rakṣasas, Kiṃpuruṣas, and others.
They possess many natures arising from passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and ignorance (tamas),
by which living beings and likewise the lords of beings are differentiated;
indeed, according to their respective natures, the diverse speech of all flows forth.

Thus, O bull among men, the minds of human beings diverge due to the diversity of material nature; some follow traditional lineages, while others hold heretical views, their intellects deluded by my illusory energy.
Some declare that the highest good is not absolute, but depends on one's actions and inclinations;
some speak of dharma, others of fame, others of desire, truth, self-restraint, and tranquility;
others speak of self-interest, sovereignty, renunciation, or the enjoyment of pleasures.
Some [practice] sacrifice, austerity, charity, vows, observances, and restraints;
yet their worlds, fashioned by karma, have both a beginning and an end.
They result in suffering, culminate in darkness, and are trivial, dull, and filled with grief.
O members of the assembly, for one who has offered his self to Me, who is indifferent to everything else,
and who finds happiness through Me by means of the self— how could such happiness belong to those whose minds are fixed on sense objects?
For one who possesses nothing, who is self-controlled, tranquil, and even-minded;
For one whose mind is satisfied by Me, all directions are filled with happiness;
there is no need for the station of Brahmā, nor the abode of Mahendra,
nor sovereignty over the entire earth, nor lordship over the netherworlds.
One who has dedicated their self to Me does not desire the perfections of yoga or even liberation from rebirth as anything other than Me.
Neither the Self-born Brahmā nor Śaṅkara is as dear to Me as he.

Neither Saṅkarṣaṇa, nor Śrī, nor even my own self are as [dear] to me as you are. I constantly follow after that sage who is independent, peaceful, free from enmity, and possessed of equal vision, so that I may be purified by the dust of his feet.
Those great souls who possess nothing, whose minds are devoted to Me, who are peaceful and compassionate toward all living beings,
whose intellects are untouched by desires— they enjoy that bliss of Mine which arises from detachment, a state which others do not know.
Even when my devotee is assailed by sense objects, his senses remain unsubdued [by them].
Generally, one is not overcome by sense objects through mature devotion;
just as a fire with well-kindled flames reduces fuel to ashes,
O Uddhava, so does devotion directed toward Me completely consume all sins.
"O Uddhava, neither yoga, nor Sāṅkhya, nor religious duty,
nor Vedic study, nor austerity, nor renunciation achieves Me as effectively as intense devotion toward Me does.
By exclusive devotion and faith, I— the Self, beloved by the virtuous— am to be grasped."
Devotion fixed upon Me purifies even dog-cookers from their very birth;
for neither virtue endowed with truth and compassion, nor knowledge accompanied by austerity,
truly purifies the self that is devoid of devotion to Me.
How could one whose sins are to be destroyed be purified without the bristling of hair, without a melting heart, and without a stream of tears of bliss, if devoid of devotion?
He whose speech is faltering, whose mind melts, who weeps incessantly, and who sometimes laughs— [he is truly purified].

Free from shame, he sings aloud and dances; endowed with devotion to me, he purifies the world. Just as gold, when smelted by fire, casts off its impurity and regains its own natural form, so too the self, having shaken off the latent impressions of karma through the yoga of devotion to me, then attains me.
To the very extent that this self is cleansed by hearing and reciting my meritorious verses,
to that same extent one perceives the subtle reality, just as an eye treated with collyrium sees clearly.
However, the mind of one who meditates upon sense objects becomes attached to those very objects.

The mind of one who remembers Me is dissolved in Me alone. Therefore, abandoning the contemplation of the unreal— such as dreams and mental fantasies— fix your mind on Me, cultivated through the state of being absorbed in My nature.
Having abandoned from afar the company of women and those attached to women, the self-possessed man,
sitting in a secure and secluded place, should meditate upon Me without weariness. For him,
there will not be such suffering or bondage as that which arises from attachment to others.
"Just as [bondage arises] for a man from association with a woman, and likewise from association with those who associate with her.
Śrī Uddhava said:
"O lotus-eyed one, in what manner, of what kind, or of what nature You are..."
"One who desires liberation should meditate upon this; you ought to describe this meditation to me.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Seated on a level seat, with the body held straight and at ease..."
Placing his hands in his lap and fixing his gaze on the tip of his own nose,
he should purify the path of the breath through inhalation (*pūraka*), retention (*kumbhaka*), and exhalation (*recaka*);
having conquered the senses, he should practice these gradually, even in reverse order.

Having projected the uninterrupted *oṃkāra*— like the sound of a bell or a lotus fiber— into the heart by means of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one should then cause that very sound to enter back into it.
In this way, one should practice the vital breath itself in conjunction with the *praṇava*.
Having mastered his breath, for less than a month he should perform the ritual three times a day tenfold; then,

meditating upon the lotus of the heart situated within— the eight-petaled lotus with its stalk pointing upward and its face downward— now turned upward, fully blossomed, and complete with its pericarp.
One should place the Sun, Moon, and Fire within the pericarp, each one higher than the last;
in the midst of the fire, one should contemplate this auspicious form of Mine for meditation—
equanimous, serene, with a beautiful face and four long, graceful arms.
With a very charming and beautiful neck, lovely cheeks, and a pure smile; with shimmering makara-shaped earrings set level upon his ears;
clad in golden garments, dark as a rain cloud, and the abode of the beauty of the Śrīvatsa mark.

Adorned with the conch, discus, mace, lotus, and a forest garland; His feet shining with anklets and endowed with the luster of the *kaustubha* gem; Possessing a radiant crown, bracelets, a waist-string, and armlets.
One should meditate upon Him who is beautiful in every limb, heart-stealing, with a gracious countenance and a pleasant gaze, and exceedingly delicate, fixing the mind on all His limbs;
having withdrawn the senses from their objects by means of the mind, one should fix that mind [upon Him].
With the intellect as his charioteer, the steadfast one should lead [the chariot] toward Me in every way;
having withdrawn that all-pervading mind, he should fix it on a single point.
He should no longer think of other things, but should meditate upon My face with a beautiful smile.
There, having withdrawn the mind that has found its footing, one should fix it upon the ether;
and abandoning even that, one who has ascended to Me should not think of anything at all.
Thus, with a concentrated mind, one perceives Me alone as the Self within the self.
O Soul of all, he perceives me— the light united within the light. As the yogi thus joins his mind through this most intense meditation,
the delusion regarding material objects, knowledge, and action will quickly lead him to liberation.
The Blessed Lord said: For the yogi who has conquered the senses, who is disciplined, who has mastered his breath,
and who fixes his mind upon Me, the perfections appear.
Śrī Uddhava said:

O Acyuta, by what means of concentration (dhāraṇā), what is it, and how is perfection (siddhi) attained? How many perfections are there? Please tell me, for you are the bestower of perfection upon yogīs.
The Blessed Lord said:
Eighteen perfections have been described by those who have reached the further shore of yoga.
Of these, eight are centered on Me, while ten are causes for the material qualities.

The powers are: *aṇimā* (atomization), *mahimā* (magnification) of the body, *laghimā* (levitation), *prāpti* (attainment) through the senses, *prākāmya* (the fulfillment of desires regarding what has been heard or seen), *īśitā* (sovereignty consisting of the power to direct),
*vaśitā* (non-attachment to the *guṇas*), and *yat-kāmāvasāyitā* (the realization of whatever one wills).
O gentle one, these eight perfections of mine are considered innate:
freedom from physical distress in this body, the power of hearing and seeing from afar, the speed of thought, the ability to assume any form at will, and the power of entering the bodies of others.
Death at will; beholding the gods sporting together; the complete fulfillment of every resolve; unimpeded movement according to one's command;
knowledge of the three periods of time; freedom from the pairs of opposites; and the superknowledge of the minds of others and so forth.
The neutralization of fire, the sun, water, poison, and so forth, as well as invincibility—
these are declared to be the perfections of yogic concentration (dhāraṇā) by way of enumeration. Learn from me which perfection arises through which concentration, and in what manner it occurs.

One who concentrates the mind upon Me, the self of the subtle elements (bhūta-sūkṣma), as consisting of those subtle elements alone, attains the power of atomization (aṇimā); such is the worshiper of My subtle form. One who fixes the mind upon Me, the self of the principle of Mahat, according to its true nature, [attains the power of becoming as large as desired].
By fixing the mind upon me while delighting in the subtle atomic nature of the elements within all beings, the yogi attains greatness over each and every creature,
as well as the power of minuteness (aṇimā) and the subtlety of time.
Fixing his entire mind upon Me as the principle of "I-ness" (ahaṃ-tattva) within the Vaikārika [ego], he whose mind is fixed on Me attains the state of being the self of all the senses.
He who fixes his mind upon Me as the Great Self (mahat), the Thread-Self (sūtra), [attains the same].

One who fixes the mind upon Viṣṇu— the Lord of the three worlds, whose birth is unmanifest, and who is the embodiment of Time— attains my supreme power of will (*prākāmya*) and the sovereignty of the Great Lord (*pārameṣṭhya*). He acquires lordship (*īśitva*) over the impelling of the field (*kṣetra*) by means of the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*).
Fixing his mind upon me as Nārāyaṇa— the one called the Fourth (turīya), designated by the word "Bhagavān"— the yogi who abides in my nature shall attain mastery.
Fixing his pure mind upon me, the Brahman devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), [he attains the same].
One attains supreme bliss wherein all desire ceases;
by fixing the mind upon Me— the pure Lord of Śvetadvīpa, who consists of dharma—
a person becomes white (pure) and is freed from the six waves [of worldly existence].
When one carries the sound within the vital breath (prāṇa), which is of the nature of space, by means of the mind,
that person, having perceived it there, hears the speech of all beings;
having joined the eye with Tvaṣṭṛ, and Tvaṣṭṛ also with the eye.
Meditating upon Me there with his mind, he perceives the universe from afar; having firmly fixed his mind on Me, along with his body and its vital breath,
the self remains wherever the mind is through the power of concentration on Me.
When, having taken hold of the mind, one desires to become whatever form one wishes,
that very form of the mind shall come to be by relying on the power of my yoga. An adept entering another's body should contemplate himself as being therein.
Having abandoned the physical body, the life-force, becoming like the wind, should enter [the ether] like a bee.

Pressing the anus with the heel, one should draw the life-force up through the heart, chest, throat, and head; having led it to Brahman through the aperture of Brahmā (*brahma-randhra*), one should cast off the body.

While sporting in the pleasure gardens of the gods, he should contemplate the mode of goodness (sattva) residing within himself. Celestial women, whose very nature is the mode of goodness, approach him in celestial chariots whenever that man, devoted to Me,
conceives such a thought through his intellect.

By fixing the mind upon Me, who am Truth, one attains that very state. Indeed, the man who has attained My nature, being under the control of the Lord, cannot be thwarted by anything; his command is just like Mine.
For that yogi who possesses pure goodness through devotion to Me and who knows the practice of *dhāraṇā*,
his intellect— though encompassing the three periods of time and augmented by birth and death—
cannot destroy the sage’s body composed of yoga-power, even by fire and other such elements.
For one whose mind is pacified through union with me, just as water [supports] aquatic creatures,
he becomes invincible by meditating upon my manifestations adorned with the Śrīvatsa mark and weapons, and equipped with banners, parasols, and fans.

O sage, for the practitioner who thus meditates upon me through the concentration of yoga— being self-controlled, disciplined, and having mastered his breath— all the perfections previously described manifest in their entirety.
For one who maintains the meditation upon Me, what perfection is so difficult to attain? These obstacles are said to exist for one practicing the supreme yoga;
they are merely causes for the wasting away of time for one who is already united with Me.
Whatever perfections are attained here through birth, herbs, austerity, or mantras, one attains them all through yoga; yet one cannot reach the goal of yoga by other means.
I alone am the Lord and Master, the cause of all perfections whatsoever.
I am the goal of yoga and sāṅkhya, and the dharma of those who discourse on Brahman;
I am the inner and outer Self of all embodied beings, unobstructed. Just as the elements exist within and without other elements, so do I myself exist [within and without all things].
Śrī Uddhava said:
You are the supreme Brahman, manifest, without beginning or end, and unconditioned; you are the source of the protection, maintenance, dissolution, and origination of all beings.
[Your nature] is difficult to be known by those of undisciplined self among beings, high and low;
yet, O Blessed One, the brāhmaṇas worship you according to reality. And in whatever beings the supreme sages worship you with devotion, [there they see you].
Those who worship You attain perfection; please tell me that. O Soul of all beings, source of all beings, You move about hidden from them;
deluded by Your power, living beings do not perceive You even as You behold them.

"O Lord of Great Power, whatever manifestations exist on earth, in heaven, in the netherworld, or in the various directions—please describe those to me, for they have been experienced by You. I bow down to Your lotus feet, the source of all sacred pilgrimage sites.
The Blessed Lord said:
O best among those who know how to ask questions, thus was I questioned by Arjuna at Vinaśana while he desired to fight his rivals;
for he knew that the slaughter of kinsmen for the sake of a kingdom was censurable and unrighteous.
Then, having turned back with the worldly thought, "I am the slayer; he is slain," that tiger among men was enlightened by me through reasoning;
he then addressed me in this manner, just as you have here at the front of the battle.
I am the Self, O Uddhava, the friend and Lord of these beings;
I am all beings, as well as their maintenance, origin, and dissolution. I am the goal of those who seek a goal, and I am Time for those who reckon time.

I am also the equilibrium of the *guṇas*, and I am the innate quality within that which possesses the *guṇas*. I am the thread of all things possessing qualities, and I am the Great One among the great.
I am the individual soul (*jīva*) within even the subtlest beings, and I am the mind within those difficult to conquer.

Among the Vedas I am Hiraṇyagarbha; among mantras I am the *praṇava*; among the threefold [sacrifices] I am the *akṣara* (the syllable Om). Among letters I am the letter *a*; and among meters I am the *padas*.
Among all the gods I am Indra; and among the Vasus I am Agni, the bearer of oblations.
Among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; among the Rudras, I am Nīlalohita.
Among the Brahman-sages I am Bhṛgu; among the royal sages, I am Manu.
Among the divine sages I am Nārada; among the cows, I am the wish-fulfilling cow Havirdhānī.
Among the perfected masters I am Kapila; among birds I am Suparṇa;
among the lords of progeny I am Dakṣa; and among the ancestors I am Aryaman.
Know me, O Uddhava, to be Prahlāda, the sovereign of the Daityas and Asuras.

He appointed Soma as the lord of the constellations and medicinal herbs, Dhaneśa as the lord of the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, Airāvata as the king of the lordly elephants, Varuṇa as the sovereign of aquatic creatures,
Sūrya as the lord of those who heat and shine, and the King of Men (Manu) as the ruler of human beings.
Among horses I am Uccaiḥśravas; among metals I am gold. Among those who exercise restraint I am Yama, and among serpents I am Vāsuki.
Among the lords of the serpent-kings I am Ananta, and among horned and fanged beasts I am the king of beasts.
O sinless one, among the stages of life I am the fourth; among the social orders, I am the first.
Among sacred fords I am the flowing Gaṅgā; among bodies of water, I am the ocean. Among weapons I am the bow; among archers, I am the destroyer of Tripura.
Among the sacrificial hearths I am Meru; among the mountain ranges I am the Himalaya.
Among the lords of the forest I am the Aśvattha tree; among medicinal herbs I am barley.
Among the family priests I am Vasiṣṭha; among those most devoted to Brahman I am Bṛhaspati.
Among all generals, I am Skanda; among the unborn lords, I am the Lord Brahmā.
Among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice to Brahman; among vows, I am non-violence.
Among the pure, I am the pure one—the self of wind, fire, sun, water, and speech.
Among those who practice yoga, I am the restraint of the self; among those seeking victory, I am the mantra.
Among those skilled in logic, I am the science of inquiry (ānvīkṣikī); among those who maintain various philosophical views, I am the doctrine of manifestation (khyāti).
Among women, I am Śatarūpā; among men, I am Svāyambhuva Manu.
Among sages I am Nārāyaṇa; among celibate students, Kumāra;
among religious duties, renunciation; and among forms of security, the inward-turning of the mind. Among secrets, I am truthful silence; and among couples, I am the unborn Aja.
Among the unblinking gods, I am the year; among the seasons, Madhu and Mādhava;
among the months, I am Mārgaśīrṣa; and likewise, among the lunar mansions, I am Abhijit.
Among the ages, I am Kṛta; and among the wise, I am Devala and Asita.

Among the Vyāsas I am Dvaipāyana, and among poets I am the self-possessed Kāvya; among the Blessed Lords I am Vāsudeva, and among the devotees I am you. Among the Kiṃpuruṣas I am Hanumān, and among the Vidyādharas I am Sudarśana.
Among gems, I am the ruby; among beautiful things, I am the lotus bud. Among types of *darbha* grass, I am the *kuśa*; among sacrificial offerings, I am the clarified butter from cows.
Among those who strive for success, I am prosperity; among gamblers, I am the deceptive throw of the dice.
I am the forbearance of the forbearing, and I am the goodness of the virtuous. Know me to be the vigor, the endurance, and the strength of the powerful; I am the action of the Sātvatas.
Among the nine forms of the Sātvatas, I am the supreme primordial form.
Among the Gandharvas and Apsarases, I am Viśvāvasu and Pūrvacitti;
among the mountains, I am stability; and of the earth, I am its mere fragrance. Among the waters, I am their supreme taste; and among the most brilliant things, I am fire.
I am the radiance of the sun, moon, and stars; I am the sound beyond the ether.
Among those devoted to Brahman, I am Bali; among heroes, I am Arjuna.
I am indeed the maintenance, the origin, and the dissolution of all beings.
I am the movement, speech, excretion, grasping, and the characteristics of pleasure and touch; I am tasting, hearing, and smelling—the sense-faculty of all the senses.
I am earth, wind, ether, water, light, and the Great Principle (mahat).
The transformation, the person (puruṣa), the unmanifest (avyakta), passion (rajas), goodness (sattva), and darkness (tamas)—
this is my enumeration, this is knowledge, the ascertainment of reality, [existing] without me as the Lord, the individual soul (jīva), the quality (guṇa), or the possessor of qualities (guṇin).
Even with my entire being and in every respect, no limit to my existence can be found anywhere.
I might, over time, count the atoms of the universe,
but I cannot likewise enumerate my own manifestations as I create millions of cosmic eggs.
Splendor, beauty, fame, sovereignty, modesty, renunciation, good fortune, fortune,
heroism, forbearance, and wisdom— wherever these are found, there is a portion of Me.
All these manifestations of Yours have thus been described in brief.
These are merely transformations of the mind, just as they are designated by speech.
Restrain your speech, restrain your mind, restrain your vital breaths and your senses;
restrain the self by means of the self, so that you no longer wander upon the path of worldly existence.
Indeed, for that ascetic who does not properly restrain his speech and mind through his intellect,
his vows, austerity, and charity flow away like water from an unbaked clay pot.
Therefore, one who has me as his supreme goal should restrain his speech, mind, and vital breaths.
"By means of an intellect joined with devotion to me, one then attains completion.
Śrī Uddhava said:
"That dharma characterized by devotion to you, which was previously described by you,"

O lotus-eyed one, you ought to explain to me how devotion to you may arise for all human beings— even for those belonging to the various social classes and stages of life who follow their respective duties— through the performance of their own specific dharma.
O mighty-armed Lord, O Mādhava, that supreme dharma which You formerly proclaimed to Brahmā while in the form of a swan— that very same dharma,
O crusher of enemies, has now [returned] after a very long time.

O Acyuta, in the mortal world, there will likely be no other than you who has been previously instructed [in this]— no one else on earth who is the speaker, the performer, and the protector of dharma—
even in the assembly of Brahmā where the personified arts reside.
O Madhusūdana, O Lord, when you— the creator, protector, and expounder—
have departed from the surface of the earth, who will proclaim that which has been lost? Therefore,
O Knower of all duties, our duty, characterized by devotion to you, [is at stake].
"O Lord, describe to me how and for whom each [dharma] is prescribed.
Śrī Śuka said:
Thus questioned by his chief servant, the Blessed Lord Hari—
Being pleased, for the welfare of mortals, he spoke of the eternal duties.
The Blessed Lord said:
This question of yours is righteous and brings about the supreme good for human beings.

O Uddhava, learn from me concerning those who follow the conduct of their respective social classes (varṇa) and stages of life (āśrama). In the beginning, during the Kṛta-yuga, the class of men was known as *haṃsa*;
because all subjects were by nature fulfilled in their duties, they know that period as the Kṛta-yuga.
In the beginning, the Veda was the syllable *praṇava* alone; I myself am Dharma, assuming the form of a bull.

Those established in austerity, freed from all taints, worship Me as the *haṃsa*. O highly fortunate one, at the commencement of the Tretā age, the threefold Veda (*trayī*) emerged from My heart as My vital breaths.
From that [union] knowledge appeared, and I was its threefold sacrifice (*tri-vṛn makha*).
From the Vairāja Puruṣa were born the Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras, born from his mouth, arms, thighs, and feet,
who are characterized by their respective natures and conduct.
The householder’s stage of life is from my hips; celibacy is from my heart; dwelling in the forest is from my chest; and renunciation is situated upon my head.
These [stages] for the social classes and the stages of life follow the land of one's birth.
The dispositions of men range from the lowest of the low to the highest of the high.
Tranquility, self-control, austerity, purity, contentment, forbearance, uprightness,
devotion to Me, compassion, and truthfulness— these, indeed, are the dispositions of those whose nature is Brahman.
Splendor, strength, fortitude, heroism, endurance, magnanimity, exertion,
stability, devotion to Brahman, and sovereignty— these are the inherent qualities of the Kṣatriya.
Furthermore, faith in the scriptures, dedication to charity, freedom from hypocrisy, and service to Brahman are also [Kṣatriya qualities].

Discontent with the accumulation of wealth—these are the natural tendencies of the Vaiśya; however, the natural tendencies of the Śūdra are as follows: service to the twice-born, cows, and the gods without guile, and contentment with whatever is obtained therein.
Impurity, falsehood, theft, atheism, and futile quarreling;
lust, anger, and thirst—these are the characteristics of those who belong to the lowest classes.
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, and freedom from lust, anger, and greed [are the virtues of the virtuous].
And this duty, which consists of the desire for the welfare and happiness of all beings, pertains to all social classes (varṇas).
Having obtained his second birth according to the prescribed sequence through the rite of initiation (upanayana),
the twice-born, dwelling in the teacher’s household and being self-controlled, should study the Veda when summoned.
Wearing a girdle, deerskin, staff, rosary, sacred thread, and water-pot,
with matted hair, unwashed garments, and an unstained seat, he carried kusha grass;
he remained restrained in speech during bathing, eating, fire-offerings, and the recitation of prayers.
One who observes the vow of Brahman should not cut his nails or the hair of his armpits or private parts, nor should he ever intentionally discharge semen.
If he should discharge it, he must immerse himself in water and, while restraining his breath, recite the three-footed Gāyatrī mantra.
Pure and composed, one should worship with self-restraint the two twilights while chanting prayers, honoring the fire, the sun, the teacher, cows, brahmins, gurus, elders, and the gods.
One should recognize the teacher as Myself and never treat him with disrespect.
One should not find fault with him, thinking him to be a mere mortal, for he is the Guru who embodies all the gods.
Having brought alms in the evening and in the morning, one should offer them to him;
and whatever else is permitted, one should consume it while remaining self-controlled.
Desiring to hear [the teachings], he should always attend upon the teacher like a servant,
remaining neither too far away while standing, sitting, traveling, or lying down, with his palms joined in reverence.
Living in the teacher’s household in this manner, he should dwell there, free from worldly enjoyments.
As long as he maintains his vow without interruption, his study of the Veda is completed; if, desiring to ascend to the world of the Vedas— the realm of Brahman—
he is one who has undertaken the great vow (*bṛhad-vrata*), he should offer his body to the guru for the sake of his own Vedic study.

One who possesses non-dual discernment should worship Me, the Supreme, within the fire, the guru, the self, and in all living beings; such a person becomes radiant with spiritual luster and free from sin.
[One should avoid] looking at, touching, conversing with, or laughing with women, and so forth.
A person who has not yet entered the householder stage should avoid passing in front of living beings engaged in sexual union.
Purification, sipping water, bathing, the twilight prayers, worship of Me,
visiting sacred fords, chanting, and the avoidance of those who are untouchable, forbidden foods, and improper conversation [are required].

O delighter of your lineage, this discipline is enjoined for all stages of life: maintaining my nature toward all beings through the restraint of mind, speech, and body. Thus, a brāhmaṇa who observes this great vow blazes like fire.
My devotee, whose latent impressions of karma have been burnt away by intense austerity and who is thus stainless,
shall thereafter— having received the sacred scriptures exactly as he desired to know them—
give the teacher his fee and, with the teacher’s permission, perform the ceremonial bath.
The best of the twice-born may enter the householder stage, retire to the forest, or renounce the world;
he may proceed from one stage of life to the next, but he should not act otherwise than with Me as his supreme goal. One who desires a household should marry a suitable wife who is beyond reproach.
But according to the sequence of age, one should approach a woman of the same caste who is younger than oneself.
Of all the twice-born, the rites of sacrifice, study, and giving are common;
however, receiving gifts, teaching, and officiating at sacrifices belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone.

Considering the acceptance of gifts to be a destroyer of austerity, luster, and fame, one who perceives faults in those two [accepting gifts and begging] should subsist by other means, such as gleaning ears of grain. For this body of a brāhmaṇa is not intended for trivial desires.

By subsisting on the practice of *śiloñcha* (gleaning grains), with a contented mind and practicing the great, stainless dharma, one whose self is offered unto Me attains peace while remaining even in the home, provided he is not overly attached. This leads to austerity and penance in this world, and to infinite happiness after death.
Those who rescue a brāhmaṇa who is sinking while devoted to Me—
I shall rescue them from their calamities before long, as a boat rescues one from the ocean.
A king should rescue all his subjects from distress, just as a father does for his children.
Just as a wise lord of elephants subdues other elephants with his own self,
so too this king, having shaken off all inauspiciousness in this world by means of a celestial chariot with the splendor of the sun, rejoices together with Indra.
A Brahmin who is sinking may cross over his distress by the occupation of a merchant, using trade goods alone; or, when overcome by calamity, he may use a sword, but never by the occupation of a dog.
A Kṣatriya, however, may live by the occupation of a Vaiśya, such as hunting, in times of distress.
Or he may act in the form of a brahmin, but never by the conduct of a dog.

A vaiśya should adopt the livelihood of a śūdra, and a śūdra the work of an artisan or a mat-maker. Once released from his difficult penance, he should not seek a livelihood through a despicable occupation.
Every day, according to one's means, one should worship the gods, sages, ancestors, and elemental spirits— who are all forms of Me— with Vedic study, *svadhā*, *svāhā*, offerings, and food,
using wealth that has come by chance or been acquired through honest means.
Without oppressing his dependents with wealth, he should perform sacrifices according to the law;
even while maintaining a family, he should not be attached to it nor become negligent. A wise man should perceive even that which is unseen as being as transitory as that which is seen.

The meeting with sons, wives, kinsmen, and friends is like the meeting of travelers; they depart with each successive body, just as a dream vanishes upon waking. Reflecting thus, one who is liberated dwells in his home like a guest.
One should not be bound by houses, being free from the sense of "mine" and free from egoism;
having worshipped Me alone through the ritual acts pertaining to the householder,
the devoted one may either remain [in that state], retire to the forest, or, if he has offspring, renounce the world entirely.

But he whose mind is attached to his home, who is distressed by the desire for children and wealth, who is devoted to women, of wretched intellect and deluded, is bound by the notions of "mine" and "I": "Alas! My parents are old; my wife is young, as are my children and grandchildren."
“Without me, how will these wretched and miserable ones live, being without a protector?
Thus, with his heart captivated by the longing for home and his intellect deluded,
this man dies while still unsatisfied and, dwelling upon them, enters the blinding darkness.
The Blessed Lord said:
Desiring to enter the forest, having entrusted his wife to his sons or taking her with him,
he should dwell peacefully in the forest during the third stage of his life.
One should provide for one's livelihood with pure wild roots, tubers, and fruits;
one should wear garments of bark, grass, leaves, or deerskins,
and one should bear the hair of the head, body hair, nails, and beard, as well as dirt, having cleansed the teeth.
One should not run, nor should one immerse oneself in water; sleeping on the bare ground at the three junctions of the day, one should perform penance:
in the summer, one should heat oneself with five fires; during the rains, enduring the downpour, one should stay in water;
and in the winter, submerged up to the neck—one who follows such conduct should thus practice austerity.

He should eat food cooked by fire or even that ripened by time; he may grind with a mortar and stone, or use his teeth as a mortar. He should personally gather everything required for his own livelihood.

One who understands the requirements of place, time, and strength should not accept food brought at an improper time; rather, one living in the forest hermitage should perform the offerings at the prescribed times with wild grains, sacrificial porridge (caru), and sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa),
but he should not sacrifice with an animal according to the Śruti injunctions.
The Agnihotra, the Darśa, and the Paurṇamāsa sacrifices were performed as before,
as well as the Cāturmāsya rites prescribed for the sage by the followers of the Vedas.
By performing such austerities, the sage became emaciated, with his veins standing out.
Having worshipped me, who am composed of austerity, one attains me from the world of the sages.
What fool other than him would employ this great austerity— which, when practiced with difficulty, leads to the supreme good— for the sake of a trivial desire?
When he is no longer capable of his religious observances due to old age and trembling has arisen within him,
he should internalize the sacred fires within himself and, with his mind fixed on Me, enter the fire.
When the worlds, which are the ripening of one's karma, have become like hells...
When dispassion arises perfectly, one who has properly laid down the sacred fires should then renounce.

Having worshipped Me according to the instructions and having given all his possessions to the officiating priest, he should enter the fires into his own vital breaths and wander forth as a mendicant, free from all expectations.

When a brāhmaṇa renounces the world, the demigods take the form of wives and other such things to create obstacles, thinking, "This man, having overcome us, will attain the Supreme. A sage should wear only a loincloth as his upper garment.
Except in times of distress, he should not set aside anything other than his staff and water-vessel;
he should place his foot down purified by sight, drink water purified by a cloth,
speak words purified by truth, and perform actions purified by the mind.
Silence, lack of exertion, and breath control are the three staffs of speech, body, and mind;
for one who does not possess these, my dear, he is no ascetic merely by means of bamboo staves.
He should wander for alms among the four social orders, avoiding those who are censurable.
He should be satisfied with whatever he obtains from seven houses without prior intention; having gone outside to a body of water and performed ritual ablutions there while restraining his speech,
he should divide the remainder of what was brought, and eat it all after it has been purified.
One should wander this earth alone, free from attachment, with senses restrained,
finding sport in the Self, delighting in the Self, self-possessed, and possessing equal vision;
taking solitude as one's secure refuge, with a heart purified by devotion to Me.
The sage should contemplate the Self as one with me without distinction;
he should investigate his own bondage and liberation through steadfastness in knowledge. Bondage is the distraction of the senses, and liberation is their restraint.

Therefore, having restrained the group of six [internal enemies], the sage should move about with the disposition of being Mine, detached from petty desires and having attained great happiness within the Self. He should wander, entering cities, villages, cow-pens, and caravans for the purpose of begging alms.

One should frequently practice begging for alms in the regions of the earth that abound with holy places, rivers, mountains, forests, and hermitages, specifically at the sites of the forest-dweller’s stage of life (*vānaprasthāśrama*).
Thus purified in essence and free from delusion, one quickly attains perfection through the food of roots and fruits.
One should not perceive this visible world as a substantial reality, for it perishes;
with an unattached mind, one should desist from all that is desired here and in the hereafter. This world, which is composed of mind, speech, and breath, exists within the Self.
Realizing through reasoning that "all is illusion," one who is established in the Self should abandon that [world] and not remember it.
Whether established in knowledge, detached, or a devotee of Mine who has no expectations,
having abandoned the stages of life along with their emblems, he should wander beyond the scope of prescribed rules.
The wise man should play like a child, the skillful one should act like a fool,
the learned man should speak like a madman, and he who knows the scriptures should follow the conduct of a cowherd.
He should not be devoted to the literal recitations of the Vedas, nor should he be a heretic or a mere rationalist.
In dry disputation and debate, one should not take recourse in any partisan position.
A wise person should not be agitated by people, nor should he cause agitation among people. He should endure harsh words and should not despise anyone.
One should not harbor enmity toward anyone on account of the body, as if toward a sacrificial animal;
for the Supreme Self alone is present within all beings and within the individual self,
just as the moon is reflected in many vessels of water, and all beings are of one essence.
One should not despair if food is not obtained at various times, nor should one rejoice upon obtaining it; being steadfast, one should recognize that both outcomes are governed by destiny.
One should strive for food only for the sake of sustenance, as that is what maintains life.

By that [discipline], reality is contemplated; having realized it, one is liberated. A sage should eat whatever food comes to him by chance, whether it be excellent or otherwise; likewise, he should accept whatever clothing and bedding are obtained.
The wise man should perform purification, sipping water, and bathing not out of ritual injunction, nor should he observe other restrictive rules, just as I, the Lord, act with ease;
for in him there is no longer the notion of dualistic discrimination, which has been destroyed by my vision.

Until the end of the body, one may occasionally attain renown; thereafter, having become weary of desires that result in suffering, the self-possessed person who has learned my dharma should approach a sage as his guru.

A devoted disciple, full of faith and free from malice, should serve with reverence until he realizes Brahman as Me alone, his Guru. But he whose six internal enemies are unsubdued and whose charioteer is the wild senses—
Devoid of knowledge and detachment, he lives off the triple staff; he denies the gods, the Self abiding within himself, and Me as well— thus, as a destroyer of dharma whose impurities are undigested,
he is deprived of both this world and the next.

The duty of the mendicant is tranquility, non-violence, austerity, and spiritual inquiry; that of the forest-dweller is residence in the woods; that of the householder is the protection and worship of living beings; and that of the twice-born student is service to the teacher.
Celibacy, austerity, purity, contentment, and friendliness toward all beings [are the duties of the student].
Even for a householder who approaches his wife during her season, my worship is present in all [actions].
Thus, he who constantly worships me through his own duty, being devoted to no other,
and who perceives my presence in all beings, attains firm devotion to me.
"O Uddhava, he who approaches Me— the Great Lord of all worlds,
the Brahman who is the cause of the origin and dissolution of all things— by means of unwavering devotion, has his being purified by his own duty and has fully realized My state."
Endowed with both theoretical knowledge (jñāna) and realized wisdom (vijñāna), he attains Me before long.
This duty, characterized by proper conduct, belongs to those following the system of social classes and stages of life;
when united with devotion to Me, it alone brings about the supreme good.
O virtuous one, that which you asked me has been explained to you:
how a devotee, united with his own duty, may attain Me, the Supreme.
The Blessed Lord said:
He who is endowed with learning and sacred scripture, who possesses self-control, and who does not rely on mere inference—
having realized that this world is nothing but me, he should surrender his knowledge into me.
To the man of knowledge, however, I alone am the desired object, the goal, and the accepted motive.
Both heaven and liberation—no other object is as dear to me as I am.
Those perfected in theoretical and realized knowledge know my supreme state;
therefore, the man of knowledge is dearest to me, for by means of that knowledge he sustains me.
Austerity, pilgrimage, chanting, charity, and other purifying acts are not capable of producing that perfection which is achieved by even a fraction of knowledge. Therefore,
O Uddhava, knowing your own self to be endowed with knowledge, [attain liberation].

Endowed with both theoretical knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*), worship Me with a spirit of devotion. Having worshipped Me— the Lord of all sacrifices— within the self by means of the sacrifice of *jñāna* and *vijñāna*, the sages have indeed attained perfection.
O Uddhava, those threefold transformations that resort to You do not enter into Your illusory power (māyā) during the periods of creation or dissolution;
how then could birth and the other states belong to You, who are beyond them?
"That which exists at the beginning and at the end of the non-existent, that alone exists in the middle.
Śrī Uddhava said:
"This ancient knowledge is pure, vast, and endowed with dispassion and realized wisdom."
O Lord of the universe, O you whose form is the universe, tell me of the yoga of devotion to you, which is sought after by the great;
for I, struck by the threefold miseries and scorched on the terrible path of worldly existence, O Lord,
see no other refuge than the pair of your feet, which are like a royal umbrella raining down nectar.

"O Great-Souled One, please lift up with compassion this person who has fallen into this pit, bitten by the black serpent of craving for petty pleasures; sprinkle him with words that lead to liberation. The Blessed Lord said:

In this manner, in former times, King Ajātaśatru, overwhelmed by the death of his kinsmen after the Bharata war had ended, questioned Bhīṣma— the best among the upholders of dharma— in the presence of all of us as we listened.
Having heard many duties, he subsequently inquired about the duties pertaining to liberation;
those I shall declare to you as they were heard from the sacrifice of Devavrata,
augmented by knowledge, detachment, realized wisdom, faith, and devotion.

That by which one indeed perceives the nine, eleven, five, and three states within all beings, or even just one among them— that, I have determined, is true knowledge. For this alone is realized wisdom, and not that by which [one perceives] through a single [state] as it truly is.

One should perceive the maintenance, origination, and dissolution of all entities composed of the three qualities (guṇas); that which is to be created follows the creator in the beginning, the end, and the middle;
and when there is a re-absorption of that [creation], whatever remains is alone real.
Scripture, perception, tradition, and inference—these four means of knowledge lead to instability due to their conceptual nature; consequently, he becomes detached from them.
Because all actions are subject to transformation, everything up to the realm of Brahmā (Viriñci) is inauspicious.
The wise man should perceive even that which is imperceptible as if it were perceived, seeing all things as transient.
O sinless one, the yoga of devotion has already been described to you who are pleased;
I shall speak again of the supreme cause of devotion to Me.
Faith in my nectar-like stories, constant chanting of my praises, complete dedication to my worship, praising me with hymns, respect for my service, and saluting me with all one's limbs.
Worshiping My devotees is superior [to all other rites]; having the mind fixed on Me toward all living beings;
moving the limbs for My sake; praising My qualities with speech;
offering the mind unto Me; and the renunciation of all desires.
The renunciation of wealth, of enjoyment, and of pleasure for my sake; whatever is sacrificed, given, offered in the fire, chanted, or whatever vow and austerity is performed for my sake—
by such duties, O Uddhava, do men offer themselves to Me.
Devotion to me arises; what other goal remains for him? When the mind is offered to the Self, peaceful and strengthened by *sattva*, one attains virtue, knowledge, dispassion, and sovereignty.
That which is offered [to the senses] wanders among the objects of the senses through the fluctuations of the mind;
know that the mind, when characterized by passion (*rajas*) and fixed upon material things, is the opposite state.
Dharma is said to be the practice of devotion to Me, and knowledge is the vision of oneness.
Non-attachment to the modes of nature, dispassion, and the lordly powers such as *aṇimā* and the rest.
Śrī Uddhava said: O taker of water, how many kinds of *yama* are declared? And what is *niyama*, O Kṛṣṇa? What is *śama* (tranquility), and what is *dama* (self-control)?
O Lord, what is endurance? What is fortitude? What is charity? What is austerity? What is heroism?

What is called truth and what is *ṛta*? What is renunciation? What is the desired wealth? O Illustrious One, what is sacrifice for a man, and what is the sacrificial fee? And what indeed is his strength?
O Keśava, what is fortune and what is gain? What is knowledge, and what is supreme modesty? What is Śrī?
What is happiness and what is indeed suffering? Who is the wise man and who is the fool?
What is the path and what is the wrong path? What is heaven and what, indeed, is hell?
"Who is a kinsman? What is a home? Who is wealthy? Who is poor?
Who is miserable? And who is a lord? O Lord of the virtuous, please answer these questions of mine, as well as their opposites. The Blessed Lord said:
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, non-attachment, modesty, lack of hoarding, faith in the scriptures, celibacy, silence, steadiness, forgiveness, fearlessness,
purity, chanting, austerity, fire-offerings, faith, hospitality, and worship of Me.
Pilgrimage to sacred fords, desire for the welfare of others, contentment, and service to the teacher—
