these twelve, O dear one, are recorded as the *yamas* and *niyamas* for both [paths].
When practiced by men, they indeed yield all desires according to one's wish.

Peace (*śama*) is the steadiness of the intellect in Me; self-control (*dama*) is the restraint of the senses; endurance (*titikṣā*) is the patient acceptance of suffering; and fortitude (*dhṛti*) is the conquest of the tongue and the genitals. Renouncing the rod of punishment is the supreme gift, and the renunciation of desire is known as austerity (*tapas*).

Victory over one's own nature, heroism, truthfulness, and equanimity; furthermore, speech that is pleasant and truthful has been proclaimed by the poets. Freedom from attachment to actions is called purity, while renunciation is termed *tyāga*.
For men, dharma is their desired wealth; I, the most worshipful Lord, am the sacrifice;
the instruction of knowledge is the sacrificial fee; and breath control is the supreme strength. My divine nature is my fortune; and devotion to me is the highest gain.
In the self that is knowledge, there is the sublation of duality, freedom from loathing, modesty regarding improper acts,
prosperity, the qualities such as detachment, and happiness which is the transcendence of both suffering and pleasure;
suffering is the longing for sensual pleasure, and the wise man is one who knows the nature of bondage and liberation.

O friend, the foolish person is one who possesses the notion of "I" regarding the body and so forth; the path is said to be my scripture (the Vedas), while the wrong path is mental distraction. Heaven is the arising of the quality of goodness (sattva), and hell is the increase of darkness (tamas). I am your kinsman and your teacher.
The human body is the house; indeed, one who is rich in virtuous qualities is called wealthy.

But he who is dissatisfied is poor, and he who has no control over his senses is a wretch. One whose intellect is unattached to the modes of nature is a master, while attachment to those modes is the opposite.
O Uddhava, all these questions of yours have been thoroughly explained.
What is the use of further description? The defining characteristic of both virtue and vice is this:
perceiving vice as virtue is a fault, whereas freedom from both is the true quality.
Śrī Uddhava said:
O lotus-eyed Lord, your scripture consists of injunctions and prohibitions;
it considers both the merit and the fault of actions.

Without the perception of distinctions between qualities and defects, your word [teaches] the classification of castes and stages of life born of inverse and natural unions, as well as substances, places, ages, times, heaven, and even hell.
O Lord, how does the Veda— characterized by prohibitions and injunctions— constitute the supreme good for men, and serve as the eye for the ancestors, the gods, and human beings? Furthermore,
O Lord, it provides guidance regarding the unperceived goal, as well as the means for its attainment.

"The perception of distinctions between qualities and defects arises from your study of the Vedas, for it does not exist inherently; and the censure of such distinctions through the Veda is likewise an illusion.
Thus spoke the Blessed Lord.
I have declared three types of yoga for the sake of securing the ultimate welfare of human beings:
knowledge, action, and devotion; there is no other means anywhere.
Among these, the yoga of knowledge is for renunciants who are weary of worldly activities.
For those whose minds are not despondent regarding these [worldly objects] but who are seekers of sense-gratification, there is indeed the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*).
However, for that man who has developed faith in my stories and other such matters by chance,
neither despondent nor overly attached, the yoga of devotion (*bhakti-yoga*) bestows perfection upon him.

One should perform ritual actions as long as one does not become weary of them, or until faith arises for hearing My stories and so forth. O Uddhava, remaining steadfast in one's own duty, one should sacrifice with sacrifices, free from desire for rewards.
One who abides by his own duty in this world— sinless and pure— does not go to heaven or hell provided he performs no other [forbidden] action;
such a person attains either purified knowledge or devotion to Me by chance.
Even those in heaven and likewise those in hell desire this world;
it is the means for achieving both through knowledge and devotion, yet it is not achieved by those lacking them.
A wise man should not long for the path of heaven nor for that of hell.
One should not desire this world, for through the obsession with the body one becomes negligent.
Knowing this, before death, one should strive for liberation; being vigilant and understanding that even this mortal life bestows the attainment of the supreme goal.
Just as a bird, seeing a tree upon which it has built its nest being cut down by these Yamas, abandons its own home and goes to a place of safety free from desire;
so too, perceiving that one's lifespan is being cut away day and night, one trembles with fear.
Free from attachment and having realized the Supreme, one becomes effortless and attains peace.
This human body— the first vessel that is both easily obtained and exceedingly difficult to find—
is a well-constructed boat with the Guru as its helmsman.
If a person does not cross the ocean of worldly existence when it is impelled by me, acting as a favorable wind, that man is a destroyer of his own self.
This occurs when one has become despondent with worldly undertakings, is free from attachment, and has restrained the senses.
Through practice, the yogi should hold his own mind steady.
When the mind being held is wandering and unstable like a runaway horse, he should,
with vigilance, bring it under his own control by means of the appropriate method.
One who has conquered the vital breaths and the senses should not allow the movement of the mind to wander;
with an intellect endowed with purity (*sattva*), one should bring the mind under the control of the Self.
This is indeed remembered as the supreme yoga: the complete restraint of the mind.
Seeking to understand the heart, as one would repeatedly train a young horse,
one should meditate through Sāṅkhya upon the origin and dissolution of all states of being, both in their direct and reverse orders, until the mind becomes serene.
For a person who is disillusioned, detached, and who knows what has been taught,
the mind abandons its wickedness by reflecting upon that which has been contemplated,
through the paths of yoga such as *yama* and others, and through the science of *ānvīkṣikī*.
Or, by means of worshiping and meditating upon Me, the mind becomes fit for yoga; it should not be fixed on anything else.
If a yogi should, through negligence, perform a censurable action, he should burn away that evil solely through yoga; there is never any other way to do so.
That which is steadfastness in one’s own respective duty is proclaimed as virtue (*guṇa*).
By this [verse], a restriction has been established for actions that are impure by nature,
with the desire to cause the abandonment of attachments through the prescription of virtues and defects.
Having developed faith in my stories and becoming disillusioned with all ritual activities,
one realizes that desires consist of suffering; yet, being unable to renounce them,
one should then worship me with love, full of faith and firm resolve.
While experiencing those desires yet censuring them as resulting in future suffering,
all the desires residing in the heart of the sage— who worships Me with the previously described yoga of devotion— perish once I am established in his heart.
The knot of the heart is severed, all doubts are cut asunder,
and one's karmas are exhausted when I, the Self of all, am seen.
Therefore, for the yogi who is endowed with devotion to Me and whose very self is absorbed in Me—
In this world, neither knowledge nor detachment generally constitutes the highest good—
that which is attained through ritual acts, through austerity, through knowledge and detachment,
through yoga, through the duty of charity, or by any other such means of excellence.
My devotee attains everything directly through the yoga of devotion to me—
whether it be heaven, liberation, or my own abode— if he so desires.
Indeed, my wise and exclusive devotees, the saintly ones, desire nothing at all.
Even though they desire from Me the state of liberation (*kaivalya*)— the non-return to rebirth—
they declare that supreme detachment is the greatest good;
therefore, let there be devotion to Me by one who is free from desires and expectations.
The qualities arising from the modes of nature— whether as virtues or defects— do not affect those who are single-mindedly devoted to Me,
the saintly ones who possess even minds and have attained the state beyond the intellect.
Thus, they follow these paths ordained by Me.
They find security in My abode, which the wise know as the supreme Brahman.
The Blessed Lord said:
Those who, having abandoned these paths of Mine—which consist of devotion, knowledge, and ritual action—[fall away...]
Those who indulge in trivial desires with their fickle vital breaths continue to wander in the cycle of transmigration.
That which is steadfastness in one’s own respective duty is proclaimed as virtue (*guṇa*);
conversely, its opposite is a fault (*doṣa*). This is the certainty regarding both.

O sinless one, purity and impurity are prescribed even for objects that are otherwise identical; the qualities and defects, whether auspicious or inauspicious, are designated for the sake of determining the nature of a substance, for the purpose of legal transactions, and for the sake of sustenance.
This conduct has been shown by me to those who bear the burden of upholding dharma;
earth, water, fire, air, and ether are the five elements of all beings.
From Brahmā down to the stationary beings, all embodied beings are joined with the Self; O Uddhava,
by means of the Veda, diverse names and forms are fashioned even within the uniform elements for the sake of accomplishing their own purposes.
O best of men, for all things— whether places, times, or conditions— their merits and defects are established by Me for the purpose of regulating ritual actions. Indeed,
a place that lacks the *kṛṣṇasāra* antelope becomes unfit for Brahmins and impure.

Even if it is black antelope skin, if it comes from Sauvīra, Kīkaṭa, or an uncultivated wasteland, it is unfit for ritual use; likewise, time that is effective and full of qualities may, by its very nature or through the material substances used,
become such that action ceases because of it— that defect is known as "akarmaka" (unfit for action).
The purity and impurity of a substance are determined by the substance itself, by scriptural injunction, by refinement, by time, or by its magnitude or smallness;
or else by one's capacity or incapacity, by intelligence, or by prosperity, according to what is appropriate for oneself.
For they commit sin according to the nature of the place and circumstances,
[using] grains, wood, bones, fibers, liquids, metals, skins,
and earthen objects, through the agency of time, wind, fire, earth, and water, in various combinations.
Whatever substance removes the odor and stain of that by which one is smeared with impurity is considered to be its purifier for that long;
[this applies] through bathing, charity, austerity, state, potency, refinement, and ritual action.
Through mindfulness of Me, a twice-born person attains personal purity; being thus purified, he should perform his duties.
Thorough knowledge of the mantra, purity of action, and dedication to Me—by these six factors, righteousness (dharma) is accomplished; unrighteousness (adharma), however, arises from their opposites.
In some cases, even a merit may become a fault, and by rule, even a fault may become a merit;
the fixed definition of merit and fault merely subverts their distinction. For those who have fallen, the performance of common actions does not constitute a sin.
Innate attachment is a defect; one who lies down [in negligence] does not fall downward.
From whatever [object] one withdraws, from that one is liberated. This is the dharma of men, which brings security and removes sorrow, delusion, and fear.
From the attribution of qualities to sense objects, attachment arises for the person;
from attachment, desire for them arises; and from desire alone comes strife for men.
From strife comes unbearable anger, and that leads one further into darkness.

The pervasive consciousness of the person is swiftly swallowed by darkness; O virtuous one, deprived of that consciousness, a living being becomes as if void. Consequently, there occurs a loss of his own true purpose, like one who is unconscious or dead.
Through attachment to sense objects, one knows neither oneself nor another;
living by the life of a tree while breathing like a bellows, such a person lives in vain. This scriptural promise of rewards for men is merely a means to make them find pleasure in the highest good.
Just as medicine is prescribed with the desire to speak of what is beneficial for one's health, so it has been said: "Indeed,
from birth, mortals have minds attached to sense objects, vital breaths, and their own kin— all of which are causes of harm to the self."

How could a wise man again engage those ignorant ones— who bow down [to him], who wander on the path of suffering for their own sake, and who are entering into darkness— in [worldly affairs]? Some of evil intellect, failing to understand his resolve, [act otherwise].
Indeed, those who know the Vedas do not speak of the promise of fruit as being like a flowering tree; for those who are lustful, wretched, and greedy perceive fruit only within the flowers.
Deluded by fire and exhausted by its smoke, they do not recognize their own true world.
My dear friend, they do not know Me, who dwells within their hearts, because of this:

those who subsist on the vital breaths (the sacrificial mantras) have eyes shrouded by mist, like those performing the *uktha* and *śastra* chants. Being devoted to sense objects, they do not understand My teaching, which is beyond their perception.
If there were attachment to violence, then sacrifice would not even be an injunction. Indeed,
the wicked worship the gods, the ancestors, and the lords of beings with sacrifices involving the slaughter of animals, which they perform as a pastime out of a desire for their own pleasure.
Having conceived desires in their hearts for this unreal world— which is like a dream and pleasant only to hear— they abandon their goals like a merchant;
those established in passion, goodness, and darkness, enjoy passion, goodness, and darkness respectively.
The gods headed by Indra worship me no differently than they do the other deities;
having sacrificed to those deities here with rituals, we shall go to heaven and rejoice there.
At the end of that merit, may we be born here again as members of great households and noble lineages.
Thus, for those men whose minds are distracted by flowery speech— those who are conceited and excessively greedy— even news of Me is not pleasing to them.
These Vedas have as their subject matter Brahman and the Self, and they comprise the three divisions [of ritual, knowledge, and yoga].
The sages speak in indirect ways, for indirectness is dear to me.
The Brahman of sound is very difficult to understand; it consists of the vital breaths, the senses, and the mind.
It is infinite, shoreless, profound, and as difficult to fathom as the ocean.
Augmented by the Infinite Power of Brahman,
that [unmanifested sound] is perceived within all beings as the form of resonance, just as a spider emits thread from its heart through its mouth.
Just as a spider emits thread from its heart through its mouth, so too does He.
From space arose the resonant vital breath (*prāṇa*), together with the mind whose form is touch; the Lord, consisting of the meters and consisting of nectar, [revealed] the path of a thousand words,
adorned with the consonants (*sparśa*), vowels (*svara*), sibilants (*ūṣman*), and semivowels (*anta-stha*) manifested from the syllable *oṃ*.
He himself creates and withdraws the vast *Bṛhatī*— which is spread across diverse languages and possesses no end— by means of the meters increasing by four syllables each:
*Gāyatrī*, *Uṣṇih*, *Anuṣṭubh*, *Bṛhatī*, and *Paṅkti*.
The *triṣṭubh*, *jagatī*, *aticchandas*, *atyaṣṭi*, *atijagat*, and *virāj*—
none other than I knows the heart of this [Vedic revelation] in the world, nor what it enjoins, what it describes, or what it restates and modifies.

"He enjoins me, he describes me, and by means of conceptualization, I am negated. Such is the entire meaning of all the Vedas: having resorted to me through words that express duality, they conclude by negating mere illusion and thus become serene.
Śrī Uddhava said:
"O Lord of the Universe, O Master, how many principles (*tattva*) have been enumerated by the sages?
We have heard You speak here of nine, eleven, five, and three."
Some say there are twenty-six; others, twenty-five;
some say seven, others nine, six, four, or eleven;
some say seventeen, others sixteen, and some thirteen.
"O long-lived one, it is for the sake of explaining these very enumerations that the sages sing variously; you ought to tell this to us.
The Blessed Lord said:
"And it is fitting that the Brahmins speak thus everywhere; for what indeed is difficult to accomplish when they rely upon my own illusory power (māyā) as they speak?
This is not as you say; it is exactly as I tell you."
Such is the cause for those who dispute thus; my powers are difficult to overcome.
From the interplay of these powers arises the conceptualization that is the domain of disputants.
Even when tranquility and self-control are attained, this conceptualization persists; yet, following that [realization], the dispute subsides.
O bull among men, because the principles (tattvas) interpenetrate one another,
their enumeration in terms of priority and posteriority depends upon the speaker's intention; for even within a single principle, all the others are seen to be included.
Whether in the prior or the subsequent principle, all principles exist in every respect;
therefore, for those desiring a systematic enumeration of these [principles],
we shall accept that which is distinguished by its source and established through reasoning.

Since self-knowledge is not possible by itself for a person joined with beginningless ignorance, another who knows reality must become the giver of that knowledge. In this regard, there is not even an atom’s worth of difference between the individual soul and the Lord.
Any other conceptualization is useless; knowledge is a quality of material nature (prakṛti).
Material nature is indeed the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas); the qualities do not belong to the Self (ātman).
Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the causes of maintenance, creation, and dissolution.
In this world, *sattva* is said to be knowledge, *rajas* action, and *tamas* ignorance;
likewise, the interaction of the *guṇas*, time, inherent nature (*svabhāva*), and the *sūtra* (the thread of life);
as well as the person (*puruṣa*), primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the manifest, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), ether, and air.
I have described to you the nine principles—light, water, and earth—as well as the powers of cognition:
hearing, touch, sight, smell, and taste;
the functions of action: speech, hands, the generative organ, the anus, and the feet; and the mind, which possesses both capacities.
Sound, touch, taste, smell, and form are the categories of objects; movement, speech, excretion, and manual skill are the accomplishments of the instruments of action.
Indeed, at the beginning of creation, primordial nature (prakṛti) assumes for him the form of both effect and cause.

Through the qualities of *sattva* and the rest, the unmanifest *puruṣa* sustains [the world] and observes it. By the gaze of the *puruṣa*, the elements, undergoing transformation from the manifest, acquire vitality; united by the power of primordial nature (*prakṛti*), they create the cosmic egg.

Regarding the statement "there are only seven constituents," the objects there are five, beginning with space (ether). Knowledge, the self, and their substratum—these constitute the body, the senses, and the vital breaths.
Furthermore, regarding the statement "there are six," the elements are five and the sixth is the Supreme Person.
Joined with those [qualities] produced from Himself, He created this [universe] and entered it. Even there, the four—namely fire, water, and food (earth)—were born from His own Self;
indeed, by means of these, this world was born as the possessor of limbs (the whole).
In the enumeration of seventeen, the elements, the subtle elements, and the senses—
five of each— along with the mind and the self, are recorded as the seventeen.
Likewise, in the enumeration of sixteen, the self itself is said to be the mind.
The elements, the senses, and the five [subtle elements]—the mind and the self make thirteen.
When the self is counted as one, there are eleven; the great elements and the senses make eight, and with the primary natures (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*), they become nine. Thus it is said.

Thus, various enumerations of the principles (*tattvas*) have been made by the seers (*ṛṣis*). Since all of them are logical and possess sound reasoning, what is not beautiful [or acceptable] to the wise?
Śrī Uddhava said:
O Kṛṣṇa, although both material nature and the person are distinct from the Self, no difference between them is perceived because they depend upon one another;
for the Self is observed within material nature, and material nature likewise within the Self.

"O lotus-eyed one, O omniscient one, you ought to sever this great doubt in my heart with your words that are so skillful in logic. For knowledge comes from you for all living beings, and its loss occurs here through the power of your [māyā]."
"For you alone, O bull among men, know the course of your own *māyā*, and no other.
The Blessed Lord said:
"Material nature (*prakṛti*) and the person (*puruṣa*)—this is a conceptual distinction (*vikalpa*)."
This is the *vaikārika* creation, consisting of the intermixture of the *guṇas*.

My *māyā*, composed of the *guṇas*, O dear one, brings forth manifold conceptualizing intellects through those *guṇas*. The *vaikārika* is threefold: one is the *adhyātma*, another the *adhidaiva*, and the other the *adhibhūta*.

The eye is the form of the sun; here, in this aperture, that which is the Self (ātman) is established by itself in the ether as the mutual [correspondence] of these [senses]. That which is their other [Self], the Primordial One, is the perfection of all perfections through His own self-experience.
Thus [are] the skin and so forth, the ear and so forth, and the eye.
The tongue and other [senses], as well as the nose and others, joined with the mind—
that modification produced by the agitation of the *guṇas*, born from the *mahat* which is rooted in *pradhāna*—
is the threefold ego (*ahaṃkāra*), the cause of delusion and conceptualization, consisting of the *vaikārika*, the *tāmasa*, and the *aindriya*.
Disputes consisting of ignorance of the Self— centered on the distinctions of "it exists" and "it does not exist"—
though futile, do not cease for those whose minds have turned away from Me, their own true world.
Śrī Uddhava said:

O Lord Govinda, tell me how those whose minds are turned away from You take up and cast off various high and low bodies through their own performed actions— a process difficult to comprehend for those who lack self-realization.
"For generally in this world, even the learned are deceived; they do not truly know this.
The Blessed Lord said:
"The mind of men, consisting of past actions, is joined with the five senses."
One person goes from world to world, while another self follows after him;
contemplating objects seen or heard, the mind pursues them,
and as the mechanism of action rises and falls, memory follows suit and eventually subsides.

When, due to attachment to sense objects, a person no longer remembers the Self for any reason whatsoever, that is death— the ultimate forgetting. O Giver of Abundance, birth, however, is the realization of one's identity as the Self through total devotion.
They say that the appropriation of sense objects is like a dream or a mental fantasy;
yet, in this state, one does not remember the dream or the fantasy from before,
for there one perceives oneself as both previously existing and as something unprecedented.
Through the creation of the pathways of the senses, this threefold division appears within the Reality;

it is the cause of the distinction between the external and the internal, just as a person creates the distinction between the virtuous and the non-virtuous. For indeed, O dear one, living beings are constantly coming into existence and passing away.
Because its speed is imperceptible and it is subtle, that time is not seen, just as the movement of flames, the flow of streams, or the growth of fruits on a tree is not perceived;
in the same way, the various stages of life and other conditions of all beings are brought about by it.
Just as this lamp is but a collection of flames and this water is but a collection of currents,
so too the notion among men that "this is a person" is a false speech and a vain intellect for those whose lives are in vain.
Furthermore, this so-called "person" is born only through the seed of his own past actions.
Or, like fire joined with wood, the immortal soul appears to die through delusion.
Conception, gestation, birth, infancy, childhood, youth,
middle age, old age, and death— these are the nine stages of the body.
These various high and low bodies, consisting of mere mental constructs, another being assumes through attachment to the modes of nature; at some point, someone abandons them.
One's birth and dissolution are to be inferred from the analogy of one's own father and son.
One who is not an expert regarding the nature of things that arise and perish is characterized by duality;
whereas the wise man knows both the birth and the restraint [of the tree] through its seed and its maturation.
Just as the observer of a tree is distinct from the tree, so too is the observer of the body separate from it.
Thus, the ignorant man, failing to distinguish the Self from material nature,
becomes deluded by contact with its reality and enters into the cycle of worldly existence;
through attachment to *sattva* he attains the state of sages and gods, and through *rajas*, that of asuras and humans.
Deluded by darkness, one wanders through the states of beings and animals due to one's past actions;
just as one who watches those dancing and singing comes to imitate them,
so too, even though free from desire, one is made to imitate the qualities of the intellect upon seeing them.
Just as trees appear to move when the water is moving,
and the earth appears to spin when the eye is being whirled around;
just as the experience of objects in the mind and imagination is false.
O descendant of Daśārha, just as one sees things in a dream, so too does the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) appear to the self;
for even when the object does not exist, the cycle of transmigration does not cease,
just as one who dwells upon sense-objects incurs misfortune in a dream.
Therefore, O Uddhava, do not enjoy sense objects with your unrefined senses;
behold this conceptual delusion manifested through the failure to grasp the Self.
Whether you are insulted, humiliated, mocked, or envied by the wicked, [remain steadfast].
Whether beaten, imprisoned, deprived of his livelihood,
spat upon, urinated upon, or otherwise greatly shaken by those in authority,
one who desires his own welfare and has fallen into distress should uplift himself by his own effort.
Śrī Uddhava said:
O best among speakers, please tell me how I may understand this exactly as it is.
O Soul of the Universe, I consider this transgression against myself to be most difficult to endure; for even among the wise, O Lord, material nature is indeed more powerful,
except for those who are peaceful, devoted to Your dharma, and whose refuge is Your feet.

Śrī Bādarāyaṇi said: Thus addressed with such aspirations by Uddhava, the foremost of the devotees, Mukunda— the chief of the Dāśārhas, whose heroic deeds are worthy of being heard— honoring the words of his servant, spoke to him.
The Blessed Lord said:
O son of Bṛhaspati, there is no truly virtuous person here who is capable of composing his own mind when it has been shattered by the ill-spoken words of the wicked.
A man pierced by arrows that strike his vital organs does not suffer so much as he is tormented by the harsh arrows of the wicked lodged in his very vitals.
O Uddhava, here I shall relate a great and meritorious ancient history.

I shall describe that; listen with a well-composed mind. It was sung by a certain mendicant who had been insulted by wicked people, yet remained steadfast in mindfulness of the ripening of his own past actions.
In the land of Avanti, there was a certain twice-born man who was most wealthy in prosperity;
however, he was a miser who lived by the profession of trade, and he was lustful, greedy, and exceedingly irascible.
His kinsmen and guests were not honored by him even with a mere word.
In an empty dwelling, even his own self is neglected at the proper time due to lack of offerings; for one of evil character and miserly nature, his sons and kinsmen turn against him,
and his wife, daughters, and servants become despondent and no longer act with affection.
When he, whose wealth was merely that of a spirit, had thus fallen from both worlds and was bereft of virtue and desire, the five sharers [of sacrificial offerings] became enraged at him—
O Bṛhadbala, for his mass of merit had been dissipated by his neglect of them.
Even his wealth, acquired through great exertion and toil, met its end;
O Uddhava, his kinsmen took some, the thieves took some,
and by fate, time, or the king, the outcaste Brahmin lost the rest.
When his wealth was thus lost, he was deprived of both virtue and pleasure;
neglected by his own kinsmen, he fell into an insurmountable anxiety. As that poor man brooded thus for a long time over his lost riches, [he became emaciated].
As he was distressed, his throat choked with tears, a profound sense of renunciation arose within him.
He thought: "Alas, what misery! I have needlessly tormented myself;
this exertion was for neither dharma nor desire."
Generally, the wealth of the miserly never leads to happiness;
in this world it results in self-torment, and after death, in hell.
The fame of the illustrious is pure, as are the praiseworthy virtues of the virtuous.
Even a slight greed destroys them, just as white leprosy destroys a desirable complexion.
In the acquisition, attainment, increase, protection,
expenditure, loss, enjoyment, and toil of wealth, men experience fear, anxiety, and delusion.
Theft, violence, falsehood, hypocrisy, lust, anger, pride, intoxication,
dissension, enmity, lack of trust, rivalry, and vices—
these fifteen are considered by men to be the roots of misfortune.

Therefore, one who seeks the highest good should abandon from afar that which is called "wealth" but is actually a source of harm. Brothers, wives, fathers, and friends— who were once united in affection— are instantly turned into enemies by the loss of even a single cowrie.
For even for the sake of a very small object, these men, their anger inflamed, become agitated; they quickly abandon their rivals and, casting aside friendship, strike them down.
Having obtained this human birth—which is sought even by the immortals—and having attained the status of the foremost among the twice-born...
Those who disregard that [instruction] and destroy their own true interest go to an inauspicious destination.
Having reached this world, which is the gateway to both heaven and liberation, what mortal man would remain attached to wealth, the abode of misfortune?

One who does not share with the gods, sages, ancestors, spirits, kinsmen, and relatives who are entitled to a portion, being like a Yakṣa in his wealth, falls downward. Through the pursuit of wealth in vain, the riches, life-span, and strength of the heedless man perish.
By what means do the skillful achieve perfection? What, then, can an old man accomplish?
Why does a wise man repeatedly distress himself with the pursuit of useless objects? Surely this world is utterly deluded by the illusory power (*māyā*) of someone.
Of what use are riches or those who bestow riches, or desires or those who grant desires, or even ritual acts that yield rebirth, for one being devoured by death?
Surely Lord Hari, who embodies all the gods, must be pleased with me.

"By him I have been brought to this state; therefore, detachment is my boat. With the remainder of my allotted time, I shall wither away my own body, remaining vigilant regarding the ultimate goal of the self, should I achieve perfection within myself."
"May the gods, the lords of the three worlds, show me favor there.
In a mere moment, Khaṭvāṅga reached the world of Brahmā.
The Blessed Lord said:
Having reflected thus in his mind, that best of the twice-born from Avanti untied the knots of his heart and became a peaceful mendicant sage.
With his self, senses, and breath restrained, he wandered over this earth.

For the sake of alms, he entered cities and villages unattached and unrecognized. Seeing that aged mendicant, who appeared as a wandering ascetic, wicked people, O gentle one, humiliated him with many insults.

Some took up the triple staff (*tri-veṇu*), others a water-pot (*pātra*) and a mendicant’s bowl (*kamaṇḍalu*); some took a seat (*pīṭha*) and a rosary (*akṣa-sūtra*), while others took a patched garment (*kanthā*) and rags (*cīrāṇi*).
Having offered these, they then took back those items which had been shown to the sage.
While he was eating food obtained through alms on the riverbank,
the most wicked of men urinated and spat upon his head;
they forced him to speak while restraining his speech, and beat him if he would not speak.

Others threatened him with words, saying, "This man is a thief! Some bound him with ropes, crying out, "Bind him! Bind him! Still others, treating him with contempt, reviled him, saying, "This rogue is merely a hypocrite who uses religion as a banner."
With his wealth exhausted and abandoned by his own people, he adopted this mode of life.
Oh, how great is his strength! Steadfast like the king of mountains, he accomplishes his purpose through silence, possessing a firm resolve like a crane.
Some laughed at him, while others reviled him;
they bound him and restrained him like a pet bird.
Thus he experienced material suffering—whether caused by fate or arising from his own body.
Realizing that whatever was destined for him had come to pass,

he remained firm in his sattvic resolve and, though insulted by those lowest of men who sought to cast him down from his own duty, he sang this verse: *“Whatever is ordained for oneself must be accepted as it arrives.”* (BhP 11.23.41)
The twice-born said:
Neither this person, nor the gods, the self, the planets, karma, or time are the causes of my happiness and suffering;
the wise declare that the mind alone is the supreme cause, which sets the wheel of worldly existence in motion.
The powerful mind indeed creates the modes of nature, and from them arise various actions—
white, black, and red— from which proceed corresponding destinies.
The inactive Self, golden-hued and my friend, looks on as the mind exerts itself.

Having seized the mind as its own characteristic, one who indulges in desires becomes bound through attachment to the modes of nature. Charity, one's own duty, observances, restraints, sacred learning, ritual acts, and virtuous vows—all these have the restraint of the mind as their ultimate goal; for the supreme yoga is the concentration of the mind.

Tell me, what further duty remains for one whose mind is concentrated and perfectly tranquil? And for one whose mind is uncontrolled and perishing, what is the use of these other practices such as charity?
Indeed, all the gods have come under the control of the mind, yet the mind does not come under the control of anything else.
For Bhīṣma is indeed a god, more powerful than the strongest; he would bring him under his control, for he is the God of gods.

Without first conquering that invincible enemy of unbearable speed who pierces the vitals, some deluded people here engage in improper conflict with mortals, regarding them as friends, neutrals, or enemies.
Having grasped this body, which is merely mind, foolish-minded men think "I" and "mine";
through the delusion that "this is I" and "that is another," they wander in darkness whose shore is difficult to reach.
If people are indeed the cause of pleasure and pain, then what is the role of the self in these two, which are products of the earth?

If one bites one's own tongue with one's own teeth at some point, toward whom should one feel anger for that sensation? If the cause of suffering were the deities, what would that have to do with the Self?
When one limb strikes another limb somewhere in the body, toward which part of one's own body should a person become angry?
If the self were the cause of pleasure and pain, then what role would anything else have there? For that would be its own inherent nature.
If there is nothing other than the self, then that [external cause] must be false; why then would one become angry, and why would there be neither pleasure nor pain?
If the planets are the cause of pleasure and pain, then how can they belong to the unborn self? They belong only to those who are born.
They say that the affliction caused by the planets is actually from the planet itself; who else could the person be angry with?

If karma were the cause of pleasure and pain, then what would be the status of the self (ātman) as conscious or unconscious? The body is insentient, while this person is like the Suparṇa bird; with whom, then, could he be angry? For karma is not the root.
If time is the cause of pleasure and pain, then how can the Self be of that nature?

For heat does not belong to fire, nor does cold belong to snow; with whom could one be angry? Duality belongs to another, not to the Supreme who is beyond all others. Indeed, for this Supreme Being, who is higher than the highest, there is no coloring by duality through anything, anywhere, or in any way.

Just as I am of the nature of worldly existence (*saṃsṛti*), so too one who is awakened does not fear material beings. Having taken recourse to this state of being established in the Supreme Self— a state practiced by the ancient great seers—
I shall cross over the darkness whose further shore is difficult to reach, solely through service to the feet of Mukunda.
The Blessed Lord said:

Having become disenchanted when his wealth was lost, and being free from fatigue as he wandered the earth after having renounced the world, this sage—though thus rejected by the wicked—remained unshakable from his own duty and spoke this verse:
BhP 11.23.058.3: "Though rejected by the wicked, the sage remained unshakable from his own dharma and spoke this verse."
There is no other giver of happiness or suffering for a person than the delusion regarding one's own self;
friends, neutrals, and enemies are created by the darkness of worldly existence.
Therefore, my dear, restrain the mind with your intellect by every means possible.
One who is disciplined by fixing their mind upon Me— this is the complete summary of yoga.
He who, being composed, maintains, causes others to hear, or hears this teaching on the realization of Brahman sung by the mendicant, is never overcome by the pairs of opposites.
The Blessed Lord said:
Now I shall fully declare to you the Sāṅkhya system as determined by the ancients,
by understanding which a person may immediately abandon the delusion of dualistic conceptualization.
In the beginning, during the Kṛta-yuga, when people were skilled in discernment, there was only one undifferentiated reality, which was both knowledge and its object. That absolute,
undifferentiated state appeared as the fruit of Māyā.
The Great Reality, which is beyond the reach of speech and mind, became twofold.
Of these two, one aspect is the object, Prakṛti, which consists of both [spirit and matter];
the other aspect is the state of knowledge, which is designated as Puruṣa.

From Prakṛti, as she was being agitated by Me with the consent of Puruṣa, there arose the qualities of Tamas, Rajas, and Sattva. From these arose the Sūtra (the subtle thread), which is joined with the Mahat.

Then, from Me as I underwent transformation, there arose the delusive ego (ahaṅkāra), which is threefold: the Vaikārika, the Taijasa, and the Tāmasa. Composed of both consciousness and the unconscious, it is the cause of the subtle elements, the senses, and the mind.

From that *tanmātra* of Tamas, the objects of sense were born; from the Taijasa [Ego], the eleven deities of the senses arose; and from the Vaikṛta [Ego], they came into being. Impelled by Me, all these entities act in concert.
They produced an egg, my supreme abode; within that egg, which rested upon the waters, I came into being. From my navel arose a lotus known as the universe, and there the Self-born (Brahmā) appeared.
Endowed with austerity and through the influence of my *rajas* grace,
that Soul of the Universe created the worlds together with their guardians— the threefold realms of *bhūḥ*, *bhuvaḥ*, and *svar*.
*Svar* became the abode of the gods, and *bhuvaḥ* the station of the elemental beings.
The Lord created the world of earth for mortals and others, the realm above the three worlds for the perfected ones (siddhas), and below the earth the abode of the asuras and nāgas;
all the destinies within the three worlds are the result of actions characterized by the three qualities.

The stainless goals of yoga, austerity, and renunciation are Mahar, Jana, Tapa, and Satya; but the goal of the yoga of devotion is My own state. By Me, the Creator, whose nature is Time, this world is bound by action.
In this flow of the modes,
whether it be minute or vast, subtle or gross— whatever state of being manifests,
all of it is joined with both nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa).
That which is the beginning and the end of something is indeed its middle as well;
modification exists for the sake of conventional usage, just like [the distinctions between] things made of gold or earth.
Whatever prior state takes up [its cause] undergoes transformation into another state.
That which has neither beginning nor end is designated as Truth (Satya).
Nature (Prakṛti) is its material cause, the Supreme Person (Puruṣa) is its support, and Time (Kāla) is that which manifests the existent; these three together are indeed Brahman, and I am that.

The creation proceeds eternally in a continuous sequence of prior and subsequent stages, for the purpose of the manifestation of the qualities (guṇas), until the end of the maintenance of the world, as long as His glance [of will] persists; the Virāṭ,
being approached by me, is the one who fashions the various forms of the worlds.
The world, together with all its elements, is reduced to the state of the five gross elements; mortal beings dissolve into food, and food dissolves into grains;
the grains dissolve into the earth, and the earth dissolves into fragrance.
Smell dissolves into water, and water dissolves into its own quality, taste;
taste dissolves into light, and light dissolves into form.
Form dissolves into air, and that [air] dissolves into touch; that too dissolves into space.

The ether dissolves into its own source, the subtle element of sound; the senses dissolve into their own source, O gentle one, into the mind, which is of the nature of the *vaikārika* (sattvic) ego under the Lord.
Sound merges into the *bhūtādi* (tāmasa ego); the *bhūtādi* merges into the Great Principle (*mahat*), the sovereign.
That Great One, the most excellent of those possessing qualities, dissolves into his own qualities;
they dissolve into the Unmanifest (avyakta), and at that time, the Unmanifest dissolves into the Imperishable.
Time dissolves into the living being (jīva) composed of Māyā; the living being dissolves into the Self, who is Me, the Unborn.
The Self is absolute, established in itself, characterized by the disappearance of all dualistic constructs.
For one who investigates in this manner, how could the delusion of duality remain in the mind? It would vanish like darkness at the rising of the sun in the sky.
This method of Sāṅkhya has been declared by me, which severs the knots of doubt through the direct and indirect perspectives of the higher and the lower.
The Blessed Lord said:
O best of men, listen as I describe to you how a person comes to possess the unmixed modes of nature.
Serenity, self-restraint, forbearance, discernment, austerity, truthfulness, compassion, and mindfulness— these are the qualities of goodness (sattva).
Contentment, renunciation, lack of desire, faith, modesty, compassion, and so forth, as well as self-satisfaction;
desire, effort, pride, thirst, arrogance, longing, duality, pleasure;
intoxication, enthusiasm, fame, affection, laughter, heroism, strength, and exertion.
Anger, greed, falsehood, violence, begging, hypocrisy, fatigue, strife,
grief, delusion, despondency, distress, sleep, desire, fear, and lack of effort—
these belong respectively to the qualities of goodness (sattva), passion (rajas), and darkness (tamas).

The modes of livelihood have been described for the most part; now hear, O Uddhava, about their combination. This combination, O Uddhava, is the notion "I" and "mine," as well as the worldly activity involving the mind, the senses, the subtle elements, and the vital breaths.
When he is fully established in virtue, wealth, and pleasure—
this conjunction of the qualities brings about faith, delight, and riches— then a man finds his final fulfillment in the householder stage of life, which is characterized by active engagement.
One should abide in one's own duty, for that is the assembly of the qualities (guṇas).
One may infer a person joined with goodness (sattva) by tranquility and other such traits;
one joined with passion (rajas) by desire and the like; and one joined with darkness (tamas) by anger and the like.
When one worships Me with devotion through one's own prescribed duties, being free from desire for rewards,
one should know that person— whether male or female— to be of the nature of *sattva*.
When one worships Me through one's own prescribed duties while praying for specific blessings, [one should know them to be of the nature of *rajas*].
One should know that [the mind] characterized by passion (rajas) is the source of violence, while that characterized by ignorance (tamas) is the source of desire.

Sattva, rajas, and tamas are the qualities (guṇas) of the individual soul (jīva), but they do not belong to Me. It is from these qualities, born of the mind, that the soul becomes attached and is bound.
When the *sattva* quality overcomes the other two— being luminous, pure, and auspicious—
then a person becomes united with happiness through virtue, knowledge, and so forth.
When *tamas* overcomes *sattva*, and *rajas* overcomes attachment, differentiation, and instability...
At that time, one may be joined with suffering, with fruitive action, fame, and prosperity;
yet when one conquers passion (*rajas*), goodness (*sattva*), and the deluded darkness (*tamas*)— which are inert and lead to dissolution—
one is joined with grief and delusion, with sleep, violence, and worldly desire.
When the mind becomes serene and the senses find their rest,
when there is fearlessness in the body and non-attachment of the mind— that, know it to be *sattva*, my state.
When one acts through activity yet remains undeluded, and there is no turning back of the consciousnesses— [that is *rajas*].
"Observe that my limbs are unwell, my mind is bewildered, and these are the effects of *rajas*.
My consciousness is sinking and dissolving, incapable of perceiving objects;
my mind is lost, there is exhaustion, and that is *tamas*—understand that to be *tamas*."
When the mode of goodness (sattva) increases, the strength of the gods flourishes;
when passion (rajas) increases, that of the asuras; and when darkness (tamas) increases, O Uddhava, that of the demons.
One should know that wakefulness arises from goodness, and one should indicate sleep as arising from passion.
The fourth state, *prasvāpa*, is characterized by darkness (*tamas*) and persists throughout the other three states for living beings.
Among these, people who are Brahmins ascend higher and higher through the quality of goodness (*sattva*).
Through darkness they go lower and lower toward the very bottom, while those characterized by passion (*rajas*) move in between.
Those merged in *sattva* go to heaven; those dissolved in *rajas* go to the world of men;
but those dissolved in *tamas* go to hell, while those free from the modes (*nirguṇa*) come to Me alone.
That one's own action which is offered to Me, whether it be fruitless or of the nature of *sattva*, is *sāttvika*.
Knowledge characterized by attachment to fruits is *rājasa*; that which consists primarily of violence and the like is *tāmasa*.

Knowledge of liberation (*kaivalya*) is *sāttvika*, while that which is based on dualistic discrimination is *rājasa*. Knowledge pertaining to material nature (*prākṛta*) is *tāmasa*; but knowledge centered on Me is remembered as being beyond the modes (*nirguṇa*).
Dwelling in the forest is said to be *sāttvika*, while dwelling in a village is *rājasa*.
Dwelling in a gambling hall is *tāmasa*, but my own abode is beyond the *guṇas*. A doer who is free from attachment is *sāttvika*; one blinded by passion is known as *rājasa*.
The *tāmasa* [faith] is that which is devoid of memory and lacks the [three] qualities, yet takes refuge in Me;
the *sāttvika* faith is spiritual, while the *rājasa* faith is directed toward ritual action.
The *tāmasa* faith is that which is fixed on unrighteousness, whereas the *nirguṇa* (transcendental) faith is directed toward service to Me.
Food that is wholesome, pure, unlabored, and easily obtained is said to be *sāttvika*;
that which is most pleasing to the senses is *rājasa*; and that which causes distress and is impure is *tāmasa*.
*Sāttvika* happiness arises from the self, while *rājasa* happiness arises from sense objects.

That which arises from delusion and wretchedness is *tāmasa*; that which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*) takes refuge in Me. Indeed, substance, place, fruit, time, knowledge, the agent, faith, state, form, and final goal—all these are composed of the three *guṇas*.
O bull among men, all states of being consist of the modes of nature and are presided over by the Person (puruṣa) and the unmanifest (avyakta).
O best of men, whether seen, heard, or contemplated by the intellect,
these transmigrations of the person are bound by the activities of the modes.
O gentle one, he by whom these qualities born of the mind have been conquered through the yoga of devotion becomes established in Me and attains My own state. Therefore,
having obtained this body which is the source of theoretical and realized knowledge, [one should strive for that goal].
"Having completely shaken off attachment to the modes of nature, let the wise devote themselves to Me.
Free from attachment, the learned man, vigilant and with senses conquered, should worship Me; as a sage, he should overcome passion and ignorance by cultivating goodness."

One who is disciplined, whose intellect is tranquil, and who is indifferent to worldly objects, should conquer the mode of goodness (sattva). Thus liberated from the modes, the individual soul (jīva), having abandoned the life-force (jīva), attains Me.
When the soul is freed from the life-force and from the modes born of its latent impressions (āśaya), it is truly liberated.
Filled by Me alone as Brahman, he would move neither outside nor within.
The Blessed Lord said:
Having obtained this body which bears My characteristics, one should remain established in My dharma.
Freed from the womb of the individual soul composed of the modes of nature through steadfastness in knowledge, he attains Me, the Supreme Self, who is bliss and resides within the self;
for the modes, which consist of mere illusion, are seen as appearing while being unreal in substance.
Even while existing in this world, a person is not joined with the qualities of the material modes, which are unreal;
one should never form an attachment to the wicked who seek only the gratification of their genitals and bellies.
A follower of such a person falls into blind darkness, just like a blind man following another blind man.

The emperor Aila, of great renown, sang this verse while bewildered by separation from Urvaśī and despondent in his effort to control his grief: "O King, having abandoned himself as she departed, he ran after her like a naked madman."
Lamenting, "Stay, O wife! he followed her in distress;
unsatiated by his desires, enjoying those brief nights and years, his mind was so captivated by Urvaśī that he did not perceive them passing away nor returning again.
Aila said:
Alas! How vast is my delusion, for my mind is defiled by lust; though my neck was grasped by the Goddess, these fragments of my life were not even noticed.
"I am not one who has turned away from the Vedas, nor is the sun risen upon me by her; alas, many years have passed while I was robbed of my days!
Oh, what self-delusion is mine, by which I have been made a slave to women!"
A mere plaything for the Lord, a universal emperor and the crest-jewel of kings,
I abandoned my own self along with all its trappings like a blade of grass; and as the Goddess departed, I followed her, naked and weeping like a madman.
Whence could he have any power, splendor, or even lordship—
he who, like a donkey, was kicked by her foot as she walked away?
What is the use of knowledge, what of austerity, what of renunciation, or what of sacred learning?
"What is the use of solitary silence for one whose mind has been stolen by women?
Fie on me, a fool who considers himself a scholar, ignorant of my own true interest,
I who, having attained lordship, have been conquered by women like a bull or a donkey!"
For many series of years, as he drank the nectar from the lips of Urvaśī,
Kāma— the progenitor of his own self— was not satiated, just as fire is never sated by oblations. Who else indeed is capable of liberating a mind that has been stolen away by a wanton woman?

Except for the Lord Adhokṣaja, the master of those who delight in the Self, the great delusion residing in the mind of this evil-minded one does not depart— even though I have been awakened by the queen’s well-spoken words— because I have failed to conquer my own self.
What harm has this [body] done to us, who— like one perceiving a snake in a rope—
fail to know our true nature as observers, being those whose senses are unsubdued? Where is this filthy body, consisting of foul odors and the like, and inherently impure?
Where indeed are qualities such as cheerfulness and the like? For this superimposition is created by ignorance.
Is anything one's own among parents, wife, master, fire, dogs, or vultures? Nor is it determined what belongs to oneself or to friends.
In that impure body, which culminates in nothingness, he becomes attached;
"Oh, how beautiful is the woman's face, with its lovely nose and gentle smile!"—
yet it is merely a conglomeration of skin, flesh, blood, sinews, fat, marrow, and bone.

What difference is there between worms that delight in feces, urine, and pus, and [those who delight in women]? Nevertheless, one who understands the true goal should not become attached to women or to those devoted to them;
for the mind becomes agitated through the contact of the senses with their objects, and not otherwise.
From an object that has not been seen or heard, no mental state arises;
when one does not engage the senses with their objects, the mind becomes tranquil and still.
Therefore, one should not form attachments to women or to things pertaining to women by means of the senses.
"Even for the wise, the sixfold group of internal enemies is untrustworthy; how much more so for those like me?
Śrī Bhagavān said:
"O King, having thus sung, that god of gods abandoned the world of Urvaśī."
Having realized the Self within the self, and having understood Me, one whose delusion has been shaken off by knowledge should indeed desist from worldly activity.
Then, abandoning bad association, the wise person should devote himself to the saintly;
for it is the saintly alone who sever the mind's attachment through their instructions.
O highly fortunate one, among those saintly persons— who are free from expectations, whose minds are fixed on Me, who are tranquil, who perceive with equanimity,
and who are devoid of possessiveness, egoism, dualities, and worldly attachments—
discourses concerning Me should always be held.
For those [stories] arise for men who take delight in them, purifying their sins;
and those who listen to them, sing them, or approve of them with respect—
being devoted to Me and full of faith— they find devotion unto Me.
For the virtuous person who has attained devotion to Me— the Infinite Brahman whose nature is the experience of bliss— what else remains to be achieved?
Just as for one who approaches the divine fire, [all else is consumed].
Cold, fear, and even darkness do not reach those who serve the saintly; likewise,

for those sinking and surfacing in the terrible ocean of worldly existence, the saintly ones— who know Brahman and are peaceful— are the supreme refuge, like a sturdy boat for those drowning in the waters.
For food is the life-breath of living beings, and I am the refuge for the distressed; dharma is the wealth of men after death, while the virtuous are the protection for those who fear in this world.
The virtuous grant the eyes of wisdom, whereas the sun that has arisen provides only external vision.

The deities, his kinsmen, the virtuous, the virtuous, the Self, and even I myself— having been thus addressed by Vaitasena, Urvaśī, and others, he thereafter wandered this earth free from desire for the world, liberated from attachment, and finding delight in the Self alone.
Śrī Uddhava said:
O Lord, please explain the yoga of action (*kriyā-yoga*), which is the means of worshiping you,
by which the *sātvatas* worship you, O bull among the *sātvatas*.
The sages repeatedly declare this to be the supreme good for human beings;
it is that which was spoken by the unborn Lord from your lotus-like mouth, as taught by the venerable Nārada, Vyāsa, and the teacher Aṅgiras.
The Blessed Lord Bhava imparted this to his sons, headed by Bhṛgu, and to the Goddess;
O giver of honor, I consider this to be the most excellent of all spiritual goals for all social classes and stages of life, as well as for women and Śūdras.
"O lotus-eyed one, O Lord of the lords of the universe, please tell this— which liberates from the bondage of karma— to a devotee who is devoted to You. The Blessed Lord said:
O Uddhava, there is indeed no end to the ritualistic section (karma-kāṇḍa) which has no limit;
therefore, I shall describe it to you concisely, according to its true nature and in proper sequence. My sacrifice is of three kinds: Vedic, Tantric, and mixed.

One should worship Me according to the very procedure desired by the three [classes]. Listen to Me as I explain how a person, having attained the status of the twice-born as declared in his own Veda, should worship Me with devotion and faith.
In an image, on a sacrificial mound, in the fire, in the sun, in water, or in the heart, a twice-born person,
endowed with devotion, should worship my own guru and myself with material offerings and without guile.
First, having cleaned one's teeth, one should perform a bath for the purification of the body.

I have been enjoined by the Veda to perform the rites of twilight worship (*sandhyopāsti*) and so forth, as well as bathing with both [the prescribed substances] using mantras and the application of clay; one who is pure in intention should properly perform worship with these, which purifies all action.
An image is recorded as being of eight kinds: made of stone, wood, metal, plaster, paint, sand, mind, or gemstone.
This consecrated abode of the living soul is of two types: mobile and immobile.
In the worship of a permanent image, O Uddhava, there is neither dismissal nor invocation;
for a temporary image, there may be an option between the two, but on a sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), both should be performed.
As for bathing, it is prescribed for an image that is not plastered; otherwise, there should be mere wiping.
O Uddhava, for one who is free from deceit, My sacrifice is performed with well-known materials in images and the like;

however, for the devotee, it is indeed performed with whatever is obtained, or even through devotion alone within the heart, while the bathing and adorning of the image is most dear when performed specifically upon the arcā.
The arrangement of the principles upon a sacrificial mound, an oblation soaked in clarified butter offered into the fire,
the most beloved worship of the Sun, and water and other offerings presented with faith in water— these, even if they be mere water, are most dear to me when offered by a devotee.
Even an abundance of offerings brought by one who is not devoted does not lead to my satisfaction; how much less so [the case of] mere perfume, incense, flowers, a lamp, and food?
Being pure and having prepared the necessary materials, one should first arrange a seat with *darbha* grass.
Seated facing either the east or the north, one should chant while facing the image;

having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), one should wipe my image with the hand upon which the *nyāsa* has been performed. One should then duly prepare the water-pot and the vessel for sprinkling (*prokṣaṇīya*).
Having sprinkled the sacrificial ground for the gods, the ritual materials, and even himself with that water, he should prepare three vessels with those various materials and water.
The preceptor should prepare three vessels for the purpose of the *pādya*, *arghya*, and *ācamanīya* offerings.
One should consecrate [the clay] with the heart-mantra, the head-mantra, the *śikhā*-mantra, and the *gāyatrī*.

Then, once the *piṇḍa* has been purified by the air and fire mantras, one should meditate upon my supreme, subtle particle of life (*jīva-kalā*) residing in the heart-lotus, which is realized at the end of the *nāda* by the perfected ones (*siddhas*).

When the body has been pervaded by that [consciousness] which has become one's own self, one who is absorbed in that [Self], having performed worship, should invoke me into the image and other representations, establish me there with the assignment of limbs (*nyāsāṅga*), and worship me. One should then offer the ritual services such as water for the feet, water for sipping, and respectful offerings (*argha*).
Having fashioned for me a seat consisting of the nine principles beginning with dharma,
an eight-petaled lotus there, radiant with its pericarp and filaments—
for my attainment of both goals through both the Vedas and the Tantras.
One should worship the Sudarśana discus, the Pāñcajanya conch, the mace, the sword, the bow, the plow, the club, the Kaustubha gem, the garland, and the Śrīvatsa mark;
as well as Nanda, Sunanda, Garuḍa, Pracaṇḍa, and Caṇḍa.
One should worship Mahābala, Bala, Kumuda, and Kamudekṣaṇa, as well as Durgā, Vināyaka, Vyāsa, Viṣvaksena, one’s gurus, and the gods,
facing their respective positions, with sprinkling and other rites.
When one has the means, one should daily bathe [the deity] with waters scented with sandalwood, uśīra, camphor, saffron,
and agallochum, while reciting the mantras of the *Svarṇagharma-anuvāka* and the *Mahāpuruṣavidyā*.

My devotee, filled with love, should worship me as is appropriate, adorning me with the Puruṣasūkta, Sāman chants such as the Rājana, and with garments, sacred threads, ornaments, leaf-designs, garlands, fragrances, and ointments.
A worshiper of Me should offer with faith water for the feet, water for sipping, fragrance, flowers, unbroken grains of rice, incense, lamps, and food offerings;
as well as jaggery, milk-rice, clarified butter, fried cakes, sweetmeats, and dumplings.
O Sati, one should prepare as an offering *saṃyāva*, curd, and soups; likewise, on a festival day— or indeed every day— there should be anointing, massaging, looking in a mirror, cleaning the teeth,
bathing, food, song, and dance.
Having established the fire in a sacrificial pit prepared according to the rules— complete with its girdle, trench, and altar— one should gather the kindled fuel around it with one's hand; then,
having strewn grass around it and performed the ritual addition of fuel (*anvādhāna*) according to the injunctions, one should sprinkle water around the fire.

Having set out the ritual substances for sprinkling and having sprinkled them, one should meditate upon Me in the fire— Me who resemble molten gold, possessing four radiant arms adorned with the conch, discus, mace, and lotus, peaceful, and clothed in the filaments of a lotus.
Meditating upon Him, whose crown, bracelets, waist-thread, and excellent armlets are shimmering,
who bears the Śrīvatsa mark on His chest, the radiant Kaustubha gem, and a forest garland;
and having worshipped Him, one should offer pieces of wood smeared with clarified butter as the sacrificial oblation.
Having offered the two portions of clarified butter (*ājyabhāga*) and the two libations (*āghāra*),

the wise one should offer the oblation soaked in clarified butter with the root mantra, using sixteen portions of the sacrificial cuttings (*avadāna*), and perform the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering for Dharma and the others according to rule with the appropriate mantras.
Then, having worshipped and offered obeisances, one should present the sacrificial offering (*bali*) to the attendants;
one should mutter the root mantra while remembering Brahman as having Nārāyaṇa as its essence.
Having offered water for sipping (*ācamana*), one should set aside the remnants for Viṣvaksena.
Then, one should offer fragrant mouth-perfumes such as betel nut and the like;
singing, chanting, dancing, enacting my deeds through mime,
and causing others to hear or listening to my stories, one should remain absorbed in me for even a moment.
Having offered praise with various hymns— whether from the Purāṇas or even in the vernacular—
one should prostrate like a staff, saying, "O Blessed One,
be gracious," while placing one's head between one's arms upon my feet.
"O Lord, protect me who have sought refuge, terrified as I am by the ocean of the crocodile of death"—
having thus respectfully placed upon his head this *śeṣā* (remnant) offered by me,
he should dismiss [the deity] if it is to be dismissed; that light, moreover, should be merged back into the light.
When one has faith in an image or any other [representation], one should worship Me therein;
for I, the Self of all, abide within all beings and within the self.
Thus, by means of the paths of ritual action—both Vedic and Tantric—a person [attains Me].
Worshipping Me on both [occasions], one attains from Me the desired perfection.
Having established My image, one should construct a firm temple,
along with beautiful flower gardens intended for worship, processions, and festivals.

By giving fields, marketplaces, cities, and villages on great festival days or daily for the sake of maintaining the flow of worship and other rites, one shall attain equality with Me; by means of a consecrated image,
one attains sovereignty over the whole earth, and by means of a temple, the three worlds.
Through worship and other such acts, one may reach the world of Brahmā; through three [lifetimes], one attains equality with Me.
But by means of the yoga of devotion (bhakti-yoga) characterized by detachment, one finds Me alone.
Thus, he who worships Me indeed attains the yoga of devotion.

He who seizes the means of subsistence given by himself or given by others to a deity or a Brahmin shall be born as a consumer of feces for ten million times ten thousand years; this applies to the one who performs the act,
the one who assists, the one who provides the cause, and even the one who approves of it.
After death, one becomes a sharer in the fruits of those actions, receiving them again and again in greater measure.
The Blessed Lord said:
One should neither praise nor disparage the actions and natures of others.
He who perceives the universe as one, consisting of both material nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa),
yet praises or censures the external nature, inherent dispositions, or actions of others, quickly falls away from his own true purpose due to his attachment to what is unreal.
When the Taijasa state has fallen into sleep, the person situated in the subtle body (piṇḍa) loses consciousness;
just as that happens, so too does the person who perceives manifold objects encounter illusion or death.
What is auspicious and what is inauspicious? How much is there of duality, which is unreal?
Whatever is uttered by speech or even meditated upon by the mind is unreal;
for like shadows, echoes, and reflections, these things are non-existent yet produce effects.
In this same way, entities such as the body and so forth cause fear until death.
The Self alone is this entire universe; as the Lord, He creates it and creates Himself;
as the Soul of the universe, He protects it and protects Himself; as the Sovereign, He withdraws it and withdraws Himself.
Therefore, no entity has ever been described that is other than the Self.
When this has been ascertained, this threefold appearance within the self is seen to be rootless;
know this threefold world to be composed of the modes of nature and created by *māyā*.
Knowing this, which I have declared, is the proficiency of knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*).

He neither censures nor praises; he moves through the world like the sun. Having realized through direct perception, inference, scripture, and self-realization that the world is unreal and possesses a beginning and an end, he should wander here free from attachment.
Śrī Uddhava said:

O Lord, neither for the self nor for the body does transmigration exist, since these two are respectively the seer and the seen. For whom, then, is it perceived, given that they are both non-self and objects of perception?
The self is imperishable, devoid of the modes of nature, pure, self-luminous, and unconditioned.
Since the insentient body is like wood to fire, whose is the cycle of birth and death in this world?
The Blessed Lord said:

As long as there is contact of the self with the body, senses, and vital breaths, so long does this worldly existence continue; though it is fruitless for the undiscriminating, it appears to bear fruit.
Indeed, even when the object [of desire] no longer exists, transmigratory existence does not cease.
As one who contemplates sense objects experiences the arrival of misfortunes in a dream,
so indeed does deep sleep bring many evils to one who has not awakened;
yet that very same sleep does not lead to delusion for one who is awakened.

Grief, joy, fear, anger, greed, delusion, longing, and so forth—these, as well as birth and death, are seen to belong to the ego (ahaṅkāra) and not to the Self (ātman). The individual soul (jīva), who is the inner self (antar-ātmā), is the identification with the body, senses, vital breaths, and mind; he is the embodiment of the qualities (guṇas) and their actions.

The Sūtra is sung as the Great Principle (Mahat), and from it the cycle of worldly existence (saṃsāra) rushes forth, governed by Time. This rootless flow, manifested in many forms through the activities of mind, speech, breath, and body, the sage cuts asunder with the sharp sword of knowledge and spiritual practice; thus, free from craving, he wanders the earth.

Knowledge, discrimination, scripture, austerity, direct perception, tradition, and inference—whatever exists at the beginning and end of this universe is that alone which exists in the middle; it is both the cause and the time.
Just as gold is present before and after everything made of gold that has been fashioned from it.

That very same [reality], when being manifested in the midst of worldly transactions through various designations, appears as "I" and "this" for him; likewise, my dear, this consciousness exists in three states consisting of the three *guṇas*, acting as the cause, the effect, and the agent.
By means of that fourth state alone—through both conjunction and separation—that very [consciousness] is the Truth.
That which does not exist before, nor after, nor in the middle—that is merely a designation.

It is my conviction that whatever has come into being and is well-known as distinct from the Supreme, that is indeed [the Supreme] itself. This manifest creation, consisting of transformations and characterized by passion (*rājasa*), appears even though it does not truly exist.
Therefore, Brahman, which is self-luminous, shines forth as the manifold variety of the senses, their objects, the self, and its transformations. Thus, through the causes for discerning Brahman,
it becomes clearly manifest by means of the expert refutation of the "other" (the non-Brahman).

Having severed the doubt regarding the self, one should desist from all objects of desire, satisfied by one's own bliss. The self is not the body made of earth, nor the senses; for the gods, the asuras, wind, water, and fire are indeed [the presiding deities of] these.
Mind, the subtle elements, intellect, the mode of goodness (*sattva*), ego, ether, earth, and the equilibrium of the objects of the senses—
what quality could there be for one who is composed with these instruments whose nature is the *guṇas*, and whose abode is perfectly distinguished from Me?
What fault indeed is there in clouds being dispersed, or what loss in their arrival when the sun has departed?
