Just as the imperishable ether is not attached to the qualities of the seasons that come and go,
so the Supreme is untouched by the impurities of goodness, passion, and ignorance, which are the causes of worldly existence for the egoistic mind.

Nevertheless, attachment to the modes of nature created by Māyā must be completely abandoned for as long as the impurity of the mind— the passion of *rajas*— is not cast out by the firm yoga of devotion to Me.
Just as a disease in men that is not properly treated recurs again and again, growing ever stronger.
In this way, the mind— when its impurities (*kaṣāya*) have not been matured through action— pierces the false yogi with all attachments.

Those false yogis who are hindered by obstacles created by human beings or by those sent by the gods, they again apply themselves to yoga by the power of their previous practice, and not to the system of ritual action (*karma-tantra*).
A living being performs action and is acted upon by another who impels him until his fall;
in this regard, the wise man, though situated in material nature, is not affected because his thirst has ceased through the experience of his own bliss.

Whether he is standing, sitting, walking, lying down, urinating, or eating food— *Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-verse; the full verse (BhP 11.28.31) continues:* "...whether he is speaking or remaining silent, the wise man is never attached to these states, nor does he feel aversion toward them."*
One whose intellect is fixed on the Self does not perceive the Self as being anything else, even while desiring some other nature here;
if he should see something unreal as an object of the senses, which is variously inferred and contradictory,
that wise man does not consider it to be a reality, just as one who has awakened does not regard a dream that vanishes upon rising.

O dear one, that ignorance which was previously grasped as variegated by the qualities and actions, and which remained undistinguished from the Self, ceases simply through right vision; it is neither grasped nor released, for the Self is not an object of action.
Just as the rising of the sun destroys the darkness of men's eyes but does not create that darkness anew.
Thus, when this subtle discernment is perfected, it destroys the darkness of the intellect of a person.
He is self-luminous, unborn, immeasurable, of great majesty, and the experience of all;
he is one without a second, beyond the reach of words, by whose will speech and the vital breaths move.

Such is the delusion regarding the self: that there is conceptualization toward the absolute Self, when in truth one has no support other than one's own Self. For that which is perceived through names and forms as having five colors is unsubstantial.
Even though this is a figurative statement (arthavāda) devoid of literal meaning, it serves as a warning for those who consider themselves wise.
When a yogi whose practice is not yet mature attempts to concentrate, his body may be struck by obstacles arising from within; in such a case, this prescribed method is ordained.

One may completely burn away certain obstacles by means of yogic concentration (*yoga-dhāraṇā*), others through postures (*āsana*) accompanied by concentration, and still others through austerity (*tapas*), mantras, and medicinal herbs; some may be destroyed by meditation upon Me, and others by the chanting of My names and so forth.

Or, by following the masters of yoga, one may gradually destroy the givers of inauspiciousness. Some wise ones, having prepared this body while it is still firm in its prime, then employ various means for the sake of spiritual perfection.

Indeed, that is not to be performed by one who seeks the good, for such exertion is useless; for the body is perishable, like the fruit of a tree. Even if the body should become perfected for one who constantly practices yoga, [it is still not to be pursued].
A wise person devoted to Me should not abandon yoga and fail to have faith in that; for the yogi who practices this yoga-conduct while taking refuge in Me,
being free from desire and experiencing his own bliss, shall not be thwarted by obstacles.
Śrī Uddhava said:

O Acyuta, I consider this practice of yoga to be very difficult to master for one who has not disciplined the self. Please tell me directly, O Unfallen One, how a person may achieve perfection easily.

O lotus-eyed one, yogīs who generally endeavor to fix their minds [upon You] become despondent due to a lack of concentration, being exhausted by the effort of restraining the mind. Therefore, O lotus-eyed one, let the swans take refuge in Your foot-lotus, which yields bliss.
O Lord of All, how could those who are proud find happiness through yogic practices or ritual actions, which are thwarted by Your illusory power?
O Acyuta, O friend of all, what wonder is there in this that You bestow Your own self upon Your servants who have no other refuge— You,
whose footstool was once pressed by the crowns of the illustrious lords of the gods, yet who now chose to dwell among the deer?
Who indeed would abandon You, the Lord who is the beloved of the Self of all, the giver of all goals to those who have taken refuge in Him, and the knower of one's own deeds?
And who would worship another, which serves only for forgetfulness and not for true realization?
Or what could possibly happen to us who serve the dust of Your feet? O Lord, the wise, their joy perfected by remembering [Your deeds], do not seek even the honor of Brahmā’s lifespan for themselves.
He who, shaking off the impurity of embodied beings both within and without,
reveals his own state of being through the forms of the teacher and the shrine—
Śrī Śuka said:

Thus questioned by Uddhava, whose heart was deeply attached, the Lord of lords— the one who sports with the world and assumes three forms through His own potencies— spoke with a charming smile of love. The Blessed Lord said:
"Come now, I shall describe to you my most auspicious duties,
by practicing which with faith a mortal conquers death, which is otherwise difficult to overcome.
One should perform all actions for My sake, remembering Me gradually."
Having dedicated his mind and consciousness to Me, with his heart and self devoted to My dharma, he should resort to holy places frequented by virtuous devotees of Mine,
as well as the deeds performed by My devotees among gods, asuras, and humans.

One should perform for me, individually or through a collective sacrificial session (*satra*), festivals and great processions on sacred days, accompanied by song, dance, and other arts, with the splendor of a great king;
[seeing] me alone, unveiled both externally and internally, within all living beings.

One whose heart is pure should perceive the Self within the self, just as one perceives space; O you of great splendor, thus honoring all beings with the realization that they are of my nature, and reflecting upon this, one relies solely on knowledge.
A wise person is considered to have equal vision toward a brāhmaṇa and a pukkasa, a thief and one devoted to sacred knowledge, the sun and a spark, and the non-cruel and the cruel;
for a man who constantly cultivates the state of being Me among men, that state arises before long.

Indeed, rivalry, envy, contempt, and egoism vanish when one casts aside pride and physical shame, and bows like a staff upon the ground before everyone— from a horse down to a cāṇḍāla, a cow, and a donkey— while smiling at one's own [former] self.
As long as the state of being absorbed in Me (mad-bhāva) does not arise within all beings,
so long should one worship in this manner through the activities of speech, mind, and body;
for everything has Brahman as its self, known through knowledge and the contemplation of the Self.

Observing this, one should desist from all [worldly activities], with all doubts dispelled; for this state of being absorbed in Me toward all beings through the functions of mind, speech, and body is, in my view, the most excellent among all spiritual disciplines.
O Uddhava, not even an atom of My dharma is ever destroyed at its commencement;
for I have perfectly resolved that it is free from desire and devoid of the material modes.
Whatever dharma is prescribed for Me, the Supreme, if it is performed for the sake of fruitless ends, [it does not lead to liberation].
O best of men, the effort for that [liberation] would be as futile as the effort for fear and the like;
this is the wisdom of the intelligent and the insight of the wise:
that by means of the mortal, which is unreal, one attains Me, the immortal, in this world.

This entire compendium of the discourse on Brahman has been declared to you according to both concise and detailed methods, which is difficult even for the gods to comprehend. This knowledge, endowed with clear reasoning, has been repeatedly spoken by me to you.

Having understood this, a person whose doubts have been destroyed is liberated. One who retains even this well-discriminated answer to your question shall attain the eternal secret of Brahman and reach the Supreme Brahman.
To him who would bestow this most abundant [gift] upon My devotees,
I, by My very self, grant My own self as a gift of Brahman to that giver of Brahman.
To him who would study this supreme, purifying, and pure [text], I grant My own self.
He shall be purified day by day as he reveals Me through the lamp of knowledge.
That man who, being undistracted, constantly hears this with faith while performing supreme devotion unto Me, is not bound by his actions.
O friend Uddhava, have you thoroughly understood the Absolute Truth?
Has your delusion and this grief born of the mind departed from you? This [knowledge] should not be told by you to a hypocrite, an atheist, or a rogue.
Let this be given to one who is disobedient, lacking devotion, and ill-behaved;
but let it be spoken to one who is free from these defects, devoted to the Brahmanas, dear to Me, virtuous, and pure. Devotion may also arise among Śūdras and women.
Having understood this, nothing further remains to be known for one who desires knowledge;
just as when one has drunk the nectar of immortality (*pīyūṣa-amṛta*), nothing further remains to be drunk.
[This applies] to knowledge, ritual action, yoga, livelihood, and the wielding of punishment.

O dear one, whatever purpose men have, that is mine in fourfold form. When a mortal has renounced all ritual action and offers himself to Me, desiring to act for My sake, then, attaining immortality, he indeed becomes fit for identity with My own Self.
Śrī Śuka said:

Having thus been shown the path of yoga and having heard the words of Uttamaśloka, he stood with palms joined in reverence; his throat choked with joy and his eyes overflowing with tears, he could say nothing at all.

O King, steadying his mind which was reeling with affection by means of fortitude, and honoring him greatly, Śrī Uddhava spoke to the hero of the Yadus with palms joined in reverence, touching the lotus feet of the Lord with his head. Śrī Uddhava said:
The great darkness of delusion has been dispelled because I have taken refuge in Your presence; O Unborn One, how could cold, darkness, or fear prevail for one who has approached the sun?
Out of compassion, You have restored to me, Your servant, this lamp consisting of realized knowledge.
O Knower of all deeds, having abandoned everything, what other refuge of Yours would one like me seek, who is grateful for Your lotus feet?
And my very firm bond of affection for the Dāśārhas, Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, and Sātvatas has been severed by You,
who, for the sake of expanding creation, have employed Your own *māyā* as a weapon that brings about the perfect realization of the Self.
"Obeisances unto You, O Great Yogin; instruct me, who have sought refuge in You, so that there may be an unswerving devotion to Your lotus feet. The Blessed Lord said:
"Go, Uddhava, as commanded by Me, to My hermitage named Badarī. There,
purified by bathing and sipping the water of the sacred ford at My feet,
and with all your sins shaken off by the sight of the Alakanandā river,"
Wearing bark garments, O dear one, subsisting on forest fare, free from desire for pleasure,
enduring the pairs of opposites, well-behaved, with senses restrained,
peaceful, with a concentrated mind, and endowed with both theoretical knowledge and realized wisdom.
Reflecting upon that which you have learned from me in solitude,
with your speech and mind absorbed in Me, remain devoted to My dharma; then,
having transcended the three goals of life, you shall come to Me thereafter.
Śrī Śuka said:
Having been thus addressed by Hari, Uddhava, his mind fixed on Him, circumambulated Him and placed his head at His feet;
though he was beyond the dualities of worldly life, his heart was moistened with tears as he wept at the time of departure.

Distressed by the unbearable pain of separation from his beloved, and unable to abandon him, the afflicted king placed the Lord’s sandals upon his head; having offered obeisances, he departed again and again.
Then, keeping him within his heart, that great devotee went to Viśālā.

Having undertaken austerity as instructed by the sole kinsman of the world, he attained the goal of Hari. Whoever, with true faith, studies this nectar of knowledge— filled with the ocean of bliss— which was spoken for the sake of the devotee of the Lord whose feet are served by the masters of yoga, is liberated from the world.
To destroy the fear of worldly existence, the author of the Vedas extracted the essence of knowledge and realization from the Vedas, just as a bee gathers the nectar of flowers;
he then caused his circle of devotees to drink that nectar of immortality from the ocean of the Upanishads.
"I bow down to the primordial Person, the bull among men, who is known by the name Kṛṣṇa.
The King said:
Then, after the great devotee Uddhava had departed for the forest...

What did the Blessed One, the creator of all beings and the bull among the Yādavas, do in Dvāravatī when his own lineage was struck by the curse of the brāhmaṇas? And how did he abandon that body which is the most beloved of all eyes?
Where women were unable to draw back their eyes once they had become fixed upon him; where that which enters the ears of the virtuous does not depart once it has attached itself to the soul;
and where his splendor produces delight even in the words of poets—what indeed can be said of his majesty?
Seeing that Arjuna had mounted his chariot in battle and attained equality with Him,
the venerable sage said:
"In heaven, on earth, and in the intermediate space, great portents have arisen."
Seeing them seated in the Sudharmā assembly hall, Kṛṣṇa spoke this to the Yadus.
The Blessed Lord said:
"These terrible and great portents in Dvārakā are the banners of Yama."
"O best of the Yadus, we must not remain here even for a moment.
Let the women, children, and the elderly depart from here for Śaṅkhoddhāra.
We shall go to Prabhāsa, where the Sarasvatī flows westward."
Having performed the consecration there, being pure, fasting, and well-composed,
we shall worship the deities with baths, ointments, and offerings;
and having performed the rites for auspiciousness, we shall honor the highly fortunate Brahmins.
With cows, land, gold, garments, elephants, horses, chariots, and houses—
this is indeed the rite that destroys misfortune and is the supreme resort of auspiciousness;
the worship of the gods, the twice-born, and cows is the highest state among all beings.
Having heard this from the enemy of Madhu, all the elders of the Yadu clan said,
"So be it," and having crossed [the river] by means of boats, they departed for Prabhāsa on chariots.
There, the Yādavas were instructed by the Blessed One, the god of the Yadus.

With supreme devotion, they prepared a great drinking vessel filled with all that promotes well-being. Then, their intellects clouded by fate, they drank the maireyaka wine, for by its liquid the mind is led astray.
A great conflict arose among those heroes who were intoxicated by the drinking of the great liquor and possessed arrogant minds, who were utterly deluded by the illusory power (*māyā*) of Kṛṣṇa;
inflamed with anger, they fought as assassins on the shore.
With bows, swords, crescent-headed arrows, maces, spears, and lances;

with falling banners, chariots, elephants, and the like; and with donkeys, camels, cattle, buffaloes, and even men—these utterly intoxicated beings, meeting one another, struck each other with arrows like elephants in a forest striking with their tusks.
Pradyumna and Sāmba, filled with fierce rivalry in battle; Akrūra and Bhoja, Aniruddha and Sātyaki;
Subhadra and Saṅgrāmajit—these were all exceedingly formidable.
Gada fought with Sumitra and Suratha;
others, such as Niśaṭha and Ulmuka, and Sahasrajit, Śatajit, Bhānu,
and their leaders, having encountered one another, blinded by intoxication and utterly deluded by Mukunda, struck each other down.
The Dāśārhas, Vṛṣṇis, Andhakas, Bhojas, and Sātvatas; the Madhus, Arbudas, Māthuras, Śūrasenas,
Visarjanas, Kukuras, and Kuntayas.
But they struck one another, utterly casting aside their affection; sons fought with fathers and brothers,
as well as with sisters' sons, grandsons, paternal uncles, and maternal uncles.
Fools indeed, they killed their friends with friends, their well-wishers with well-wishers, and their kinsmen with kinsmen,
while their arrows were being exhausted and their bows were breaking.
As their weapons were being worn away, they struck with their fists at the *erakā* grass;
for those blades, grasped in their fists, became like thunderbolts and iron clubs.
With these they struck their enemies, even though they were being restrained by Kṛṣṇa, and they likewise struck him.
O King, regarding Balarāma as an adversary, they were deluded and resolved to kill him; having encountered him, they became assailants.
Then, O descendant of Kuru, those two also became enraged and raised [their weapons].

Moving about with clumps of *erakā* grass as clubs, they struck one another in battle; for those who were afflicted by the curse of a Brahmin and whose minds were shrouded by the illusory power (*māyā*) of Kṛṣṇa,
their rivalry and anger brought about their destruction, just as fire from bamboo destroys a forest.

When all his own clans had thus perished, Keśava, remaining behind, thought: "The burden of the earth has been removed. Then Rāma, having resorted to his human prowess, applied himself to yoga on the shore of the ocean.
Having united his self with the Supreme Self, he abandoned the human world.
Beholding the departure of Rāma, the Blessed Lord, the son of Devakī,
sat upon the surface of the earth, having approached a *pippala* tree in silence.
Bearing a four-armed form that shone with its own radiance,
dispelling the darkness from all directions like a smokeless fire,
He was marked with the Śrīvatsa, dark as a rain cloud, and possessed the luster of refined gold.
Enveloped in a pair of silken garments, most auspicious,
with a lotus-face graced by a beautiful smile and adorned with dark locks of hair; his eyes were as delightful as white lotuses, and he wore shimmering earrings shaped like sea-monsters.
He was resplendent with a waist-thread, a sacred thread, a crown, bracelets, and armlets; with necklaces, anklets, and hand-seals, and with the Kaustubha gem;
his body was encircled by a forest garland, and he was accompanied by his own weapons personified.
Having placed his foot upon his right thigh, he sat there with a complexion as red as a lotus;
then the hunter Jarā, mistaking that foot— which was shaped like a deer— for a deer, pierced it with an arrow made from a fragment of iron left over from the *muśala* weapon.
Seeing that four-armed Person, he, whose sins had been committed,
fell in fear with his head at the feet of the enemy of the demons.
"O Madhusūdana, this was done by me, a sinner, unknowingly."

O sinless one, O Lord of excellent renown, you ought to forgive my sin, for they say that the remembrance of you, O Viṣṇu, destroys the darkness of ignorance in men; yet, O Lord, I have acted wickedly toward you.
Therefore, O Vaikuṇṭha, quickly slay me, this sinful deer-hunter,
so that I may never again commit such an offense against the virtuous.
You, whose self-mastery Viriñca does not understand—

Rudra and the others are his sons, those who are the lords of speech; yet, their vision being obscured by Your māyā, they perceive this [universe] directly. What can we—who have resorted to the unreal—possibly proclaim of You?
The Blessed Lord said:
"Do not fear, O Jarā; arise! This desire has indeed been fulfilled by me. Depart, permitted by me, to heaven, the abode of those who have performed meritorious deeds."
Thus instructed by the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, whose body was at his own will, Dāruka circumambulated him three times, bowed down to him, and departed for heaven in a celestial chariot;
meanwhile, having sought the path of Kṛṣṇa, he reached it.

Having smelled the fragrance of the *tulasī* carried by the wind, he went toward him; there, at the foot of an *aśvattha* tree, he saw his lord, who had made that his dwelling and was surrounded by weapons as radiant as the sun.
His soul overflowing with affection, he leaped down from the chariot and fell at [the Lord's] feet with eyes full of tears; yet,
O Lord, as he failed to see Your lotus feet, his vision was lost and entered into darkness.

"I do not know the directions, nor do I find peace, as if the moon had vanished in the night. While the charioteer was speaking thus, O King of kings, the chariot marked with the emblem of Garuḍa, together with its horses and banner, leapt up into the sky even as he looked on.
The divine weapons of Viṣṇu followed him as well.
Then Janārdana, his mind filled with great wonder at this, said to the charioteer:
"O charioteer, go to Dvāravatī and report the mutual destruction of our kinsmen."
Tell my kinsmen of Saṅkarṣaṇa’s departure and of my own condition;
you and your own relatives must no longer remain in Dvārakā,
for the ocean will submerge the city of the Yadus once it has been abandoned by me.
"Taking each your own possessions and our parents as well,
all of you, protected by Arjuna, shall go to Indraprastha.
But you, however, abiding in my dharma, remain indifferent, established in knowledge."
"Recognizing this world as fashioned by my *māyā*, attain tranquility.
Thus addressed, he circumambulated Him, bowed down again and again,
placed His feet upon his head, and departed for the city with a heavy heart.
Śrī Śuka said:
Then Brahmā arrived there, along with Bhavānī and Śiva,
as well as the gods headed by Mahendra, the sages, and the lords of created beings.
The ancestors, Siddhas, Gandharvas, Vidyādharas, Mahoragas,
Cāraṇas, Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Kinnaras, Apsarases, and the twice-born—
all were intensely eager and desirous of beholding the departure of the Blessed One.
Singing and praising the deeds and birth of Śauri,
O King, they showered rains of flowers from rows of celestial chariots, filling the sky with supreme devotion.

The all-pervading Lord, beholding his grandfather and having withdrawn his own manifestations into himself, closed his lotus-eyes. He then withdrew his body, which was delightful to the worlds and auspicious for concentration and meditation.
Having burned [all obstacles] with the fiery power of yogic concentration (yoga-dhāraṇā), he entered his own abode.
In the heavens, kettledrums resounded and flowers fell from the sky;
Truth, Dharma, Fortitude, Glory, and Prosperity followed after him.
The gods and others, headed by Brahmā, were utterly amazed; they beheld Kṛṣṇa entering His own abode, His path unknown to them,
just as a flash of lightning is seen when it vanishes from the circle of clouds.
The movement of Kṛṣṇa could not be perceived by mortals, nor even by the gods;
however, when Brahmā, Rudra, and the others beheld that yogic departure of Hari,
they were filled with wonder and, praising it, then returned each to his own world.
O King, understand that the activity of embodied beings— their birth and dissolution—
is a mere imitation of Māyā, like that of an actor; for after creating this world by Himself and entering into it to sport, He withdraws it at the end.

Having withdrawn [the world] by His own majesty, He remains at rest— He who, as a mortal, brought back the son of His preceptor who had been led to the realm of Yama, and You, O giver of refuge, who were consumed by the supreme weapon.
Though powerless himself, he conquered even the Lord who is the end-maker of Death;
yet, while leading the hunter with his body into his own forest,
he remained the master of the maintenance, creation, and dissolution of all things without exception.
He who possesses all powers and has no other cause [for his existence] did not wish to leave behind a physical form here, demonstrating to mortals the path of abiding in one's own true self.
He who, having risen at dawn, recites with devotion and self-restraint this supreme path of Kṛṣṇa, attains that very same unsurpassed state.
Dāruka, having arrived at Dvārakā, [reported this] to Vasudeva and Ugrasena.
Falling at his feet, he drenched Kṛṣṇa’s feet with tears;
O King, he related in its entirety the destruction of the Vṛṣṇis.
Upon hearing this, the people, their hearts agitated and overwhelmed by grief, fainted away.
There they went in haste, overwhelmed by separation from Kṛṣṇa,
to where their kinsmen lay lifeless with their faces covered as they were being slain.
Devakī, Rohiṇī, and Vasudeva likewise [beheld] their two sons.
Not seeing Kṛṣṇa and Rāma, they were afflicted with grief and lost their senses;
tormented by separation from the Blessed Lord, they gave up their lives there.
O dear one, embracing their husbands, the women ascended the funeral pyres.
The wives of Rāma embraced his body and entered the fire;
the wives of Vasudeva, along with Pradyumna and the other daughters-in-law of Hari, [did the same];
and the wives of Kṛṣṇa, headed by Rukmiṇī, being absorbed in him, entered the fire.
Arjuna, distressed by separation from his beloved friend Kṛṣṇa,
consoled himself with the well-spoken verses sung by Kṛṣṇa. Arjuna then performed the funeral rites for his kinsmen whose lineages had been lost.
He had the funeral rites for the slain performed properly and in due order.
Then, O Great King, the ocean submerged Dvārakā— which had been abandoned by Hari— in an instant,
with the exception of the glorious abode of the Blessed Lord.
The Blessed Lord Madhusūdana is eternally present there,
the remover of all inauspiciousness through mere remembrance and the most auspicious of all auspicious things.
Taking with him the women, children, and the elderly who remained after the slaughter, Dhanañjaya—
Having established Indraprastha, he consecrated Vajra there as its ruler.
O King, having heard of the slaughter of their kinsmen by Arjuna, your grandfathers,
after making you the bearer of their lineage, all departed upon the great path.
The mortal who with faith glorifies these deeds and the birth of Viṣṇu, the God of gods, is liberated from all sins. Thus [ends the account of] the beautiful incarnations of the Blessed Lord Hari.
By chanting the heroic deeds and most peaceful childhood exploits of the Lord,
heard elsewhere and here,
a person shall attain supreme devotion directed toward the goal of the Paramahaṃsas.
